# Architecture principles

## What this set governs

This is the architecture-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product is designed — its regions, their boundaries, and the entities
that build and evolve them. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity is
performed; this set governs what the designed system must look like.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working set. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
contract, relationship kind, and intent are defined in the
[glossary](glossary.md). Two distinctions those terms carry are used
throughout. A shop is either the lead shop — the system-level
coordinator, owning the product-level artifacts and no Bounded
Context — or a BC-shop, owning exactly one. A contract is offered
either as a product contract, on a Bounded Context, or as an
operational contract, on a shop.

Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle at the
architecture level, this document declares the lineage in its
frontmatter — `derives-from` maps the principle in this set to the
working-scope principle it applies — instead of restating the rule as a
second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.

A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects work we
would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it
implies at least one practice and one check. The fitness screen at the
end of this document applies these tests to the principles above it.

---

## Every first-class entity has a knowable shape (`knowable-shape`)

**Statement.**

- The product MUST have exactly two kinds of first-class entity: the
  Bounded Context and the shop.
- Each Bounded Context MUST be contained and produced by exactly one
  BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT contain one.
- Every first-class entity MUST carry a description, maintained as an
  artifact, from which an outside reader can name what the entity is
  for, what it accepts and produces, what it guarantees, and the
  contracts it offers.
- The description MUST suffice without reading the entity's internal
  code or configuration and without asking its maintainers.

**Rationale.** When an entity's shape lives only in its internals, every
consumer, coordinator, and reviewer pays to rediscover it, and each
rediscovery reaches a different answer: nobody can say what a service
guarantees without opening its source, the answer holds only until the
next commit, and no description can be trusted without re-inspecting
the thing it describes. Parnas made the design case in 1972: a module
is known by what its interface states, not by what its implementation
happens to do. Without `knowable-shape`,
`contracts-between-contexts` is speculative — no one can write a
contract for an entity whose shape no one can state.

**Implications.**

- Whoever creates a Bounded Context or a shop writes its description at
  creation; an entity without a description is not yet created,
  whatever code exists.
- Maintainers keep the description authoritative: when an outside
  reader must open internals to answer a question the description
  claims to cover, the description is the defect and its maintainer
  repairs it.
- Architects reason from descriptions; opening an entity's internals is
  audit work — checking that a description is true — not the normal way
  to learn what the entity is.

## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)

**Statement.**

- Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass through a
  named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the meaning
  of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind.
- A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's
  contract does not state.
- Bounded Contexts MUST NOT share state or coordinate outside their
  contracts.

**Rationale.** Unstated expectations cannot be reviewed, versioned, or
deliberately kept — they are discovered when they break. Hyrum's law
(Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, *Software Engineering at Google*)
records the observed endpoint: with enough consumers, every observable
behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the
contract says — the only defense is making the contract the sole thing a
consumer is entitled to. Evans (*Domain-Driven Design*, 2003) draws
context boundaries for the same reason: models stay coherent only when
what crosses between them is explicit. Without this rule,
`local-comprehension` collapses — a consumer must read a counterpart's
internals to learn what is safe to use.

**Implications.**

- Contract authors put every promise in the contract document —
  schemas, semantics, errors, relationship kind; a promise made
  anywhere else is not owed.
- Reviewers of a consuming context treat reliance on unstated behavior
  as that context's defect, and treat the underlying need as a
  contract-change request, not a license to work around the contract.
- Integrators who need a channel the contract lacks amend the contract
  first or do not integrate.

## Discipline attaches to activities, not actors (`actor-neutral-discipline`)

**Statement.**

- Rules, authority, and required records MUST attach to the activity
  and the role performing it, never to the kind of actor filling the
  role.
- An activity MUST NOT record less, skip checks, or gain authority
  because a particular kind of actor — human, agent, or service —
  performs it.

**Rationale.** Rules forked by actor kind create bypasses: whichever
fork is weakest becomes the route around the discipline, and social
routes — "just ask the team next door" — are exactly the moves agents
scale beyond anyone's review. Role-based access control (Ferraiolo and
Kuhn, 1992; the NIST RBAC model) grounds the mechanism: grant to roles,
and the actor mix can change without regranting authority. The working
set's `no-orphan-activities` already places every activity in a process;
this rule keeps those processes actor-neutral, which is what keeps
`contracts-between-contexts` binding on whoever shows up — an actor that
could renegotiate the rules by kind could talk its way around a
contract.

**Implications.**

- Process authors demand the same inputs, checks, and records from a
  step whoever performs it; "it was just an automation" excuses no
  missing record.
- Reviewers strike rule text that splits one activity by actor kind —
  "humans may, agents must" — the rule attaches to the activity or it
  goes.
- Whoever grants authority grants it to a role within a process; a
  standing grant to an individual actor is a defect whoever holds it.

## Comprehension is local at every level (`local-comprehension`)

**Statement.**

- A participant MUST NOT need to read beyond the level they are
  working at.
- The design MUST designate, for each level, the description artifacts
  sufficient for that level's work. The levels, and their designated
  artifacts, are (a closed set):
  - working inside a shop — that shop's own records and code;
  - consuming a Bounded Context — that context's contracts;
  - working across Bounded Contexts — the contracts and the
    system-level map of the contexts and their relationships;
  - coordinating the system — the product-level descriptions the lead
    shop owns.
- Work at a level MUST be performable from its designated artifacts
  alone.
- A task that can be done only by reading below its level MUST be
  treated as a design defect — a missing or incomplete description or
  contract — not as the reader's burden.

**Rationale.** The cost of working on one part of the product has to
stay proportional to that part, or growth taxes every participant; for
agents the tax is literal — context loaded is context paid for. The
familiar endpoint of the failure: a corpus with no designated reading
levels grows until a one-line change is one nobody dares make without
reading the whole system first, and every newcomer must read far beyond
the task at hand before starting it. This rule applies the
working set's `least-context` to the designed system — the lineage is
declared in this document's frontmatter: `least-context` caps what an
activity loads, and a design obeying this rule is what makes that cap
reachable, because the artifacts an activity needs exist at its own
level.

**Implications.**

- Designers ship each level's designated artifacts as part of the
  design; a level whose work demands undesignated reading is unfinished
  design.
- Whoever hits a task that requires reading below its level files the
  defect against the design and does not normalize the deep read into
  practice.
- Reviewers of a design check the reading bound: the artifacts a task
  needs stay proportional to the task's level, not to the product's
  size.

## Design is authoritative, conformance runs both ways (`bidirectional-conformance`)

**Statement.**

- The design — descriptions, contracts, recorded decisions — MUST be
  the authoritative statement of what the product is and does, and code
  MUST conform to it.
- Conformance MUST be checked in both directions: forward — every
  design element MUST have code implementing it (did we build what we
  said?) — and reverse — every code element MUST be called for by the
  design (did we build only what we said?).
- A design change MUST itself be a recorded activity.
- Retirement and refactoring MUST be gated on both conformance checks.

**Rationale.** When code is the authority, descriptions decay into
folklore and `knowable-shape` drifts false — the description stops
matching the entity it claims to describe. Forward checking alone
misses half the failure: features removed on paper live on as unowned
code, and undecided behavior accumulates until the design describes a
product that no longer exists. Murphy, Notkin, and Sullivan's reflexion
models (1995) demonstrated the two-directional comparison this
statement requires — computing both what the design promises that the
code lacks, and what the code contains that the design never called
for. The working set holds the two flanking rules at working scope:
`single-source-of-truth` gives every fact one authoritative home, and
`delivery-verified` demands the forward direction be demonstrated in
the running system; this rule adds the reverse direction and gates
retirement and refactoring on the pair.

**Implications.**

- Whoever changes behavior records the design change — before the code
  change or in the same recorded activity; silent drift is reverted,
  never adopted after the fact.
- Whoever retires a feature removes it from the design first; the
  reverse check then names the code that may be deleted, and nothing
  else is.
- Refactorers demonstrate both checks unchanged — no behavior lost
  forward, none gained in reverse.
- Reviewers reject code no design element calls for, however good it
  is.

## Intent enters through contracts and keeps its provenance (`intent-provenance`)

**Statement.**

- Intent — a desired outcome expressed by an originator at the
  product's edge — MUST enter the product through a contract: a product
  contract on a Bounded Context or an operational contract on a shop.
- The shop that receives intent MAY translate it, and MAY delegate it
  to other shops, only ever through those shops' contracts.
- Every receipt, translation, and delegation MUST be recorded, so that
  any activity can be traced back to the originating expression without
  ambiguity.

**Rationale.** Intent that loses its origin cannot be re-decided: when
priorities shift, no one can tell which work still serves a live desire
and which serves a decision nobody remembers making — "why did we build
this?" becomes answerable only by whoever happened to be present.
IEEE 29148 (requirements engineering) standardizes exactly the chain
this statement demands: each requirement traceable to its source and to
what implements it. Routing intent through contracts keeps
`contracts-between-contexts` whole at the product's edge — a backlog
living outside the product's contracts is an out-of-band channel like
any other, aimed at the builders instead of the contexts. And the trace
is what gives `bidirectional-conformance` its meaning: conformance can
verify that code matches design, but only provenance can verify that
either matches what anyone asked for.

**Implications.**

- Whoever accepts intent records it at the contract where it entered
  before working on it.
- Whoever translates or delegates intent records each translation
  against the original, at every step.
- Reviewers may demand the originator chain for any activity; a trace
  that dead-ends is a recording defect to repair, not a question to
  drop.

# Founding principles

> Amended 2026-08-23 by authority direction: rationale examples
> referencing the pre-migration corpus removed — the specific examples
> are not necessary to rationalize the principles, and this branch
> carries no referent for them. Statements unchanged.

> Amended 2026-08-23 by authority direction (form only): statements and
> implications re-formed as one obligation or implication per bullet;
> wording preserved modulo the sentence splits. No obligation added,
> removed, or reworded.

## What a good principle looks like

A principle is a standing rule about how we work, in four parts: a name, a
statement, a rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it. Rationales stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.

A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects something
we would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it implies at least one practice and one
check. The fitness screen at the end of this document applies these tests
to the principles above it.

---

## Define what good looks like up front (`define-good-up-front`)

**Statement.**

- Every activity MUST operate from a stated definition of what good
  looks like.
- That definition MUST drive both the performance of the activity and
  its check.
- The check MUST sit with a different role holding a different
  accountability.

**Rationale.** A definition applied only at the check puts the full weight
of quality after implementation, where rework is most frequent and most
expensive. A definition applied only up front invites gaming and closes
off outside perspective. Two roles reading one definition give both
prevention and challenge. (Deming: cease dependence on inspection; build
quality in — and still inspect.)

**Implications.**

- Authors of new activities ship the definition with the activity, or
  the activity does not enter the system.
- A check that cannot cite the definition clause it projects has no
  standing; anyone may remove it without a new decision.
- Reviewers compare work to the written definition; their own taste is
  not the standard.
- The same role never both performs and checks an activity — process
  definitions name both roles, so this is checkable mechanically.
- A failed spot check sends the maintainer to the definition or the
  check, not only to the artifact.
- Whoever proposes a new activity writes the proposal as a draft
  instance of the activity's type, so the type's derived checks run on
  the proposal before any reviewer reads it.

## Govern the generating context (`governed-context`)

**Statement.**

- Everything loaded into an agent's generating context — prompts,
  skills, memories, primers — MUST trace to a approved definition or a
  governed record.
- An unsanctioned context channel MUST NOT be created or retained.

**Rationale.** What an agent reads determines what it produces, so an
ungoverned context input is an ungoverned generator. The failure
mode this prevents: notes accumulate in channels no process governs, and
work comes to depend on content no one has ever reviewed.

**Implications.**

- Maintainers version every context input, promote changes through a
  gated step, and can audit which definition version was in force when
  an artifact was produced.
- Whoever operates a context channel closes it when it lacks a defined
  process and a consumer.
- Tool owners ship each tool's skill with the tool, in lockstep.

## Every activity belongs to a process (`no-orphan-activities`)

**Statement.**

- Every activity in the system MUST be part of a defined process with
  stated expected outcomes, expected outputs, and possible resulting
  actions.
- Every long-running loop MUST declare its exit — a reached-state
  success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.

**Rationale.** An activity outside a process has no consumer for its
output, so the output piles up unread or is thrown away. Both
failure modes follow: feedback stops flowing when nothing consumes it, and
the signal migrates into ungoverned channels instead. Any runtime can follow a process defined at this
level — the requirement is a definition, not a workflow engine.

**Implications.**

- Reviewers treat an activity with no process as a defect, not a
  convenience.
- Authors have no cost excuse: a process definition is a header plus a
  data section and a steps section.
- Reviewers fail any loop without a declared exit.

## Use defined terms (`use-defined-terms`)

**Statement.**

- Important terms MUST be defined in the system, in the glossary or as
  a schema element.
- When more than one term could carry a statement, the writer MUST use
  a defined term if one is available.

**Rationale.** The defined-term list — glossary entries plus schema
element names — restricts the available language, and a restricted
language aids clarity and reduces drift. The failure is cheap to reach:
two words for one thing appear within days of each other, and every
reader of both must learn they are the same.
(Controlled-vocabulary practice: ASD-STE100, ISO 704.)

**Implications.**

- Writers check the glossary and the schemas before coining a term; an
  undefined important term is a defect the author repairs by defining
  it or replacing it with a defined one.
- Schema authors are vocabulary authors: naming a field adds a term to
  the restricted language.
- Reviewers flag near-synonym pairs as drift; the losing term is
  removed everywhere, not deprecated in place.
- A term is important when a reader must know it to perform or check
  the work; when in doubt, the writer defines it.

## Use external standards first (`external-standards-first`)

**Statement.**

- A definition MUST adopt an established external form where one fits.
- Bespoke structure MUST be justified by a recorded gap in the form it
  rejects.

**Rationale.** Established forms carry decades of failure-tested
decisions no fresh invention can match, and readers arrive already
knowing them. In practice every element of a
definition system has an established form, and the only bespokeness that
survives review is the composition of adopted parts.

**Implications.**

- Authors search prior art before drafting and name every adopted form
  in the definition's Sources section.
- Reviewers ask "what standard is this from" and treat unjustified
  invention as a defect.

## Single source of truth (`single-source-of-truth`)

**Statement.**

- Every fact, rule, or definition MUST have exactly one authoritative
  home.
- Every other appearance MUST be a reference or a generated rendering.

**Rationale.** Copies drift and each drifting copy trains a different
behavior. Copies of schemas drift from their source, and
pinned example links stop conforming as the source moves on.

**Implications.**

- Writers link or `$ref` instead of restating.
- Only the compiler touches renderings; a hand edit to a rendering is
  reverted, not merged.
- Reviewers treat a second authoritative statement of one rule as a
  defect and remove the losing copy everywhere.

## Feedback loops have consumers (`feedback-loops-with-consumers`)

**Statement.**

- Every feedback channel MUST name its consumer and the resulting
  action.
- The effectiveness of processes, tools, and prompts MUST be measured,
  and their definitions MUST be updated from what is measured.

**Rationale.** A channel without a consumer dies silently and takes its
signal with it: when nothing consumes a channel, senders stop sending
and the signal moves into ungoverned channels. Judged checks decay the same way when no one
grades the judge.

**Implications.**

- Whoever opens a channel names its consumer and resulting action at
  creation, or the channel is closed.
- Owners of judged checks grade a sample of verdicts on a standing
  calibration schedule.
- Definition owners treat measured ineffectiveness as an obligation to
  update the definition, not as background noise.

## Delivery is verified in the running system (`delivery-verified`)

**Statement.**

- Work MUST be counted done only when its effect is demonstrated in
  the running system.
- Artifacts existing, checks passing, or reviews approving MUST NOT
  count as done on their own.

**Rationale.** The gap between green artifacts and working systems is
where the worst defects live: builds publish without the built thing
ever running, and checks stay green while decided behavior goes
unrealized.

**Implications.**

- Definition authors name the runtime demonstration in every
  Definition of Done.
- Reviewers reject completion claims that cite only artifacts.
- Whoever closes work cites the demonstration evidence in the close
  reason — the reconcile process already enforces this shape.

## Load the least context (`least-context`)

**Statement.**

- An activity MUST load the minimum context necessary to accomplish
  its task.
- The activity's process MUST name what loads into context and the
  source each input comes from.
- Context from an unapproved source MUST NOT be loaded.

**Rationale.** Extraneous context costs twice: tokens spent carrying it,
and drift when the agent follows something it was never meant to read.
The failure mode this prevents: unreviewed notes loading into every
session regardless of task, and unscoped conversations no one can
associate with specific work. (Least privilege, applied to context.)

**Implications.**

- Process authors declare a step's context inputs the way they declare
  data inputs — the declared list is the load list.
- A session loads a conversation's anchor and its definition chain,
  nothing ambient.
- Maintainers keep historical stores — archives, transcripts — out of
  ambient context; reading one is a deliberate, declared act.
- Reviewers treat an undeclared context load as a defect.

---

## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)

| Screen | define-good-up-front | governed-context | no-orphan-activities | use-defined-terms | external-standards-first | single-source-of-truth | feedback-loops-with-consumers | delivery-verified | least-context |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most systems do NOT work this way | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Implies ≥1 practice and ≥1 check (this document's intro) | shared-definition practice; role-separation check | promotion gate; provenance audit | process-membership lint; loop-exit review | term lookup before writing; undefined-term and near-synonym lint | prior-art search; Sources-section audit | link-or-ref practice; duplicate-statement review | consumer named at creation; calibration schedule | demonstration named in DoD; close-reason citation check | per-step context declaration; undeclared-load audit |

| Implications derivable and actor-named, one per bullet (judged) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |

+  actions.

output, so the output piles up unread or is thrown away. Both
failure modes follow: feedback stops flowing when nothing consumes it, and

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render the principle set into a prompt block.

Experiment apparatus, like compile_process.py. Emits a compact rendering
of the principle set — name, slug, and statement per principle — for
inclusion in an agent's generating context. Statements carry the norms;
rationales and implications stay in the source document.

Usage:
  compile_principles.py <principles.md> <out.md>
"""
import hashlib
import pathlib
import re
import sys

import yaml


def main() -> None:
    source = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
    out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])
    text = source.read_text()
    fm_match = re.match(r"---\n(.*?)\n---\n", text, re.S)
    front = yaml.safe_load(fm_match.group(1))
    digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

    principles = re.findall(
        r"^## ([^\n]+?) \(`([^\n`]+)`\)\n\n\*\*Statement\.\*\* (.*?)(?=\n\n\*\*)",
        text,
        re.S | re.M,
    )
    if not principles:
        sys.exit(f"{source}: no principles parsed")

    fm = {
        "type": "principles-rendering",
        "id": f"{front['id']}-rendering",
        "status": front.get("status"),
        "generated": True,
        "generated-by": "basis/tools/compile_principles.py",
        "derived-from": front["id"],
        "source": "basis/principles.md",
        "source-digest": f"sha256:{digest}",
        "scope": front.get("scope"),
    }
    lines = [
        "---\n" + yaml.safe_dump(fm, sort_keys=False).rstrip() + "\n---",
        "",
        "# Working principles (compiled into every session)",
        "",
        "These statements govern every activity in this shop. The full set —",
        "rationales, implications, fitness screen — is the source document",
        "named in the front-matter; on conflict the source wins.",
        "",
    ]
    for name, slug, statement in principles:
        stmt = " ".join(statement.split())
        lines.append(f"- **{name}** (`{slug}`): {stmt}")
    out.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print(f"{out}: rendered {len(principles)} principles (digest {digest})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render the principle set into a prompt block.

Experiment apparatus, like compile_process.py. Emits a compact rendering
of the principle set — name, slug, and statement per principle — for
inclusion in an agent's generating context. Statements carry the norms;
rationales and implications stay in the source document.

Usage:
  compile_principles.py <principles.md> <out.md>
"""
import hashlib
import pathlib
import re
import sys

import yaml


def main() -> None:
    source = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
    out = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[2])
    text = source.read_text()
    fm_match = re.match(r"---\n(.*?)\n---\n", text, re.S)
    front = yaml.safe_load(fm_match.group(1))
    digest = hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]

    principles = re.findall(
        r"^## ([^\n]+?) \(`([^\n`]+)`\)\n\n\*\*Statement\.\*\*\s*(.*?)(?=\n\n\*\*)",
        text,
        re.S | re.M,
    )
    if not principles:
        sys.exit(f"{source}: no principles parsed")

    fm = {
        "type": "principles-rendering",
        "id": f"{front['id']}-rendering",
        "status": front.get("status"),
        "generated": True,
        "generated-by": "basis/tools/compile_principles.py",
        "derived-from": front["id"],
        "source": "basis/principles.md",
        "source-digest": f"sha256:{digest}",
        "scope": front.get("scope"),
    }
    lines = [
        "---\n" + yaml.safe_dump(fm, sort_keys=False).rstrip() + "\n---",
        "",
        "# Working principles (compiled into every session)",
        "",
        "These statements govern every activity in this shop. The full set —",
        "rationales, implications, fitness screen — is the source document",
        "named in the front-matter; on conflict the source wins.",
        "",
    ]
    for name, slug, statement in principles:
        block = statement.strip()
        if not re.search(r"^\s*- ", block, re.M):
            # prose statement: collapse to one line, as before
            lines.append(f"- **{name}** (`{slug}`): {' '.join(block.split())}")
            continue
        # bulleted statement: one obligation per bullet, nesting preserved
        items, lead = [], []
        for raw in block.splitlines():
            m = re.match(r"^(\s*)- (.*)$", raw)
            if m:
                items.append([len(m.group(1)), m.group(2).strip()])

        if lead:
            head += " " + " ".join(lead)
        lines.append(head)
        for indent, item in items:
            lines.append("  " * (1 + indent // 2) + "- " + item)
    out.write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
    print(f"{out}: rendered {len(principles)} principles (digest {digest})")

id: definition-typedef
defines: definition
owner: product-authority

# Artifact type: definition

## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `definition` — the generic root for documents that state what
  good looks like for something else: a process, a document type, a role,
  a term list, a rule set. Specializations (e.g. `process-definition`,
  `artifact-typedef`) declare it in their ancestry, so a validator that
  knows only `definition` can check any definition document against the
  two requirements below.
- **Produced by:** seed drafting, or governed evolution of a approved
  definition. **Consumed by:** every agent whose work the definition
  governs; compilers and validators that render or check against it.

## Required frontmatter

`type`, `id`, `status` (draft | approved | superseded), `owner` (the seat
that approves changes), `created`, `updated`; `approved` (date of the most recent approval) once approved — retained
through a later draft amendment to mark the last approved version.

## Required sections

1. An **opening** that states what the document defines before the
   first section heading.
2. A closing **checks section** (its heading contains "check") — every
   definition implies at least one check; a definition no check can cite
   does not govern anything.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A definition is done when the governed work can be performed and checked
from it alone. **Consequence on failure:** the definition — and any
activity that would depend on it — does not enter the system
(`define-good-up-front`).

## Sources

Deming's operational definitions (a definition others can work from:
test, criterion, decision); the `define-good-up-front` principle.

## Derived review checklist

- Frontmatter complete; owner named. *(schema)*
- The opening states what the document defines. *(§Required sections 1)*
- At least one derived check exists and cites a clause. *(§Required sections 2)*

1	#!/usr/bin/env python3
2	"""Lint the basis corpus: structure, references, vocabulary.
3	
4	Experiment apparatus; the production linter is a BC deliverable
5	(shopsystem-knowledge owns the type system). Each check cites the clause
6	it projects, per the cite-or-delete rule.
7	
8	Checks:
9	  1. Front-matter parses and carries the identity base
10	     (definition typedef §Required frontmatter).
11	  2. `defines` values are unique across the registry
12	     (artifact-typedef + data-type typedefs: defines is what $ref resolves).
13	  3. Every distinct `$ref` in a process data block carries a `from:`
14	     source at least once — a relative link to the defining file, or a
15	     `pkg:<package>/<type>` reference to another package
16	     (process-definition typedef §Data). Local sources must exist and
17	     their `defines` must match.
18	  4. Relative markdown links resolve to existing files.
19	  5. Required headings per type are present
20	     (each type's typedef §Required sections).
21	  6. Banned vocabulary does not reappear
22	     (use-defined-terms: the losing term is removed everywhere).
23	
24	Modes:
25	  lint_basis.py                     # lint the whole basis tree
26	  lint_basis.py --derive-chain X    # print the derived definition chain
27	                                    # for artifact type X (definition-chain
28	                                    # is assembled from references, never
29	                                    # hand-written)
30	"""
31	import pathlib
32	import re
33	import sys
34	
35	import yaml
36	
37	BASIS = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
38	
39	IDENTITY_BASE = ["type", "id", "status", "created", "updated"]
40	OWNER_EXEMPT = {"experiment-index", "skill", "principles-rendering", "review-record"}
41	REQUIRED_HEADINGS = {
42	    # artifact-typedef §Required sections 1-6
43	    "artifact-typedef": ["Identity and ancestry", "Required frontmatter",
44	                         "Required sections", "Commitment (Definition of Done)",
45	                         "Sources", "Derived review checklist"],
46	    # process-definition typedef §Required sections 5-8
47	    "process-definition": ["Flow (compiled)", "Data", "Steps", "Derived checks"],
48	    # data-type typedef §Required sections 1-2
49	    "data-type": ["Purpose", "Schema"],
50	    # fitness-set typedef §Required sections 1-2
51	    "fitness-set": ["Scenarios", "Compile mapping"],
52	    # glossary typedef §Required sections 1-2
53	    "glossary": ["How the list combines", "Terms"],
54	    # review-record typedef §Required sections 1-3
55	    "review-record": ["Material", "Rulings", "State"],
56	}
57	BANNED = ["ratif", "disposition", "rebaseline bill"]
58	PKG_RE = re.compile(r"^pkg:[a-z0-9-]+/[a-z0-9_-]+$")
59	
60	
61	def front_matter(path):
62	    text = path.read_text()
63	    m = re.match(r"---\n(.*?)\n---\n", text, re.S)
64	    if not m:
65	        return None, text
66	    try:
67	        return yaml.safe_load(m.group(1)), text
68	    except yaml.YAMLError:
69	        return None, text
70	
71	
72	def yaml_blocks(text):
73	    out = {}
74	    for fence in re.findall(r"```yaml\n(.*?)```", text, re.S):
75	        block = yaml.safe_load(fence)
76	        if isinstance(block, dict):
77	            out.update(block)
78	    return out
79	
80	
81	def collect_refs(node):
82	    refs = set()
83	    if isinstance(node, dict):
84	        for k, v in node.items():
85	            if k == "$ref":
86	                refs.add(v)
87	            else:
88	                refs |= collect_refs(v)
89	    elif isinstance(node, list):
90	        for item in node:
91	            refs |= collect_refs(item)
92	    return refs
93	
94	
95	def registry():
96	    reg = {}
97	    for tree in ("artifacts", "types"):
98	        for path in (BASIS / tree).glob("*.md"):
99	            fm, _ = front_matter(path)
100	            if fm and fm.get("defines"):
101	                reg[fm["defines"]] = path
102	    return reg
103	
104	
105	def lint():
106	    errors = []
107	    reg = registry()
108	
109	    seen_defines = {}
110	    for path in sorted(BASIS.rglob("*.md")):
111	        rel = path.relative_to(BASIS)
112	        fm, text = front_matter(path)
113	
114	        # 1. identity base
115	        if fm is None:
116	            errors.append(f"{rel}: front-matter missing or unparseable (definition §Required frontmatter)")
117	            continue
118	        for field in IDENTITY_BASE:
119	            if field not in fm:
120	                errors.append(f"{rel}: front-matter lacks `{field}` (definition §Required frontmatter)")
121	        if fm.get("type") not in OWNER_EXEMPT and "owner" not in fm:
122	            errors.append(f"{rel}: front-matter lacks `owner` (definition §Required frontmatter)")
123	
124	        # 2. defines uniqueness
125	        if fm.get("defines"):
126	            if fm["defines"] in seen_defines:
127	                errors.append(f"{rel}: duplicate defines `{fm['defines']}` (also {seen_defines[fm['defines']]})")
128	            seen_defines[fm["defines"]] = rel
129	
130	        # 4. relative links resolve
131	        for target in re.findall(r"\]\(([^)#\s]+)\)", text):
132	            if target.startswith(("http://", "https://", "pkg:")):
133	                continue
134	            if not (path.parent / target).exists():
135	                errors.append(f"{rel}: broken link `{target}`")
136	
137	        # 5. required headings
138	        headings = re.findall(r"^#{1,3} (.+)$", text, re.M)
139	        for req in REQUIRED_HEADINGS.get(fm.get("type"), []):
140	            if not any(h.strip().startswith(req) for h in headings):
141	                errors.append(f"{rel}: missing required heading `{req}` ({fm.get('type')} typedef §Required sections)")
142	
143	        # 6. banned vocabulary
144	        if rel.name != "README.md":
145	            for i, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), 1):
146	                if "Replaces" in line or line.lstrip().startswith(("approved:", "ratified:")):
147	                    continue
148	                for term in BANNED:
149	                    if term in line.lower():
150	                        errors.append(f"{rel}:{i}: banned term `{term}` (use-defined-terms; see glossary)")
151	
152	        # 3. $ref sources in process data blocks
153	        if fm.get("type") == "process-definition":
154	            spec = yaml_blocks(text)
155	            data = spec.get("data", {})
156	            refs = collect_refs(data)
157	            sourced = {}
158	            def walk(node):
159	                if isinstance(node, dict):
160	                    if "$ref" in node and node.get("from"):
161	                        sourced[node["$ref"]] = node["from"]
162	                    for v in node.values():
163	                        walk(v)
164	                elif isinstance(node, list):
165	                    for i in node:
166	                        walk(i)
167	            walk(data)
168	            for ref in sorted(refs):
169	                src = sourced.get(ref)
170	                if not src:
171	                    errors.append(f"{rel}: $ref `{ref}` has no `from:` source (process-definition §Data)")
172	                elif src.startswith("pkg:"):
173	                    if not PKG_RE.match(src):
174	                        errors.append(f"{rel}: `{src}` is not pkg:<package>/<type> (process-definition §Data)")
175	                else:
176	                    target = (path.parent / src).resolve()
177	                    if not target.exists():
178	                        errors.append(f"{rel}: from `{src}` does not exist")
179	                    else:
180	                        tfm, _ = front_matter(target)
181	                        if not tfm or tfm.get("defines") != ref:
182	                            errors.append(f"{rel}: from `{src}` does not define `{ref}`")
183	    return errors
184	
185	
186	def derive_chain(artifact_type):
187	    """definition-chain is derived from document references, never authored:
188	    typedef by `defines`, guideline and fitness by `target-type`, process by
189	    `produces`, roles from the process steps, skill by `derived-from`."""
190	    chain = {"artifact_type": artifact_type, "typedef": "", "guideline": "",
191	             "fitness": "", "process": "", "roles": [], "skill": "", "status": "draft"}
192	    docs = []
193	    process_id = None
194	    for path in sorted(BASIS.rglob("*.md")):
195	        fm, text = front_matter(path)
196	        if not fm:
197	            continue
198	        t = fm.get("type")
199	        if t == "artifact-typedef" and fm.get("defines") == artifact_type:
200	            chain["typedef"] = fm["id"]; docs.append(fm)
201	        elif t == "quality-guideline" and fm.get("target-type") == artifact_type:
202	            chain["guideline"] = fm["id"]; docs.append(fm)
203	        elif t == "fitness-set" and fm.get("target-type") == artifact_type:
204	            chain["fitness"] = fm["id"]; docs.append(fm)
205	        elif t == "process-definition" and artifact_type in (fm.get("produces") or []):
206	            chain["process"] = fm["id"]; process_id = fm["id"]; docs.append(fm)
207	            spec = yaml_blocks(text)
208	            roles = {s["run-by"]["role"] for s in spec.get("steps", [])
209	                     if s.get("run-by", {}).get("role")}
210	            chain["roles"] = sorted(roles)
211	    if process_id:
212	        for path in (BASIS / "skills").rglob("SKILL.md"):
213	            fm, _ = front_matter(path)
214	            if fm and fm.get("derived-from") == process_id:
215	                chain["skill"] = fm["id"]; docs.append(fm)
216	    if docs and all(d.get("status") == "approved" for d in docs) and \
217	       all(chain[k] for k in ("typedef", "guideline", "fitness", "process", "skill")):
218	        chain["status"] = "approved"
219	    return chain
220	
221	
222	def main():
223	    if len(sys.argv) > 2 and sys.argv[1] == "--derive-chain":
224	        print(yaml.safe_dump(derive_chain(sys.argv[2]), sort_keys=False).rstrip())
225	        return
226	    errors = lint()
227	    for e in errors:
228	        print(e)
229	    print(f"{'FAIL' if errors else 'PASS'}: {len(errors)} violation(s)")
230	    sys.exit(1 if errors else 0)
231	
232	
233	if __name__ == "__main__":
234	    main()

import pathlib, re

BASIS = pathlib.Path("basis")

t = p.read_text()

t = p.read_text()
t = re.sub(r"\nverified-by:\n(?:  .*\n|    .*\n)+(?=---)", "", t)
p.write_text(t)

# shorten the six pending markers

# remove dated historical annotations (may span lines)
t = re.sub(r"\s*\*\((?:added|amended) 2026-08-2\d[^*]*?\)\*", "", t, flags=re.S)

def add_version(fm_text, version):
    if re.search(r"^version:", fm_text, re.M):
        fm_text = re.sub(r"^version:.*$", f"version: {version}", fm_text, flags=re.M)
        return fm_text
    return re.sub(r"^(created:)", f"version: {version}\n\\1", fm_text, count=1, flags=re.M)

changed = 0
for path in sorted(BASIS.rglob("*.md")):
    text = path.read_text()
    m = re.match(r"---\n(.*?)\n---\n", text, re.S)
    if not m:
        continue
    import yaml
    fm = yaml.safe_load(m.group(1))
    if fm.get("generated"):
        continue
    rel = str(path.relative_to(BASIS))
    if rel in CUSTOM:
        version, hist = CUSTOM[rel]
    else:
        version = 1
        created = fm.get("created", "2026-08-22")
        hist = H + f"| 1 | {created} | update | Authored (seed layer); earlier history, if any, in the review record ledger on `main`. |\n"
        if fm.get("approved"):
            hist += f"| 1 | {fm['approved']} | state | draft → approved. |\n"
    new_fm = add_version(m.group(1), version)
    body = text[m.end():]
    if "## Document History" not in body:
        body = body.rstrip() + "\n\n" + hist
    else:
        body = re.sub(r"## Document History.*$", hist.rstrip() + "\n", body, flags=re.S)
    path.write_text("---\n" + new_fm + "\n---\n" + body)
    changed += 1
print(f"{changed} artifacts stamped")

12	# Architecture principles
13	
14	## What this set governs
15	
16	This is the architecture-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
17	the product is designed — its regions, their boundaries, and the entities
18	that build and evolve them. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
19	[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity is
20	performed; this set governs what the designed system must look like.
21	Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
22	defined in the working set. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
23	contract, relationship kind, and intent are defined in the
24	[glossary](glossary.md). Two distinctions those terms carry are used
25	throughout. A shop is either the lead shop — the system-level
26	coordinator, owning the product-level artifacts and no Bounded
27	Context — or a BC-shop, owning exactly one. A contract is offered
28	either as a product contract, on a Bounded Context, or as an
29	operational contract, on a shop.
30	
31	Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle at the
32	architecture level, this document declares the lineage in its
33	frontmatter — `derives-from` maps the principle in this set to the
34	working-scope principle it applies — instead of restating the rule as a
35	second authority.
36	
37	## What a good principle looks like
38	
39	This section restates the shared definition from the
40	[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
41	be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.
42	
43	A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
44	rationale, and implications.
45	
46	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
47	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
48	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
49	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
50	  presents one obligation per bullet.
51	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
52	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
53	  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
54	  stay prose.
55	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
56	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
57	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
58	  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.
59	
60	A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects work we
61	would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
62	(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it
63	implies at least one practice and one check. The fitness screen at the
64	end of this document applies these tests to the principles above it.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## Every first-class entity has a knowable shape (`knowable-shape`)
69	
70	**Statement.**
71	
72	- The product MUST have exactly two kinds of first-class entity: the
73	  Bounded Context and the shop.
74	- Each Bounded Context MUST be contained and produced by exactly one
75	  BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT contain one.
76	- Every first-class entity MUST carry a description, maintained as an
77	  artifact, from which an outside reader can name what the entity is
78	  for, what it accepts and produces, what it guarantees, and the
79	  contracts it offers.
80	- The description MUST suffice without reading the entity's internal
81	  code or configuration and without asking its maintainers.
82	
83	**Rationale.** When an entity's shape lives only in its internals, every
84	consumer, coordinator, and reviewer pays to rediscover it, and each
85	rediscovery reaches a different answer: nobody can say what a service
86	guarantees without opening its source, the answer holds only until the
87	next commit, and no description can be trusted without re-inspecting
88	the thing it describes. Parnas made the design case in 1972: a module
89	is known by what its interface states, not by what its implementation
90	happens to do. Without `knowable-shape`,
91	`contracts-between-contexts` is speculative — no one can write a
92	contract for an entity whose shape no one can state.
93	
94	**Implications.**
95	
96	- Whoever creates a Bounded Context or a shop writes its description at
97	  creation; an entity without a description is not yet created,
98	  whatever code exists.
99	- Maintainers keep the description authoritative: when an outside
100	  reader must open internals to answer a question the description
101	  claims to cover, the description is the defect and its maintainer
102	  repairs it.
103	- Architects reason from descriptions; opening an entity's internals is
104	  audit work — checking that a description is true — not the normal way
105	  to learn what the entity is.
106	
107	## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)
108	
109	**Statement.**
110	
111	- Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass through a
112	  named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the meaning
113	  of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind.
114	- A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's
115	  contract does not state.
116	- Bounded Contexts MUST NOT share state or coordinate outside their
117	  contracts.
118	
119	**Rationale.** Unstated expectations cannot be reviewed, versioned, or
120	deliberately kept — they are discovered when they break. Hyrum's law
121	(Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, *Software Engineering at Google*)
122	records the observed endpoint: with enough consumers, every observable
123	behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the
124	contract says — the only defense is making the contract the sole thing a
125	consumer is entitled to. Evans (*Domain-Driven Design*, 2003) draws
126	context boundaries for the same reason: models stay coherent only when
127	what crosses between them is explicit. Without this rule,
128	`local-comprehension` collapses — a consumer must read a counterpart's
129	internals to learn what is safe to use.
130	
131	**Implications.**
132	
133	- Contract authors put every promise in the contract document —
134	  schemas, semantics, errors, relationship kind; a promise made
135	  anywhere else is not owed.
136	- Reviewers of a consuming context treat reliance on unstated behavior
137	  as that context's defect, and treat the underlying need as a
138	  contract-change request, not a license to work around the contract.
139	- Integrators who need a channel the contract lacks amend the contract
140	  first or do not integrate.
141	
142	## Discipline attaches to activities, not actors (`actor-neutral-discipline`)
143	
144	**Statement.**
145	
146	- Rules, authority, and required records MUST attach to the activity
147	  and the role performing it, never to the kind of actor filling the
148	  role.
149	- An activity MUST NOT record less, skip checks, or gain authority
150	  because a particular kind of actor — human, agent, or service —
151	  performs it.
152	
153	**Rationale.** Rules forked by actor kind create bypasses: whichever
154	fork is weakest becomes the route around the discipline, and social
155	routes — "just ask the team next door" — are exactly the moves agents
156	scale beyond anyone's review. Role-based access control (Ferraiolo and
157	Kuhn, 1992; the NIST RBAC model) grounds the mechanism: grant to roles,
158	and the actor mix can change without regranting authority. The working
159	set's `no-orphan-activities` already places every activity in a process;
160	this rule keeps those processes actor-neutral, which is what keeps
161	`contracts-between-contexts` binding on whoever shows up — an actor that
162	could renegotiate the rules by kind could talk its way around a
163	contract.
164	
165	**Implications.**
166

def add_version(fm_text, version):
    if re.search(r"^version:", fm_text, re.M):
        return re.sub(r"^version:.*$", f"version: {version}", fm_text, flags=re.M)
    return re.sub(r"^(created:)", f"version: {version}\n\\1", fm_text, count=1, flags=re.M)

changed = []
for path in sorted(BASIS.rglob("*.md")):
    text = path.read_text()
    m = re.match(r"---\n(.*?)\n---\n", text, re.S)
    if not m:
        continue
    fm = yaml.safe_load(m.group(1))
    if fm.get("generated"):
        continue
    rel = str(path.relative_to(BASIS))
    if rel in CUSTOM:
        version, hist = CUSTOM[rel]
    else:
        version = 1
        created = fm.get("created", "2026-08-22")
        hist = H + f"| 1 | {created} | update | Authored (seed layer); earlier history, if any, in the review record ledger on `main`. |\n"
        if fm.get("approved"):
            hist += f"| 1 | {fm['approved']} | state | draft → approved. |\n"
    new_fm = add_version(m.group(1), version)
    body = text[m.end():]
    if "## Document History" in body:
        body = re.sub(r"## Document History.*$", hist.rstrip() + "\n", body, flags=re.S)
    else:
        body = body.rstrip() + "\n\n" + hist
    path.write_text("---\n" + new_fm + "\n---\n" + body)
    changed.append(rel)

for c in changed:
    print(" ", c)

13	
14	# Architecture principles
15	
16	## What this set governs
17	
18	This is the architecture-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
19	the product is designed — its regions, their boundaries, and the entities
20	that build and evolve them. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
21	[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity is
22	performed; this set governs what the designed system must look like.
23	Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
24	defined in the working set. The terms Bounded Context, shop, activity,
25	contract, relationship kind, and intent are defined in the
26	[glossary](glossary.md). Two distinctions those terms carry are used
27	throughout. A shop is either the lead shop — the system-level
28	coordinator, owning the product-level artifacts and no Bounded
29	Context — or a BC-shop, owning exactly one. A contract is offered
30	either as a product contract, on a Bounded Context, or as an
31	operational contract, on a shop.
32	
33	Where a principle here applies a working-scope principle at the
34	architecture level, this document declares the lineage in its
35	frontmatter — `derives-from` maps the principle in this set to the
36	working-scope principle it applies — instead of restating the rule as a
37	second authority.
38	
39	## What a good principle looks like
40	
41	This section restates the shared definition from the
42	[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
43	be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.
44	
45	A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
46	rationale, and implications.
47	
48	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
49	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
50	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
51	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
52	  presents one obligation per bullet.
53	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
54	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
55	  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
56	  stay prose.
57	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
58	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
59	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
60	  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.
61	
62	A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects work we
63	would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
64	(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it
65	implies at least one practice and one check. The fitness screen at the
66	end of this document applies these tests to the principles above it.
67	
68	---
69	
70	## Every first-class entity has a knowable shape (`knowable-shape`)
71	
72	**Statement.**
73	
74	- The product MUST have exactly two kinds of first-class entity: the
75	  Bounded Context and the shop.
76	- Each Bounded Context MUST be contained and produced by exactly one
77	  BC-shop; the lead shop MUST NOT contain one.
78	- Every first-class entity MUST carry a description, maintained as an
79	  artifact, from which an outside reader can name what the entity is
80	  for, what it accepts and produces, what it guarantees, and the
81	  contracts it offers.
82	- The description MUST suffice without reading the entity's internal
83	  code or configuration and without asking its maintainers.
84	
85	**Rationale.** When an entity's shape lives only in its internals, every
86	consumer, coordinator, and reviewer pays to rediscover it, and each
87	rediscovery reaches a different answer: nobody can say what a service
88	guarantees without opening its source, the answer holds only until the
89	next commit, and no description can be trusted without re-inspecting
90	the thing it describes. Parnas made the design case in 1972: a module
91	is known by what its interface states, not by what its implementation
92	happens to do. Without `knowable-shape`,
93	`contracts-between-contexts` is speculative — no one can write a
94	contract for an entity whose shape no one can state.
95	
96	**Implications.**
97	
98	- Whoever creates a Bounded Context or a shop writes its description at
99	  creation; an entity without a description is not yet created,
100	  whatever code exists.
101	- Maintainers keep the description authoritative: when an outside
102	  reader must open internals to answer a question the description
103	  claims to cover, the description is the defect and its maintainer
104	  repairs it.
105	- Architects reason from descriptions; opening an entity's internals is
106	  audit work — checking that a description is true — not the normal way
107	  to learn what the entity is.
108	
109	## Contracts are the only channel between Bounded Contexts (`contracts-between-contexts`)
110	
111	**Statement.**
112	
113	- Anything one Bounded Context expects of another MUST pass through a
114	  named, versioned contract stating the schemas exchanged, the meaning
115	  of each operation, the error behavior, and the relationship kind.
116	- A Bounded Context MUST NOT rely on anything its counterpart's
117	  contract does not state.
118	- Bounded Contexts MUST NOT share state or coordinate outside their
119	  contracts.
120	
121	**Rationale.** Unstated expectations cannot be reviewed, versioned, or
122	deliberately kept — they are discovered when they break. Hyrum's law
123	(Winters, Manshreck, and Wright, *Software Engineering at Google*)
124	records the observed endpoint: with enough consumers, every observable
125	behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody, whatever the
126	contract says — the only defense is making the contract the sole thing a
127	consumer is entitled to. Evans (*Domain-Driven Design*, 2003) draws
128	context boundaries for the same reason: models stay coherent only when
129	what crosses between them is explicit. Without this rule,
130	`local-comprehension` collapses — a consumer must read a counterpart's
131	internals to learn what is safe to use.
132	
133	**Implications.**
134	
135	- Contract authors put every promise in the contract document —
136	  schemas, semantics, errors, relationship kind; a promise made
137	  anywhere else is not owed.
138	- Reviewers of a consuming context treat reliance on unstated behavior
139	  as that context's defect, and treat the underlying need as a
140	  contract-change request, not a license to work around the contract.
141	- Integrators who need a channel the contract lacks amend the contract
142	  first or do not integrate.
143	
144	## Discipline attaches to activities, not actors (`actor-neutral-discipline`)
145	
146	**Statement.**
147	
148	- Rules, authority, and required records MUST attach to the activity
149	  and the role performing it, never to the kind of actor filling the
150	  role.
151	- An activity MUST NOT record less, skip checks, or gain authority
152	  because a particular kind of actor — human, agent, or service —
153	  performs it.
154	
155	**Rationale.** Rules forked by actor kind create bypasses: whichever
156	fork is weakest becomes the route around the discipline, and social
157	routes — "just ask the team next door" — are exactly the moves agents

`type: principle-set`, `id`, `scope` (the level the set governs and whose
context it loads into: `working` — how every activity is performed, loads
everywhere — or `architecture` — how the system is designed, loads where
design work happens), `owner`, `status`, `created`, `updated`.

## Rules

- Content in an undefined format never enters a set as-is: it is source
  material for a rewrite through this typedef, or it retires.
- Where a principle in one set applies another set's principle to its own
  level, it declares the lineage (`derives-from`) rather than restating
  the rule as a second authority.
- A rationale MUST use generic examples and MUST NOT reference the
  product's operational history — other artifacts, issues, incidents,
  rulings, counts; it MAY cite well-known external references as
  support. *(amended 2026-08-23 by authority direction.)*

## Required sections

1. **What a good principle looks like** — the opening self-definition:
   the four parts (name, statement, rationale, implications) and the
   tests a good principle passes. The document obeys its own first rule
   by defining good before presenting instances.
2. **The principles** — each: a heading with name and kebab-case slug,
   then **Statement** (the rule; carries the only normative keywords —
   MUST/SHOULD/MAY per BCP 14 — and is yes/no testable; one or more
   sentences, and a statement with more than one obligation presents
   one obligation per bullet), **Rationale**
   (the failure prevented, shown as a generic example; well-known
   external sources may support it), **Implications**
   (the price tag: one implication per bullet, each derivable from the
   statement and naming the actor who absorbs the change; never a new
   obligation).
3. **Fitness screen** — a table applying the opening's tests to every
   principle, including the two mechanical/judged rows: normative
   keywords in statements only; implications derivable and actor-named.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A principle set is done when every principle passes every screen row and
the screen covers every principle. **Consequence on failure:** the
failing principle is repaired or removed before the set is citable.

TOGAF architecture principles (Name/Statement/Rationale/Implications);

13	# Founding principles
14	
15	## What a good principle looks like
16	
17	A principle is a standing rule about how we work, in four parts: a name, a
18	statement, a rationale, and implications. Terms the principles use —
19	rendering, anchor, definition chain, and the rest — are defined in the
20	[glossary](glossary.md); the processes and tools the implications name
21	are defined in this basis's sibling documents.
22	
23	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
24	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
25	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
26	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
27	  presents one obligation per bullet.
28	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
29	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
30	  may support it. Rationales stay prose.
31	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
32	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
33	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
34	  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.
35	
36	A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects something
37	we would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
38	(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it implies at least one practice and one
39	check. The fitness screen at the end of this document applies these tests
40	to the principles above it.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Define what good looks like up front (`define-good-up-front`)
45	
46	**Statement.**
47	
48	- Every activity MUST operate from a stated definition of what good
49	  looks like.
50	- That definition MUST drive both the performance of the activity and
51	  its check.
52	- The check MUST sit with a different role holding a different
53	  accountability.
54	
55	**Rationale.** A definition applied only at the check puts the full weight
56	of quality after implementation, where rework is most frequent and most
57	expensive. A definition applied only up front invites gaming and closes
58	off outside perspective. Two roles reading one definition give both
59	prevention and challenge. (Deming: cease dependence on inspection; build
60	quality in — and still inspect.)
61	
62	**Implications.**
63	
64	- Authors of new activities ship the definition with the activity, or
65	  the activity does not enter the system.
66	- A check that cannot cite the definition clause it projects has no
67	  standing; anyone may remove it without a new decision.
68	- Reviewers compare work to the written definition; their own taste is
69	  not the standard.
70	- The same role never both performs and checks an activity — process
71	  definitions name both roles, so this is checkable mechanically.
72	- A failed spot check sends the maintainer to the definition or the
73	  check, not only to the artifact.
74	- Whoever proposes a new activity writes the proposal as a draft
75	  instance of the activity's type, so the type's derived checks run on
76	  the proposal before any reviewer reads it.
77	
78	## Govern the generating context (`governed-context`)
79	
80	**Statement.**
81	
82	- Everything loaded into an agent's generating context — prompts,
83	  skills, memories, primers — MUST trace to an approved definition or a
84	  governed record.
85	- An unsanctioned context channel MUST NOT be created or retained.
86	
87	**Rationale.** What an agent reads determines what it produces, so an
88	ungoverned context input is an ungoverned generator. The failure
89	mode this prevents: notes accumulate in channels no process governs, and
90	work comes to depend on content no one has ever reviewed.
91	
92	**Implications.**
93	
94	- Maintainers version every context input.
95	- Maintainers promote changes through a gated step.
96	- Maintainers can audit which definition version was in force when an
97	  artifact was produced.
98	- Whoever operates a context channel closes it when it lacks a defined
99	  process and a consumer.
100	- Tool owners ship each tool's skill with the tool, in lockstep.
101	
102	## Every activity belongs to a process (`no-orphan-activities`)
103	
104	**Statement.**
105	
106	- Every activity in the system MUST be part of a defined process with
107	  stated expected outcomes, expected outputs, and possible resulting
108	  actions.
109	- Every long-running loop MUST declare its exit — a reached-state
110	  success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
111	
112	**Rationale.** An activity outside a process has no consumer for its
113	output, so the output piles up unread or is thrown away. Both
114	failure modes follow: feedback stops flowing when nothing consumes it, and
115	the signal migrates into ungoverned channels instead. Any runtime can follow a process defined at this
116	level — the requirement is a definition, not a workflow engine.
117	
118	**Implications.**
119	
120	- Reviewers treat an activity with no process as a defect, not a
121	  convenience.
122	- Authors have no cost excuse: a process definition is a header plus a
123	  data section and a steps section.
124	- Reviewers fail any loop without a declared exit.
125	
126	## Use defined terms (`use-defined-terms`)
127	
128	**Statement.**
129	
130	- Important terms MUST be defined in the system, in the glossary or as
131	  a schema element.
132	- A term is important when a reader must know it to perform or check
133	  the work.
134	- When more than one term could carry a statement, the writer MUST use

136	
137	**Rationale.** The defined-term list — glossary entries plus schema

139	language aids clarity and reduces drift. The failure is cheap to reach:
140	two words for one thing appear within days of each other, and every
141	reader of both must learn they are the same.
142	(Controlled-vocabulary practice: ASD-STE100, ISO 704.)
143	
144	**Implications.**
145	
146	- Writers check the glossary and the schemas before coining a term; an
147	  undefined important term is a defect the author repairs by defining
148	  it or replacing it with a defined one.
149	- Schema authors are vocabulary authors: naming a field adds a term to
150	  the restricted language.
151	- Reviewers flag near-synonym pairs as drift; the losing term is
152	  removed everywhere, not deprecated in place.
153	- When in doubt whether a term is important, the writer defines it.
154	
155	## Use external standards first (`external-standards-first`)
156	
157	**Statement.**
158	
159	- A definition MUST adopt an established external form where one fits.
160	- Bespoke structure MUST be justified by a recorded gap in the form it
161	  rejects.
162	
163	**Rationale.** Established forms carry decades of failure-tested
164	decisions no fresh invention can match, and readers arrive already

168	
169	**Implications.**
170	
171	- Authors search prior art before drafting and name every adopted form
172	  in the definition's Sources section.
173	- Reviewers ask "what standard is this from" and treat unjustified
174	  invention as a defect.
175

180	- Every fact, rule, or definition MUST have exactly one authoritative

1	---
2	type: principle-set
3	id: principles
4	scope: working
5	owner: product-authority
6	status: approved
7	approved: 2026-08-22
8	version: 5
9	created: 2026-08-10
10	updated: 2026-08-23
11	---
12	
13	# Founding principles
14	
15	## What a good principle looks like
16	
17	A principle is a standing rule about how we work, in four parts: a name, a
18	statement, a rationale, and implications. Terms the principles use —
19	rendering, anchor, definition chain, and the rest — are defined in the
20	[glossary](glossary.md); the processes and tools the implications name
21	are defined in this basis's sibling documents.
22	
23	- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
24	  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
25	  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
26	  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
27	  presents one obligation per bullet.
28	- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
29	  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
30	  may support it. Rationales stay prose.
31	- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
32	  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
33	  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
34	  statement, or it is a misfiled rule.
35	
36	A principle is good when its statement is testable, it rejects something
37	we would otherwise do (Spool), it directs without prescribing method
38	(Rumelt), it is not a claim every shop would make (Lencioni), and it implies at least one practice and one
39	check. The fitness screen at the end of this document applies these tests
40	to the principles above it.
41	
42	---
43	
44	## Define what good looks like up front (`define-good-up-front`)
45	
46	**Statement.**
47	
48	- Every activity MUST operate from a stated definition of what good
49	  looks like.
50	- That definition MUST drive both the performance of the activity and
51	  its check.
52	- The check MUST sit with a different role holding a different
53	  accountability.
54	
55	**Rationale.** A definition applied only at the check puts the full weight
56	of quality after implementation, where rework is most frequent and most
57	expensive. A definition applied only up front invites gaming and closes
58	off outside perspective. Two roles reading one definition give both
59	prevention and challenge. (Deming: cease dependence on inspection; build
60	quality in — and still inspect.)
61	
62	**Implications.**
63	
64	- Authors of new activities ship the definition with the activity, or
65	  the activity does not enter the system.
66	- A check that cannot cite the definition clause it projects has no
67	  standing; anyone may remove it without a new decision.
68	- Reviewers compare work to the written definition; their own taste is
69	  not the standard.
70	- The same role never both performs and checks an activity — process
71	  definitions name both roles, so this is checkable mechanically.
72	- A failed spot check sends the maintainer to the definition or the
73	  check, not only to the artifact.
74	- Whoever proposes a new activity writes the proposal as a draft
75	  instance of the activity's type, so the type's derived checks run on
76	  the proposal before any reviewer reads it.
77	
78	## Govern the generating context (`governed-context`)
79	
80	**Statement.**
81	
82	- Everything loaded into an agent's generating context — prompts,
83	  skills, memories, primers — MUST trace to an approved definition or a
84	  governed record.
85	- An unsanctioned context channel MUST NOT be created or retained.
86	
87	**Rationale.** What an agent reads determines what it produces, so an
88	ungoverned context input is an ungoverned generator. The failure
89	mode this prevents: notes accumulate in channels no process governs, and
90	work comes to depend on content no one has ever reviewed.
91	
92	**Implications.**
93	
94	- Maintainers version every context input.
95	- Maintainers promote changes through a gated step.
96	- Maintainers can audit which definition version was in force when an
97	  artifact was produced.
98	- Whoever operates a context channel closes it when it lacks a defined
99	  process and a consumer.
100	- Tool owners ship each tool's skill with the tool, in lockstep.
101	
102	## Every activity belongs to a process (`no-orphan-activities`)
103	
104	**Statement.**
105	
106	- Every activity in the system MUST be part of a defined process with
107	  stated expected outcomes, expected outputs, and possible resulting
108	  actions.
109	- Every long-running loop MUST declare its exit — a reached-state
110	  success exit, a round or budget cap, or both.
111	
112	**Rationale.** An activity outside a process has no consumer for its
113	output, so the output piles up unread or is thrown away. Both
114	failure modes follow: feedback stops flowing when nothing consumes it, and
115	the signal migrates into ungoverned channels instead. Any runtime can follow a process defined at this
116	level — the requirement is a definition, not a workflow engine.
117	
118	**Implications.**
119	
120	- Reviewers treat an activity with no process as a defect, not a
121	  convenience.
122	- Authors have no cost excuse: a process definition is a header plus a
123	  data section and a steps section.
124	- Reviewers fail any loop without a declared exit.
125	
126	## Use defined terms (`use-defined-terms`)
127	
128	**Statement.**
129	
130	- Important terms MUST be defined in the system, in the glossary or as
131	  a schema element.
132	- A term is important when a reader must know it to perform or check
133	  the work.
134	- When more than one term could carry a statement, the writer MUST use
135	  a defined term if one is available.
136	
137	**Rationale.** The defined-term list — glossary entries plus schema
138	element names — restricts the available language, and a restricted
139	language aids clarity and reduces drift. The failure is cheap to reach:
140	two words for one thing appear within days of each other, and every
141	reader of both must learn they are the same.
142	(Controlled-vocabulary practice: ASD-STE100, ISO 704.)
143	
144	**Implications.**
145	
146	- Writers check the glossary and the schemas before coining a term; an
147	  undefined important term is a defect the author repairs by defining
148	  it or replacing it with a defined one.
149	- Schema authors are vocabulary authors: naming a field adds a term to
150	  the restricted language.
151	- Reviewers flag near-synonym pairs as drift; the losing term is
152	  removed everywhere, not deprecated in place.
153	- When in doubt whether a term is important, the writer defines it.
154	
155	## Use external standards first (`external-standards-first`)
156	
157	**Statement.**
158	
159	- A definition MUST adopt an established external form where one fits.
160	- Bespoke structure MUST be justified by a recorded gap in the form it
161	  rejects.
162	
163	**Rationale.** Established forms carry decades of failure-tested
164	decisions no fresh invention can match, and readers arrive already
165	knowing them. The failure a bespoke form invites: a home-grown format
166	half-copies the standard it ignored, every reader must learn it from
167	scratch, and it silently diverges from the tooling and expectations the
168	standard would have supplied for free. In practice every element of a
169	definition system has an established form, and the only bespokeness that
170	survives review is the composition of adopted parts.
171	
172	**Implications.**
173	
174	- Authors search prior art before drafting and name every adopted form
175	  in the definition's Sources section.
176	- Reviewers ask "what standard is this from" and treat unjustified
177	  invention as a defect.
178	
179	## Single source of truth (`single-source-of-truth`)
180	
181	**Statement.**
182	
183	- Every fact, rule, or definition MUST have exactly one authoritative
184	  home.
185	- Every other appearance MUST be a reference or a generated rendering.
186
