cat > basis/experience-principles.md <<'EOF'
---
type: principle-set
id: experience-principles
scope: experience
owner: product-authority
status: draft
version: 1
created: 2026-08-26
updated: 2026-08-26
derives-from:
  agent-is-a-user: actor-neutral-discipline
---

# Experience principles

## What this set governs

This is the experience-scope principle set: the standing rules for how
the product's interactions are designed, whichever interaction type a
person or an agent reaches the product by — command line, terminal,
graphical or web, API and SDK, conversational, voice, or a generated
document. It is a peer of the working-scope set,
[Founding principles](principles.md), which governs how every activity
is performed, and of the architecture-scope set,
[Architecture principles](architecture-principles.md), which governs
what the designed system must look like; this set governs what a person
or an agent meets when they use it. It is the first layer of the
experience guidance corpus the
[product designer role](roles/lead-product-designer.md) owns; the
guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it.
Backticked slugs cite principles; a slug not defined in this document is
defined in the working or architecture set. The terms interaction type,
experience guidance corpus, contract, and intent are defined in the
[glossary](glossary.md). Where a principle here applies another set's
principle at the experience level, the frontmatter declares the lineage
in `derives-from` instead of restating the rule as a second authority.

## What a good principle looks like

This section restates the shared definition from the
[principle-set typedef](artifacts/principle-set.md) so this document can
be read alone; the restatement is a rendering, not a second authority.

A principle is a standing rule, in four parts: a name, a statement, a
rationale, and implications.

- The **statement** is the rule. It carries the only normative keywords
  (MUST, SHOULD, MAY — interpreted per BCP 14 when, and only when, they
  appear in capitals) and is testable: shown a piece of work, you can
  answer yes or no. A statement carrying more than one obligation
  presents one obligation per bullet.
- The **rationale** says why the rule earns its place: the failure it
  prevents, shown as a generic example; well-known external references
  may support it, the product's own history never appears. Rationales
  stay prose.
- The **implications** are the price tag: one implication per bullet,
  the concrete change each named actor absorbs to honor the rule. They
  add no obligations — every implication must be derivable from the
  statement.

A good principle passes five tests, applied in the fitness screen at the
end: its statement is testable (TOGAF's understandable, complete,
consistent); it helps you say no (Jared Spool, "Creating Great Design
Principles"); it is not fluff and not a goal in disguise (Richard
Rumelt, *Good Strategy/Bad Strategy*); it is not permission-to-play —
something every competent product already does (Patrick Lencioni, "Make
Your Values Mean Something"); and it implies at least one practice and
at least one check.

## The principles

### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type MUST use the product's one vocabulary: the same
  name for the same thing, the same word for the same action.
- Every interaction type MUST honour the conventions of the platform it
  lives on, over the product's own conventions where the two conflict.
- A rule of the experience guidance corpus MAY be varied for one
  interaction type only with the variation and its reason recorded in
  the corpus.

**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. Users carry their
expectations from the platform they are on (Nielsen Norman Group's
usability heuristic "consistency and standards"; Jakob's law), and from
the last place they met the product. The GOV.UK design principles put it
as "be consistent, not uniform": the same language and patterns wherever
possible, without a straitjacket. Consistency of words and rules,
freedom of form.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary and voice as part
  of the corpus, and every interaction type's text is screened against
  it.
- Bounded Context shops building an interaction of any type follow that
  type's platform conventions — the command-line guidelines for a CLI,
  the platform's interface guidelines for a GUI — and cite them.
- The product designer role records each per-type variation with its
  reason; an unrecorded variation is a conformance finding.

### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support the product's
  core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete wherever the
  product is reached.
- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
  task.

**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
interface shows teaches users that the product hides things. The
conversation-design guidance from Google and Amazon converges on the
rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in one
modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
interaction types without relearning what the product can do.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role keeps the list of core tasks in the corpus,
  and each new interaction type is screened against it before delivery.
- Bounded Context shops that add an option to one interaction type add
  it to every other type presenting that task, or file the gap with the
  product designer role.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
  types it must hold on.

### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)

**Statement.**
- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
  definition, a command line, an API or SDK — MUST be designed and
  screened as an interface: named, predictable, and documented for its
  user.
- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
  not reach through some interaction type.

**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group now
states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer synonymous with "human"
— and vendor guidance on building agents asks for as much care in the
agent-computer interface as in the human one. An interface no one
designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.

**Implications.**
- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
  tool definitions to the product designer role for ergonomic review
  before they are published.
- Bounded Context shops write tool and API documentation for the caller,
  with the same care as user-facing help.
- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against the
  corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.

### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)

**Statement.**
- A claim that an interaction is usable MUST rest on observed use — a
  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion — or be
  labeled a hypothesis.
- A preference — a stakeholder's, a maker's, the designer's own — MUST
  NOT decide a design question that observed use can answer.

**Rationale.** Design by committee, where every opinion in the room
weighs the same, produces the least-common-denominator interface; the
alternative is not one taste in charge but one decision-maker deciding
on evidence. Human-centred design as ISO 9241-210 describes it is
"driven and refined by user-centred evaluation"; GOV.UK's third design
principle is "design with data." A sketch handed over as a requirement
is the recorded failure mode in the product-management literature: the
designer is asked to polish it instead of to test it.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role records the evidence behind each design
  decision in the corpus's findings, and labels the rest hypotheses.
- The PM role treats a wireframe or sketch from any role as input to be
  tested, never as a requirement.
- Bounded Context shops run or request a usability test before an
  interaction is delivered, not after a complaint.

### Accessible by standard (`accessible-by-standard`)

**Statement.**
- Every graphical, web, and document interaction MUST meet WCAG 2.2 at
  level AA.
- Every non-web interaction — command line, terminal, voice, agent —
  MUST apply the WCAG 2.2 success criteria as WCAG2ICT describes for
  non-web software, and record which criteria do not apply and why.
- Accessibility conformance MUST be established before an interaction
  is delivered, never as a later pass.

**Rationale.** An interface that conveys meaning by colour alone, or a
terminal screen that a screen reader cannot follow, excludes the people
who depend on assistive technology and, increasingly, the agents that
read the same structure. The W3C's guidelines are the one shared
standard — WCAG 2.2 is ISO/IEC 40500 — and "accessible design is good
design" (GOV.UK) because the discipline it imposes, clear names and
predictable structure, serves every user. Retrofitting accessibility
costs more than building it and reaches fewer.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role names the accessibility target per
  interaction type in the corpus, with the WCAG2ICT applicability
  record for non-web types.
- Bounded Context shops test each interaction with assistive technology
  before delivery and attach the result.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for an interaction include its
  accessibility criteria.

### Errors guide recovery (`errors-guide-recovery`)

**Statement.**
- Every error the product shows MUST say what happened, in the user's
  language, and what the user can do next.
- An error MUST NOT expose an internal identifier or message in place
  of that explanation, though it MAY carry one alongside it.

**Rationale.** A command that fails with a stack trace, a form that
says "invalid input" without saying which field, a chat assistant that
answers a misunderstanding with silence — each leaves the person to
guess, and in a command line, where there is no interface to guide
them, the error message is the interface. The command-line guidelines
say it directly: catch errors and rewrite them for humans. Microsoft's
human-AI guidelines ask the same of agents — support efficient
correction — and Google's conversation design warns that one poorly
handled error outweighs dozens of successful turns.

**Implications.**
- Bounded Context shops write every user-facing error with its next
  step, and keep the internal detail in a log or an alongside field.
- The product designer role screens error text against the vocabulary
  and voice as part of conformance.
- The solutions architect role's contracts define error responses that
  carry a human-readable explanation, not only a code.

### Control stays with the person (`control-stays-with-the-person`)

**Statement.**
- An interaction in which the product acts on an inferred intent — a
  conversational, voice, or agent interaction — MUST make clear what it
  can do and what it is about to do before an action that is hard to
  reverse.
- Such an interaction MUST let the person correct, dismiss, or stop it
  at any point, and MUST hand control back when it fails.
- A generated interface MUST stay within the constraints the corpus
  states; it MAY vary its form within them.

**Rationale.** Intent-based interaction reverses the locus of control:
the person states an outcome and the system chooses the steps. That is
its value and its danger. An assistant that books the wrong thing
silently, or cannot be interrupted, or shows a different interface each
visit, loses the trust that makes delegation possible. Microsoft's
guidelines for human-AI interaction — make clear what the system can do,
support efficient invocation, dismissal, and correction, provide global
controls — and Shneiderman's case that high automation and high human
control are compatible, not a trade-off, both point the same way: the
system may act, and the person stays in charge.

**Implications.**
- Bounded Context shops building a conversational, voice, or agent
  interaction implement the confirm, correct, dismiss, and stop
  controls before the interaction is delivered.
- The product designer role screens such interactions against the
  human-AI guidelines named in the corpus.
- The product designer role states, in the corpus, the constraints a

Required changes, most important first.

## Mechanical check (guideline rule 2) — pass

Grep for BCP 14 capitals: the only occurrence outside a statement is the opening's keyword-definition sentence (line 48). Every other hit sits inside a **Statement** bullet.

## Findings (required changes)

### 1. `control-stays-with-the-person` — fused obligations, an undefined decision term, and an ambiguity that may conflict with `agent-is-a-user`

- Rule 7 / scenario 2 fail: bullet 2 carries two MUSTs in one bullet — "Such an interaction MUST let the person correct, dismiss, or stop it at any point, and MUST hand control back when it fails." Split it.
- Scenario 2 fail (undefined decision term): bullet 3, "A generated interface MUST stay within the constraints the corpus states", turns on "generated interface", defined nowhere — not in the statement, the opening, or the glossary (the glossary has "generated document or notification", a different thing). Define it.
- Ambiguity with a possible cross-principle conflict: bullet 1 scopes the rule to "a conversational, voice, or agent interaction". In `agent-is-a-user`, "agent" is the caller (an external agent using a tool definition or API). Here "agent interaction" appears to mean the product acting on inferred intent. If the first reading applies, an API delete called by an agent must "make clear ... what it is about to do" to "the person" — colliding with `agent-is-a-user` and any API convention. The two uses of "agent" need one definition each.
- Wobbly: "hard to reverse" and "make clear what it can do" have no test; acceptable if the corpus is named as the place defining them, as bullet 3 does for constraints.

### 2. `consistent-not-uniform` — the three bullets conflict with each other

Bullet 1: "Every interaction type MUST use the product's one vocabulary". Bullet 2: "MUST honour the conventions of the platform it lives on, over the product's own conventions where the two conflict." The vocabulary is a product convention; when a platform names an action differently (the CLI's `rm` against the GUI's "Remove"), bullets 1 and 2 give opposite answers. Bullet 3 then makes variation optional-with-record ("MAY be varied ... only with ... recorded"), whereas bullet 2 makes it mandatory. A reviewer holding one CLI against this statement cannot answer yes or no. State the precedence inside the bullets.

Also wobbly: "the conventions of the platform" names no convention set; decidability rests on the implication's "and cite them". The statement should name the authority for which conventions bind.

### 3. `core-task-parity` — circular decision term; an implication adds an escape

- Bullet 1 defines its term circularly: "the product's core tasks — the tasks a person must be able to complete wherever the product is reached." The implication reveals the real referent ("keeps the list of core tasks in the corpus"); the statement should point at that list.
- Scenario 4 fail: implication 2, "add it to every other type presenting that task, **or file the gap** with the product designer role", adds an alternative the statement forbids — bullet 2 says the option "MUST be reachable in every other interaction type". Either the statement carries the exception or the implication loses it.

### 4. Implications failing scenario 4 — and the screen row claiming they pass

- `consistent-not-uniform` implication 1: "maintains the vocabulary and voice as part of the corpus, **and every interaction type's text is screened against it**" — two implications, the second passive with no actor.
- `core-task-parity` implication 1: "keeps the list of core tasks in the corpus, **and each new interaction type is screened against it** before delivery" — same defect.
- `evidence-not-opinion` implication 3: "Bounded Context shops run or request a usability test before an interaction is delivered" — the statement permits delivering a claim "labeled a hypothesis" with no test; the implication adds a test-before-delivery obligation.
- `consistent-not-uniform` implication 2 ends "and cite them" — an obligation not in the statement (but it is what makes bullet 2 decidable; move it up, finding 2).

Scenario 5 consequence: "Implications derivable and actor-named, one per bullet: pass" is not reproducible for `consistent-not-uniform`, `core-task-parity`, `evidence-not-opinion`; "Statement testable: pass" is not reproducible for `consistent-not-uniform`, `core-task-parity`, `control-stays-with-the-person`. Repair the principles and the cells become true.

### 5. Enumerations in statements do not say whether they are closed (rule 7)

The exemplar marks its ladder "(a closed set)". Here: "a tool definition, a command line, an API or SDK" (`agent-is-a-user`); "a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion" (`evidence-not-opinion`); "command line, terminal, voice, agent" (`accessible-by-standard`); "a conversational, voice, or agent interaction" (`control-stays-with-the-person`). Each is a decision term (is a survey "observed use"? is a TUI covered?). Also, `accessible-by-standard` bullet 2 lists "agent" as a non-web interaction, but "agent" is not an interaction type in the glossary.

### 6. Rationales — unnamed or ambiguous external sources, one factual error (scenario 3)

No rationale references the product's operational history; each carries a generic failure example. But these sources are not checkable as written:

- "The command-line guidelines say it directly: catch errors and rewrite them for humans" (`errors-guide-recovery`) and "the command-line guidelines for a CLI" (`consistent-not-uniform` impl. 2). After line 30 ("the guidelines that apply it to each interaction type sit beneath it") this reads as the corpus's own unwritten CLI guideline — an internal artifact. If the external *Command Line Interface Guidelines* (clig.dev) is meant, name it.
- "vendor guidance on building agents" (`agent-is-a-user`) — no vendor, no work.
- "the recorded failure mode in the product-management literature" (`evidence-not-opinion`) — no work named.
- "The conversation-design guidance from Google and Amazon" (`core-task-parity`) — nameable; name it.
- "Nielsen Norman Group now states the shift plainly — 'user' is no longer synonymous with 'human'" — quotation without its article.
- Factual: "WCAG 2.2 is ISO/IEC 40500" — ISO/IEC 40500:2012 is WCAG 2.0. Correct or drop.

### 7. `derives-from: agent-is-a-user → actor-neutral-discipline` — real lineage, undeclared in the body

The lineage holds: `actor-neutral-discipline` says an activity gains no authority and drops no records by actor kind; `agent-is-a-user` bullet 2 ("MUST NOT expose a capability a person could not reach") is that rule at the interface, and bullet 1 is "design discipline does not lapse because the user is an agent". But the rationale never mentions it, whereas the exemplar's `local-comprehension` rationale states its lineage explicitly. A cold reader finds the frontmatter claim unexplained. Add one sentence.

Also bullet 1: "named, predictable, and documented for its user" — "predictable" is not decidable; the decision rests on "screened", which the statement leaves without a screener.

### 8. Undefined terms and stumbles, in reading order

- Line 61: "passes five tests, applied in the fitness screen" — the screen has seven rows. Polish.
- Line 98 and throughout: "Bounded Context shops" — the defined term is "BC-shop" (used by the architecture set). `use-defined-terms`.
- Line 102: "a conformance finding" — "conformance" elsewhere means design/code conformance; here, conformance to the corpus. Undefined in this sense.
- Line 153: "ergonomic review" — undefined; the statement says "screened".
- Line 180: "the corpus's findings" — the glossary's corpus contents include no findings record.
- Line 250: "generated interface" — finding 1.
- Spelling drifts between "honour"/"colour" and "labeled".
- No banned words; no metaphors used as terms.

## Permission-to-play

None fails outright. Two are closest and their screen cells justify the pass on one bullet only:

- `accessible-by-standard` bullet 1 (WCAG 2.2 AA for web) is a legal minimum in several jurisdictions — permission-to-play alone. The principle earns its place on bullets 2 (WCAG2ICT for non-web, with the record) and 3 (before delivery); the cell should say bullet 2 carries it.
- `errors-guide-recovery` bullet 1 is Nielsen's heuristic 9. Bullet 2 (no internal identifier in place of the explanation) is what rejects real work. The opposite is adoptable by an API-first shop, so scenario 6 passes.

## Conflicts between principles

- Internal: `consistent-not-uniform` bullets 1/2/3 (finding 2).
- Cross-principle, contingent on a term: `control-stays-with-the-person` bullet 1 against `agent-is-a-user` bullet 2, if "agent interaction" includes an external agent's calls (finding 1).
- `evidence-not-opinion` bullet 2 binds "a stakeholder's" preference without exception — read cold, that includes the product authority's decisions. Intended or not, say so. Cannot decide as written.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| core-task-parity | wobbly — "core tasks" circular | generic ("voice assistant that can start an order but only a screen can confirm it"); Google/Amazon unnamed | fail — impl. 1 fused/passive; impl. 2 adds "or file the gap" | pass | pass |
| agent-is-a-user | wobbly — "predictable", screener unnamed | generic ("parameters named for the implementer ... misread by the agent"); "vendor guidance" unnamed | pass ("ergonomic review" undefined) | pass | pass |
| evidence-not-opinion | pass; authority scope cannot decide | generic ("design by committee ... least-common-denominator"); "PM literature" unnamed | fail — impl. 3 adds obligation; "corpus's findings" undefined | pass | pass |
| accessible-by-standard | pass; "agent" not an interaction type | generic ("meaning by colour alone"); ISO 40500 claim wrong | pass | pass | pass on bullets 2–3 |
| errors-guide-recovery | pass | generic ("'invalid input' without saying which field"); "command-line guidelines" ambiguous | pass | pass | pass on bullet 2 |
| control-stays-with-the-person | fail — bullet 2 fused; "generated interface" undefined; "agent" ambiguous | generic ("books the wrong thing silently"); Microsoft, Shneiderman named | pass | pass | pass |

p="basis/experience-principles.md"; t=open(p).read()

Two words carry one\nsense each here: an *agent* is a software caller using the product on\nsomeone's behalf; an *assistant interaction* is one in which the\nproduct itself acts on an intent the person stated rather than on a\ncommand — conversational, voice, or an assistant acting for the person.")
body='''## The principles

### Consistent, not uniform (`consistent-not-uniform`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type MUST name the product's things and actions with
  the product's one vocabulary, as the experience guidance corpus
  records it.
- Every interaction type MUST follow, for its form and idiom, the
  platform interface guidelines the corpus names for that type.
- Where a platform guideline names an action differently from the
  vocabulary, the platform's word MUST be used in that interaction
  type and the mapping recorded in the vocabulary.
- A rule of the corpus MAY be varied for one interaction type only
  with the variation and its reason recorded in the corpus.

**Rationale.** A product reached through a command line, a web page,
and a chat window is three products when each names the same object
differently, and a foreign one when its command line ignores the
terminal's conventions to imitate its web page. People carry their
expectations from the platform they are on — Nielsen Norman Group's
usability heuristic "consistency and standards" and Jakob's law of
internet user experience — and from the last place they met the
product. The GOV.UK design principles put it as "be consistent, not
uniform": the same language and patterns wherever possible, without a
straitjacket. Words and rules are shared; form follows the platform.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role maintains the vocabulary, its per-platform
  mappings, and the named platform guidelines per interaction type in
  the corpus.
- The product designer role screens every interaction type's text
  against the vocabulary.
- BC-shops building an interaction cite the platform guideline the
  corpus names for its type.
- The product designer role records each variation with its reason; an
  unrecorded variation is a finding against the corpus.

### Core-task parity (`core-task-parity`)

**Statement.**
- Every interaction type the product offers MUST support every task on
  the corpus's core-task list.
- An option the product offers in one interaction type MUST be
  reachable in every other interaction type that presents the same
  task.

**Rationale.** A voice assistant that can start an order but only a
screen can confirm it strands the person who has no screen; a chat
interface that offers three choices only one of which the graphical
interface shows teaches people that the product hides things. Google's
conversation design guidelines and Amazon's Alexa design guide converge
on the rule: voice-first but not voice-only, every option offered in
one modality reachable in the other, the core message the same across
them. Parity of tasks and options is what lets a person move between
interaction types without relearning what the product can do.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role keeps the core-task list in the corpus.
- The product designer role screens each new interaction type against
  the list before delivery.
- BC-shops that add an option to one interaction type add it to every
  other type presenting that task.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for a task name the interaction
  types it must hold on.

### The agent is a user (`agent-is-a-user`)

**Statement.**
- Every interface an agent uses to reach the product — a tool
  definition, a command line, an API, or an SDK (a closed set) — MUST
  be designed as an interface: named for its caller, its behavior
  stated in its documentation, and screened by the product designer
  role.
- An agent-facing interface MUST NOT expose a capability a person could
  not reach through some interaction type.

**Rationale.** A tool whose parameters are named for the implementer
rather than the caller is misread by the agent calling it, and the
agent's failure is recorded as the agent's. Nielsen Norman Group's "AI
Agents as Users" states the shift plainly — "user" is no longer
synonymous with "human" — and Anthropic's guidance on building agents
asks for as much care in the agent-computer interface as in the human
one. This principle is `actor-neutral-discipline` applied at the
interface: the discipline of design does not lapse because the user is
an agent, and an agent gains no capability a person lacks. An interface
no one designed is still an interface; it is only an undesigned one.

**Implications.**
- The solutions architect role submits contracts, command lines, and
  tool definitions to the product designer role's screen before they
  are published.
- BC-shops write tool and API documentation for the caller, with the
  same care as user-facing help.
- The product designer role screens agent-facing interfaces against
  the corpus with the same patterns as human-facing ones.

### Evidence, not opinion (`evidence-not-opinion`)

**Statement.**
- A claim that an interaction is usable MUST rest on observed use — a
  user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion (a closed
  set the corpus may extend) — or be labeled a hypothesis.
- A preference — a stakeholder's, a maker's, the designer's own — MUST
  NOT decide a design question that observed use can answer; what the
  product is for is the PM role's decision, not a design question.

**Rationale.** Design by committee, where every opinion in the room
weighs the same, produces the least-common-denominator interface; the
alternative is not one taste in charge but one decision-maker deciding
on evidence. Human-centred design as ISO 9241-210 describes it is
driven and refined by user-centred evaluation; GOV.UK's third design
principle is "design with data." Nielsen Norman Group's "The
Product-Manager Archetype" names the failure the second bullet
prevents: a sketch handed over as a requirement, with the designer
asked to polish it instead of to test it.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role records the evidence behind each design
  decision in the corpus's evidence record, and labels the rest
  hypotheses.
- The PM role treats a wireframe or sketch from any role as input to be
  tested, never as a requirement.
- BC-shops label an untested interaction's usability a hypothesis when
  they deliver it.

### Accessible by standard (`accessible-by-standard`)

**Statement.**
- Every graphical, web, and document interaction MUST meet WCAG 2.2 at
  level AA.
- Every non-web interaction — command line, terminal, voice, and
  assistant interactions (a closed set) — MUST apply the WCAG 2.2
  success criteria as WCAG2ICT describes for non-web software, with a
  record of which criteria do not apply and why.
- Accessibility conformance MUST be established before an interaction
  is delivered.

**Rationale.** An interface that conveys meaning by color alone, or a
terminal screen that a screen reader cannot follow, excludes the people
who depend on assistive technology and, increasingly, the agents that
read the same structure. The W3C's guidelines are the one shared
standard — WCAG 2.2 is ISO/IEC 40500:2025 — and, as GOV.UK's sixth
design principle has it, accessible design is good design: the
discipline it imposes, clear names and predictable structure, serves
every user. Retrofitting accessibility costs more than building it and
reaches fewer.

**Implications.**
- The product designer role names the accessibility target per
  interaction type in the corpus, with the WCAG2ICT applicability
  record for non-web types.
- BC-shops test each interaction with assistive technology before
  delivery and attach the result.
- The PO role's acceptance scenarios for an interaction include its
  accessibility criteria.

### Errors guide recovery (`errors-guide-recovery`)

**Statement.**
- Every error the product shows MUST say what happened, in the user's
  language, and what the user can do next.
- An error MUST NOT expose an internal identifier or message in place
  of that explanation, though it MAY carry one alongside it.

**Rationale.** A command that fails with a stack trace, a form that
says "invalid input" without saying which field, a chat assistant that
answers a misunderstanding with silence — each leaves the person to
guess, and in a command line, where there is no interface to guide
them, the error message is the interface. The Command Line Interface
Guidelines (clig.dev) say it directly: catch errors and rewrite them
for humans. Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction ask the
same of assistants — support efficient correction — and Google's
conversation design guidelines warn that one poorly handled error
outweighs dozens of successful turns.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops write every user-facing error with its next step, and keep
  the internal detail in a log or an alongside field.
- The product designer role screens error text against the vocabulary
  and voice.
- The solutions architect role's contracts define error responses that
  carry a human-readable explanation, not only a code.

### Control stays with the person (`control-stays-with-the-person`)

**Statement.**
- An assistant interaction MUST make clear what the product can do and
  what it is about to do before an action the corpus classes as hard to
  reverse.
- An assistant interaction MUST let the person correct, dismiss, or
  stop it at any point.
- An assistant interaction MUST hand control back to the person when it
  fails.
- A generated interface MUST stay within the constraints the corpus
  states for it; it MAY vary its form within them.

**Rationale.** Intent-based interaction reverses the locus of control:
the person states an outcome and the system chooses the steps. That is
its value and its danger. An assistant that books the wrong thing
silently, or cannot be interrupted, or shows a different interface each
visit, loses the trust that makes delegation possible. Microsoft's
Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction — make clear what the system can
do, support efficient invocation, dismissal, and correction, provide
global controls — and Ben Shneiderman's *Human-Centered AI*, which
holds that high automation and high human control are compatible
rather than a trade-off, point the same way: the system may act, and
the person stays in charge.

**Implications.**
- BC-shops building an assistant interaction implement the confirm,
  correct, dismiss, and stop controls before the interaction is
  delivered.
- The product designer role screens assistant interactions against the
  human-AI guidelines named in the corpus.
- The product designer role states, in the corpus, which actions are
  hard to reverse and the constraints a generated interface varies
  within.

## Fitness screen (the intro's tests; sources: TOGAF, Spool, Rumelt, Lencioni)

| Screen | consistent-not-uniform | core-task-parity | agent-is-a-user | evidence-not-opinion | accessible-by-standard | errors-guide-recovery | control-stays-with-the-person |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Statement testable (TOGAF: understandable, complete, consistent) | pass — precedence stated between vocabulary and platform | pass — against the corpus's list | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Helps you say no (Spool) | yes: rejects a second name for one thing and a CLI that imitates a web page | yes: rejects a task or option offered on one type only | yes: rejects an undesigned tool definition and an agent-only capability | yes: rejects a preference deciding a testable question | yes: rejects color-only meaning and accessibility as a later pass | yes: rejects a bare code or stack trace as an error | yes: rejects silent action, uninterruptible assistants, and unconstrained generated interfaces |
| Not fluff, not a goal-in-disguise (Rumelt) | pass — directs without prescribing form | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Not permission-to-play (Lencioni) | pass — most multi-interface products drift into several vocabularies | pass — most voice and chat interfaces are subsets of the screen | pass — most tool definitions are named for the implementer | pass — most design questions are settled by the loudest preference | pass on bullets 2 and 3 — web AA is a legal floor in places; non-web application before delivery is rare | pass on bullet 2 — most CLI errors are stack traces | pass — most assistants act without confirming and cannot be stopped mid-action |
| Implies ≥1 practice and ≥1 check (this document's intro) | vocabulary and mappings maintained; text screened | core-task list kept; new type screened | screen before publication; agent-interface screen | evidence recorded per decision; sketches tested not adopted | target named per type; assistive-technology test before delivery | next-step in every error; error-text screen | controls implemented before delivery; human-AI guideline screen |
| Normative keywords used in statements only; capitals elsewhere only as the opening's mentions (mechanical) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| Implications derivable and actor-named, one per bullet (judged) | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass | pass |

'''

The screen caught three places where the old prompts had the agent deciding rather than preparing, now repaired: `review-conversation`'s apply step could apply a decision its own answer produced (now: offered to you as the next observation, never applied); `definition-chain-migration`'s rewrite step demoted keepers with no review behind it (now: nominates, you decide at close-out); `work-conversation`'s header said "prepares" where the prompt performs (header now matches).

**2. Experience principle set — draft v2, awaiting your `authority-approve`** (`basis/experience-principles.md`; screened clean at round 2 against the principle-set chain). Seven principles, scope `experience`:

- **`consistent-not-uniform`** — one vocabulary for the product's things and actions; each interaction type follows its platform's named guidelines for form; where the platform's word differs, the platform wins and the mapping is recorded.
- **`core-task-parity`** — every interaction type supports the corpus's core-task list; an option offered in one is reachable in every other presenting that task.
- **`agent-is-a-user`** — tool definitions, CLIs, APIs, SDKs are designed and screened as interfaces; no agent-only capability. Derives from `actor-neutral-discipline`.
- **`evidence-not-opinion`** — usability claims rest on observed use or are labeled hypotheses; no preference decides a testable design question (what the product is *for* stays yours).
- **`accessible-by-standard`** — WCAG 2.2 AA for web/GUI/documents; WCAG2ICT applied, with an applicability record, for CLI/terminal/voice/assistant; before delivery, never after.
- **`errors-guide-recovery`** — every error says what happened and what to do next; no bare code or stack trace in place of it.
- **`control-stays-with-the-person`** — assistant interactions say what they can do and what they're about to do before hard-to-reverse actions; correct/dismiss/stop always; control returns on failure; generated interfaces stay within stated constraints.

Two new glossary terms carry the set's distinctions: *assistant interaction* (the product acting on stated intent) and *generated interface*. The typedef gained the `experience` scope.

**Open after this:** the per-type guidelines beneath the set (the corpus's second layer); criteria sets for the PO artifact types; brief-030's typedef v3 and skills import plan.

=====QG
## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `quality-guideline` — the definition of well-made prose for
  an artifact type or for all prose (the base writing style is a
  quality-guideline every other one layers on and never overrides).
- **Produced by:** the owner (authority-authored styles are stored verbatim as guideline documents) or
  a definition author deriving type-specific rules. **Consumed by:**
  authors at write time (the Highlights block is the layer compiled into
  generating context); mechanical style checks and judges, which cite
  rules by number.

## Required frontmatter

`type: quality-guideline`, `id`, `owner`, `status`, `created`,
`updated`; `target-type` (the artifact type governed; absent for the
base style, which governs all prose).

## Required sections

1. **Voice principle** — one sentence naming the reader and the stance.
2. **Highlights** — the compressed layer compiled into the author's
   context.
3. **Layers** — what this guideline sits on and the precedence order when
   rules conflict (an approved principle beats the artifact type's typedef, which beats
   any guideline; the base writing style is a guideline other guidelines
   never override, and it yields to principles and typedefs like any
   guideline).
4. **Rules** — each numbered, with a before/after pair and Deming's three
   elements: a test, a criterion, a yes/no decision — plus the derived
   check it feeds (mechanical, judged, or both).

Sections 1–3 may appear as bolded labels; Rules is a heading. The base
writing style is stored verbatim, so its structure is the authority's
own and is exempt from the section requirements.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A quality guideline is done when every rule
is decidable yes/no on real text and feeds a named check — a check that
exists, or a filed work item for the tool that will run it; "tool chosen
later" with no work item fails. **Consequence on failure:** the rule is
advice, not a definition, and is removed.

## Sources

Google and Microsoft style-guide anatomy (principle → highlights → rules
with examples → precedence); Deming's operational definitions; Federal
Plain Language guidelines.

## Derived review checklist

- Highlights block present and shorter than the rules. *(§Required sections 2)*
- Precedence stated. *(§Required sections 3)*
- Every rule: before/after + test + criterion + decision + derived check.
  *(§Required sections 4)*

## Document History
=====FS
## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `fitness-set` — a small set of Given/When/Then scenarios that
  a judge scores against an artifact type's instances. Judged, never
  executed: there are no step definitions, and the schema says so where
  tools can read it.
- **Produced by:** the author of the target type's quality definition.
  **Consumed by:** the judging role named in the frontmatter, at the
  review step of the producing process and at any later re-verification.

## Required frontmatter

`type: fitness-set`, `id`, `target-type` (the artifact type judged),
`judged: true`, `executable: false`, `judged-by` (the role), `owner`,
`status`, `created`, `updated`.

## Required sections

1. **Scenarios** — Given/When/Then, each `Then` falsifiable: a competent
   judge shown a failing instance can say "fails" and point at why.
2. **Compile mapping** — a table taking every `Then`, one for one, into a
   judge-rubric assertion, proving the set rests on established
   evaluation practice and not a bespoke engine.

## Rules

- **Hard segregation from executable scenarios:** fitness sets never live
  in `features/`, and `executable: false` is schema-level, so no test
  runner can pick one up by accident.
- Judge verdicts are recorded with the judge's model and prompt version
  pinned; the owner grades a sample on a standing calibration loop.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A fitness set is done when every `Then` is falsifiable and mapped to a
rubric assertion. **Consequence on failure:** its verdicts carry no
standing in review.

Gherkin syntax (the readable G/W/T frame — syntax only, no runner);
LLM-judge practice (G-Eval–style rubric decomposition, promptfoo's
llm-rubric assertions); EvalGen-style human calibration of judges.

# Guideline: role definition

**Voice principle.** Write for the runtime that must instantiate the
role tomorrow and the reviewer who must catch it acting outside its
domain: every line either contracts a capability, names an
accountability, or claims the role's one decision — nothing narrates.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** who and
what for, never when · the capability contract enforces the stance
mechanically · exactly one exclusive domain, phrased as a decision ·
accountabilities are answerable after a run · no actor-kind commitments
unless the role is an owner's human-held role.

**Layers:** this guideline adds role-definition rules on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
beats the [role-definition typedef](../artifacts/role-definition.md),
which beats this guideline.

---

## Rules

**1. Say who and what for — never when.**
Before: "After the author finishes the draft, the reviewer reads it
and returns findings."
After: "Accountable for: reporting stumbles in reading order, with
quotes."

# Fitness set: decision-brief

These scenarios are evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never executed —
no step definitions exist or will exist. The judge's model and prompt
version are recorded with each round verdict. The mapping table at the end
compiles each Then into the judge-rubric assertion the reviewer scores.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: decidable without the annex
  Given the decision-brief and its labeled annex
  When the stakeholder reads only the brief
  Then every requested decision can be made without opening the annex

Scenario 2: the first paragraph answers
  Given the first paragraph of the brief alone
  When the reader stops there
  Then it states the answer or recommendation, not background

Scenario 3: no unintroduced terms
  Given any proper noun or coinage in the brief
  When it first appears
  Then a gloss appears with it, or the term is recorded shop or product
  vocabulary (in the glossary or the product's own documents)

Scenario 4: asks are complete and honest about gating
  Given each ask read in isolation
  When it is parsed
  Then it carries a recommendation, inline evidence, and a default
  And the ask set states which asks gate work and which resolve on silence

## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion (established format, tool chosen later) |
|---|---|
| 1 — decidable without annex | "Could a reader make every numbered decision using only this document? Cite any decision that needs outside context." |
| 2 — first paragraph answers | "Does paragraph 1 state a recommendation or answer? Quote the sentence, or answer no." |
| 3 — no unintroduced terms | "List every proper noun whose first mention lacks a gloss and is not recorded shop or product vocabulary. Empty list = pass." |
| 4 (Then) — each ask complete | "For each ask: recommendation present? evidence present? default present? Any 'no' = fail, cite the ask." |
| 4 (And) — gating stated for the set | "Does the ask set state which asks gate work and which resolve on silence? Yes/no; cite the sentence or its absence." |

  executed: there are no step definitions, and the schema says so where
  tools can read it.
- **Produced by:** the author of the target type's quality definition.
  **Consumed by:** the judging role named in the frontmatter, at the
  review step of the producing process and at any later re-verification.

## Required frontmatter

`type: fitness-set`, `id`, `target-type` (the artifact type judged),
`judged: true`, `executable: false`, `judged-by` (the role), `owner`,
`status`, `created`, `updated`.

## Required sections

1. **Scenarios** — Given/When/Then, each `Then` falsifiable: a competent
   judge shown a failing instance can say "fails" and point at why.
2. **Compile mapping** — a table taking every `Then`, one for one, into a
   judge-rubric assertion, proving the set rests on established
   evaluation practice and not a bespoke engine.

## Rules

- **Hard segregation from executable scenarios:** fitness sets never live
  in `features/`, and `executable: false` is schema-level, so no test
  runner can pick one up by accident.
- Judge verdicts are recorded with the judge's model and prompt version
  pinned; the owner grades a sample on a standing calibration loop.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A fitness set is done when every `Then` is falsifiable and mapped to a
rubric assertion. **Consequence on failure:** its verdicts carry no
standing in review.

## Sources

Gherkin syntax (the readable G/W/T frame — syntax only, no runner);
LLM-judge practice (G-Eval–style rubric decomposition, promptfoo's
llm-rubric assertions); EvalGen-style human calibration of judges.

## Derived review checklist

- Frontmatter guardrails present (`judged`, `executable`, `judged-by`).
  *(schema)*
- Not under `features/` — mechanical path check. *(§Rules)*
- Every `Then` appears in the compile-mapping table. *(§Required sections 2)*

**Voice principle.** Write for the runtime that must instantiate the
role tomorrow and the reviewer who must catch it acting outside its
domain: every line either contracts a capability, names an

# Fitness set: decision-brief

These scenarios are evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never executed —
no step definitions exist or will exist. The judge's model and prompt
version are recorded with each round verdict. The mapping table at the end
compiles each Then into the judge-rubric assertion the reviewer scores.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: decidable without the annex
  Given the decision-brief and its labeled annex
  When the stakeholder reads only the brief
  Then every requested decision can be made without opening the annex

Scenario 2: the first paragraph answers
  Given the first paragraph of the brief alone
  When the reader stops there
  Then it states the answer or recommendation, not background

Scenario 3: no unintroduced terms
  Given any proper noun or coinage in the brief
  When it first appears
  Then a gloss appears with it, or the term is recorded shop or product
  vocabulary (in the glossary or the product's own documents)

Scenario 4: asks are complete and honest about gating
  Given each ask read in isolation
  When it is parsed
  Then it carries a recommendation, inline evidence, and a default
  And the ask set states which asks gate work and which resolve on silence

## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion (established format, tool chosen later) |
|---|---|
| 1 — decidable without annex | "Could a reader make every numbered decision using only this document? Cite any decision that needs outside context." |
| 2 — first paragraph answers | "Does paragraph 1 state a recommendation or answer? Quote the sentence, or answer no." |
| 3 — no unintroduced terms | "List every proper noun whose first mention lacks a gloss and is not recorded shop or product vocabulary. Empty list = pass." |
| 4 (Then) — each ask complete | "For each ask: recommendation present? evidence present? default present? Any 'no' = fail, cite the ask." |
| 4 (And) — gating stated for the set | "Does the ask set state which asks gate work and which resolve on silence? Yes/no; cite the sentence or its absence." |

# Guideline: command-line and terminal interactions

**Voice principle.** Write the command line for the person at the
prompt who has not read the manual and the script that will run the
same command unattended: every command is guessable, every output
readable by both, and every failure a sentence that says what to do.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** humans
first, machines second — a TTY gets prose, a pipe gets data · flags
over positional arguments, and a flag for anything a prompt would ask ·
help at every level, fitting one screen · errors say what happened and
what next · one vocabulary, the terminal's idiom · a full-screen
terminal interaction keeps keyboard reach and screen-reader order.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`consistent-not-uniform`, `errors-guide-recovery`,
`accessible-by-standard`, `agent-is-a-user` — to the command-line and
full-screen terminal (TUI) interaction types, on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md) for every string the
interaction shows. Its external standard is the Command Line Interface
Guidelines (clig.dev) with the Heroku CLI style guide for output
conventions; where the two differ, clig.dev governs. When rules
conflict, an approved principle beats this guideline. The check every
rule feeds is the product designer role's conformance screen against
the corpus; the process that runs that screen is a filed work item,
named in the Document History.

---

## Rules

**1. Detect the reader: prose for a terminal, data for a pipe.**
Before: a table with box-drawing characters and colour written to
stdout whether or not stdout is a terminal.
After: the table when stdout is a TTY; one record per line, no colour,
when it is not; `--json` for a structured form on request.
*Test:* run the command with stdout as a TTY and with stdout piped.
*Criterion:* the TTY output is readable prose or a table; the piped
output is line-oriented data without escape codes; a `--json` or
`--plain` flag exists where the output has structure. *Decision:*
yes/no per command.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen, clig.dev "Output".

**2. Prefer flags; never require a prompt.**
Before: `deploy production main` — three positionals whose order the
user must remember; a confirmation prompt with no way to pre-answer.
After: `deploy --env production --ref main --yes`, with the prompt
shown only when stdin is a TTY and `--yes` absent.
*Test:* list each command's inputs and each prompt. *Criterion:* every
input beyond one primary argument is a named flag; every prompt has a
flag that supplies its answer, and no prompt is shown when stdin is not
a TTY. *Decision:* yes/no per command.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen, clig.dev "Arguments and
flags", "Interactivity".

**3. Help at every level, on one screen.**
Before: `tool --help` prints forty options in alphabetical order with
no example.
After: `tool --help` shows the purpose in one line, the three most
common commands with an example each, and where to find the rest;
`tool <command> --help` does the same for the command.
*Test:* run `--help` at the top level and for each command; count
screen lines at 80 columns. *Criterion:* purpose, examples, and the
common path fit one screen; every flag has a one-line description
beginning lowercase without a trailing period. *Decision:* yes/no per
help text.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen, clig.dev "Help".

**4. Errors say what happened, in the product's words, and what to do.**
Before: `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'cfg.yml'`
After: `No config file at ./cfg.yml. Create one with \`tool init\` or
pass --config <path>.` — the original error on stderr behind
`--verbose`.
*Test:* trigger each error path. *Criterion:* the message names the
thing in the product's vocabulary, states the cause, and gives at
least one next step; internal identifiers appear only alongside or
behind a verbosity flag; the exit code is non-zero and distinct from
success. *Decision:* yes/no per error.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

**5. Same words as every other interaction type; terminal idiom for
form.**
Before: the web interface says "Remove", the command is `delete`, the
chat assistant says "drop".
After: the vocabulary names the action once; each interaction type uses
that name unless its platform guideline names it otherwise, and the
mapping is recorded in the corpus.
*Test:* list each command's nouns and verbs against the corpus
vocabulary and its platform mappings. *Criterion:* every term is the
vocabulary's or a recorded platform mapping; subcommand shape (`noun
verb`) and flag naming follow clig.dev. *Decision:* yes/no per
command.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.

**6. A full-screen terminal interaction stays reachable.**
Before: a TUI whose only affordance for the current selection is a
colour change, and whose panes redraw in an order a screen reader
cannot follow.
After: the selection is marked by a glyph and a label as well as
colour; every action has a key shown on screen; the reading order of
panes is fixed and announced; a `--no-tui` path exists for the same
tasks.
*Test:* walk the interaction without colour and with a screen reader;
list each action's key. *Criterion:* meaning never rests on colour
alone; every action is keyboard-reachable and labeled; the same core
tasks are reachable through a non-full-screen path; the WCAG2ICT
applicability record for the interaction exists. *Decision:* yes/no
per TUI.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `accessible-by-standard`,
`core-task-parity`.

# Guideline: API, SDK, and agent tool interactions

**Voice principle.** Write the interface for the caller — a developer
reading the reference at two in the morning, or an agent reading the
tool definition with nothing else — so that the name says what it does,
the documentation says what will happen, and the error says what to do.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** names for
the caller, not the implementer · one vocabulary with every other
interaction type · behaviour stated, including what does not change ·
errors carry a human explanation beside the code · idempotent where the
caller may retry · no agent-only capability · reveal power gradually.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`agent-is-a-user`, `consistent-not-uniform`, `errors-guide-recovery`
— to the API, SDK, and agent tool-definition interaction types, on top
of the [base writing style](base-writing-style.md) for documentation
and error text. External standards: Google's API Improvement Proposals
for resource naming and standard methods; the Azure REST API guidelines
for compatibility and idempotency; Anthropic's guidance on the
agent-computer interface for tool definitions. The contract itself —
what is promised — is the solutions architect role's; this guideline
governs how the promise reads to its caller. When rules conflict, an
approved principle beats this guideline. Every rule feeds the product
designer role's conformance screen (process a filed work item).

---

## Rules

**1. Name for the caller.**
Before: a tool parameter `tgt_ctx_id` and a method `procRq2`.
After: `target_context` and `submit_request`, named with the corpus
vocabulary; the same noun the web interface and the command line use.
*Test:* read each name without its implementation. *Criterion:* a
caller can say what it is or does from the name and the vocabulary
alone; abbreviations appear only when the vocabulary records them.
*Decision:* yes/no per name.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.

**2. State the behaviour, including what it does not do.**
Before: "Updates the record."
After: "Replaces the record's mutable fields with the values given;
fields omitted are left unchanged; returns the record as stored.
Fails with `not_found` if the id is unknown."
*Test:* read each operation's documentation. *Criterion:* it states
the effect, the treatment of omitted inputs, the return, and each
failure case with its error; an agent could plan a call from it
without trial. *Decision:* yes/no per operation.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `agent-is-a-user`.

**3. Errors explain beside the code.**
Before: `{"error": "E4031"}`
After: `{"code": "quota_exceeded", "message": "The workspace has used
its 500 requests for today; the limit resets at 00:00 UTC.", "next":
"Retry after the reset or raise the limit in workspace settings."}`
*Test:* trigger each documented failure. *Criterion:* the response
carries a stable code, a human-readable explanation in the product's
vocabulary, and a next step; the code set is documented and closed.
*Decision:* yes/no per error.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

**4. Safe to retry.**
Before: a `create` call that makes a second record when the caller
times out and retries.
After: `create` accepts an idempotency key and returns the first
result on replay; every operation documents whether a retry is safe.
*Test:* replay each mutating call. *Criterion:* the second call has
no further effect, or the documentation states the operation is not
idempotent and why. *Decision:* yes/no per mutating operation.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; Azure guidelines on
idempotency.

**5. Nothing only an agent can do.**
Before: a tool `bulk_purge` with no counterpart in any interaction a
person uses.
After: the same capability offered through a person-facing interaction
type, or the tool withdrawn.
*Test:* list each agent-facing operation against the core-task list
and the person-facing interaction types. *Criterion:* every capability
is reachable by a person through some interaction type. *Decision:*
yes/no per operation.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `agent-is-a-user`.

**6. Reveal power gradually.**
Before: a first-call example that requires nine parameters.
After: a first call that works with the required ones and sensible
defaults; the reference shows the rest in order of likely need.
*Test:* follow the quick-start as a new caller. *Criterion:* a first
useful call needs only what has no sensible default; optional
parameters are documented after required ones with their defaults
stated. *Decision:* yes/no per operation.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen.

The conformance-screen process is a filed work item for the product designer role. |

# Guideline: graphical and web interactions

**Voice principle.** Design the screen for the person who arrives from
another part of the product and expects to recognise it, and for the
person using it without a mouse, without colour, or through a screen
reader.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** one
vocabulary, the platform's patterns · design tokens as the single
source of every visual decision · WCAG 2.2 AA before delivery ·
every core task reachable · errors at the field, in words · the
platform's own interface guidelines for form.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`consistent-not-uniform`, `core-task-parity`, `accessible-by-standard`,
`errors-guide-recovery` — to graphical and web interaction types, on
top of the [base writing style](base-writing-style.md) for every
string shown. External standards: WCAG 2.2 at level AA; the platform's
published interface guidelines (the web platform's own conventions, or
the operating system's human interface guidelines for a native
application); Nielsen Norman Group's usability heuristics for review.
When rules conflict, an approved principle beats this guideline. Every
rule feeds the product designer role's conformance screen (process a
filed work item).

---

## Rules

**1. Tokens, not values.**
Before: `color: #1a73e8; padding: 13px` written in a component.
After: `color: var(--action-primary); padding: var(--space-3)` from the
corpus's design tokens.
*Test:* scan the interaction's styles for literal colour, spacing, and
type values. *Criterion:* every visual decision references a token
the corpus defines; a needed value with no token is a token request,
not a literal. *Decision:* yes/no per component.
*Derived check:* mechanical — a token lint (tool a filed work item);
judged until it exists.

**2. Recognisable from the rest of the product.**
Before: a settings page whose primary action sits bottom-left while
every other page puts it top-right, labeled "Apply" where the rest say
"Save".
After: the same placement and the vocabulary's word.
*Test:* compare the interaction's labels and pattern placements with
the corpus's interaction patterns and vocabulary. *Criterion:* every
label is the vocabulary's; every pattern is the corpus's or a recorded
variation. *Decision:* yes/no per screen.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.

**3. WCAG 2.2 AA, before delivery.**
Before: a status shown by colour alone; a modal the keyboard cannot
leave; contrast at 3:1 for body text.
After: status by colour and text; focus trapped and released; 4.5:1
for text, 3:1 for large text and graphics; every control reachable and
named for assistive technology.
*Test:* run the automated accessibility check and a manual keyboard
and screen-reader walk. *Criterion:* no AA failure; the test result
is attached to the delivery. *Decision:* yes/no per screen.
*Derived check:* mechanical — automated WCAG check (tool a filed work
item); judged — the manual walk.

**4. Every core task, here too.**
Before: an export available only through the command line.
After: the export in the graphical interaction, or the core-task list
amended by the product designer role with the reason.
*Test:* walk the corpus's core-task list in the interaction.
*Criterion:* every task completes; every option offered elsewhere for
the task is present. *Decision:* yes/no per task.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `core-task-parity`.

**5. Errors at the field, in words.**
Before: a red banner "Invalid input" at the top of a long form.
After: the failing field outlined, labeled with what is wrong and what
would be right, focus moved to it.
*Test:* submit each form with each invalid input. *Criterion:* the
error appears at the field, says what is wrong in the vocabulary, and
says what to do; a form-level message summarises and links to fields.
*Decision:* yes/no per form.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

# Guideline: conversational, voice, and assistant interactions

**Voice principle.** Write the assistant for the person who states
what they want and needs to know, at every turn, what the product
understood, what it can do, what it is about to do, and how to stop
it.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** say what
you can do and how well · confirm before the hard-to-reverse · correct,
dismiss, stop — always · spoken first, then condensed for a screen ·
every option offered is reachable by voice and by touch · errors
recover the turn · one persona, the product's vocabulary.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`control-stays-with-the-person`, `core-task-parity`,
`errors-guide-recovery`, `consistent-not-uniform` — to assistant
interactions (conversational, voice, and an assistant acting for the
person), on top of the [base writing style](base-writing-style.md).
External standards: Microsoft's Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
(the eighteen, cited by number); Google's conversation design
guidelines, resting on Grice's cooperative principle; Amazon's Alexa
design guide for multimodal parity; Google's People + AI Guidebook for
errors and control. When rules conflict, an approved principle beats
this guideline. Every rule feeds the product designer role's
conformance screen (process a filed work item).

---

## Rules

**1. State capability and confidence.**
Before: an assistant that answers every request as if it could do it.
After: an opening and a help turn that say what the assistant can do;
an answer that says when it is unsure ("I found two matches; which did
you mean?").
*Test:* ask the assistant what it can do; ask it something outside its
scope; ask something ambiguous. *Criterion:* it names its capabilities;
it declines out-of-scope requests with the nearest thing it can do; it
disambiguates rather than guessing. *Decision:* yes/no per assistant.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; HAX G1, G2, G10.

**2. Confirm before the hard-to-reverse; act freely otherwise.**
Before: "Done — I've cancelled your subscription." with no prior turn.
After: "This cancels the subscription now and cannot be undone. Go
ahead?" — and for a reversible action, no such gate.
*Test:* trigger each action the corpus classes as hard to reverse, and
one it does not. *Criterion:* every hard-to-reverse action is stated
and confirmed first; reversible actions are not gated. *Decision:*
yes/no per action.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen;
`control-stays-with-the-person`; HAX G16.

**3. Correct, dismiss, stop.**
Before: an assistant that cannot be interrupted mid-task and offers no
way to undo what it just did.
After: "stop" halts the current action; "no, I meant…" re-routes; the
last action can be undone or its result edited.
*Test:* interrupt a multi-step action; correct a misunderstanding;
dismiss an unwanted suggestion. *Criterion:* each works at any turn
and the assistant confirms what it stopped or changed. *Decision:*
yes/no per assistant.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; HAX G8, G9, G17.

**4. Spoken first, condensed for the screen, parity between them.**
Before: a screen prompt with five choices and a spoken prompt that
names two.
After: the spoken prompt written first and carrying the core message;
the screen prompt condensed from it; every choice shown on screen is
speakable, and every choice spoken is tappable.
*Test:* compare each turn's spoken and displayed forms. *Criterion:*
same core message; every option reachable in both modalities; the
spoken form stands alone without the screen. *Decision:* yes/no per
turn.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `core-task-parity`;
Google "scale your design"; Alexa "be multimodal".

**5. Errors recover the turn.**
Before: "Sorry, I didn't get that." repeated three times.
After: a first repair that narrows ("Did you mean the invoice from
March or April?"), a second that offers the choices, a third that
hands off ("I'll show you the list instead.").
*Test:* give unrecognised, ambiguous, and out-of-context input.
*Criterion:* each repair turn adds information and the third hands
control back to a non-conversational path. *Decision:* yes/no per
assistant.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`;
PAIR "errors and graceful failure".

**6. One persona, the product's words.**
Before: an assistant that is chatty on one turn and clipped on the
next, and calls a "workspace" a "project".
After: a persona defined in the corpus; the vocabulary's nouns; tone
varied to the person's state within one personality.
*Test:* read a full dialogue against the corpus's persona and
vocabulary. *Criterion:* every noun is the vocabulary's; the
personality is constant while tone varies; the assistant never claims
to be a person. *Decision:* yes/no per dialogue.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`;
HAX G5.

# Guideline: generated documents and notifications

**Voice principle.** Write the document or notification the product
sends for the person who will read it away from the product, later,
possibly on a phone or through a screen reader, and who must know from
it alone what happened and what to do.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** answer
first · the product's vocabulary and voice · one action, one link ·
accessible as a document · a notification names what changed and why
the person is told · the same event reads the same everywhere.

**Layers:** this guideline applies the
[experience principles](../experience-principles.md) —
`consistent-not-uniform`, `errors-guide-recovery`,
`accessible-by-standard` — to generated documents (reports, receipts,
exports) and notifications (email, chat message, push), on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md). External standards: WCAG
2.2 AA as applied to documents; Nielsen Norman Group's tone-of-voice
dimensions for notifications. When rules conflict, an approved
principle beats this guideline. Every rule feeds the product designer
role's conformance screen (process a filed work item).

---

## Rules

**1. Answer first.**
Before: a notification that opens with the product's name and a
greeting and states the event in its fourth line.
After: the first line states what happened: "Your export is ready —
2,140 records, valid until Friday."
*Test:* read only the first line or subject. *Criterion:* it states the
event or result; nothing before it. *Decision:* yes/no per document.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen.

**2. One action, one link.**
Before: a notification with four links and no indication which to use.
After: the one next action, as one link, with the rest in a footer if
they must exist.
*Test:* count actions and links. *Criterion:* one primary action;
secondary links separated and labeled. *Decision:* yes/no per
notification.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen.

**3. The vocabulary and voice, and the same event everywhere.**
Before: an email that says "job failed" for what the interface calls a
"run" and the chat message calls a "task".
After: the vocabulary's noun in every channel; the same event carrying
the same sentence in email, chat, and the interface's own notice.
*Test:* compare the same event across every channel that carries it.
*Criterion:* the noun and the core sentence are the same; tone follows
the corpus's voice dimensions for the event's weight. *Decision:*
yes/no per event.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `consistent-not-uniform`.

**4. A failure notification says what to do.**
Before: "Run 4412 failed."
After: "Run 4412 failed while writing to the archive: the archive is
full. Free space or raise the limit, then rerun."
*Test:* trigger each failure that notifies. *Criterion:* the message
names the cause in the vocabulary and a next step; an internal
identifier appears only alongside. *Decision:* yes/no per failure.
*Derived check:* judged — conformance screen; `errors-guide-recovery`.

**5. Accessible as a document.**
Before: a PDF export of a table as an image; an email whose meaning is
in an unlabeled icon.
After: real text with headings and a tagged table; the icon's meaning
in words.
*Test:* open the document with a screen reader and without images.
*Criterion:* reading order, headings, and tables are tagged; no
meaning rests on an image or colour alone; contrast meets AA.
*Decision:* yes/no per document type.
*Derived check:* mechanical — document accessibility check (tool a
filed work item); judged until it exists.

## Document History

| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-26 | update | Authored by owner direction as the second layer of the experience guidance corpus, applying the approved experience principles to generated documents and notifications. The document accessibility check tool and the conformance-screen process are filed work items. |
EOF

# Fitness set: brief

A brief is the PO role's bounded statement of a problem and its scope
for a Bounded Context shop (the typedef is pending on this branch; the
frozen corpus on `main` is the reference). These scenarios are the
criteria set the [PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md)
screens a brief against, alongside the PM role's framing, which is
always the criterion named `framing`. They are evaluated by the
`cold-reviewer` role, never executed — no step definitions exist or
will exist. The judge's model and prompt version are recorded with each
round verdict.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: every part traces to the framing
  Given the brief and the framing it names
  When each statement of scope, problem, or constraint is read
  Then it serves the framed outcome, or is marked out of scope with a
  reason

Scenario 2: the problem, not the solution
  Given the brief's statement of what the shop is asked for
  When it is parsed for design or implementation choices
  Then it states the problem and the outcome and names no how — no
  technology, structure, or interface form the shop would otherwise
  choose

Scenario 3: scope has an edge
  Given the brief's scope
  When a competent reader imagines a neighbouring piece of work
  Then the brief says whether it is in or out, or names the rule that
  decides

Scenario 4: the shop can act from it alone
  Given the brief without its author present
  When the receiving shop reads it
  Then every term is the glossary's or defined in the brief, every
  referenced artifact is linked, and no question the shop must ask
  before starting is left open — or the open questions are listed as
  such

Scenario 5: readable in one sitting
  Given the brief alone
  When the reader stops after the first paragraph
  Then the problem and the outcome are already stated

## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
|---|---|
| 1 — traces to the framing | "For each scope, problem, or constraint statement: does it serve the framed outcome, or carry an out-of-scope mark with a reason? Cite any that does neither." |
| 2 — problem, not solution | "List every sentence that chooses a technology, structure, or interface form. Empty list = pass." |
| 3 — scope has an edge | "Name a neighbouring piece of work; does the brief say in or out, or name the deciding rule? Cite the sentence or its absence." |
| 4 — actionable alone | "List undefined terms, unlinked references, and unlisted open questions a shop must resolve before starting. Empty list = pass." |
| 5 — first paragraph | "Does paragraph 1 state the problem and the outcome? Quote it, or answer no." |

## Document History

| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-26 | update | Authored by owner direction as the criteria set the PO output check screens briefs against; the brief typedef is pending, so scenarios rest on the lead-po role's accountabilities and the framing. |
EOF

# Fitness set: product decision record

A product decision record is the PO role's record of one product-level
decision and its reasons (the typedef is pending on this branch; the
frozen corpus on `main` is the reference). These scenarios are the
criteria set the [PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md)
screens a record against, alongside the framing (criterion `framing`).
Evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never executed. The judge's
model and prompt version are recorded with each round verdict.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: one decision
  Given the record
  When its decision statement is parsed
  Then it states exactly one decision, as a sentence a reader can act
  on, and names the framing it serves

Scenario 2: the alternatives were real
  Given the record's alternatives section
  When each alternative is read
  Then at least one alternative is stated that a competent shop could
  have chosen, with the reason it was not

Scenario 3: the decider is the right role
  Given the record's statement of who decided
  When it is checked against the roles' decision rights
  Then the decision falls in the deciding role's domain — value and
  viability the PM's, scope and backlog order the PO's, the stack and
  contracts the solutions architect's, the experience corpus the
  product designer's — or the record names the escalation that settled
  it

Scenario 4: consequences are priced
  Given the record's consequences section
  When each consequence is read
  Then it names what changes, for whom, and what it costs or forecloses

Scenario 5: reversibility is stated
  Given the record
  When a reader asks how hard the decision is to reverse
  Then the record says so and, for a hard-to-reverse decision, names
  what would trigger revisiting it

## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
|---|---|
| 1 — one decision, framed | "Quote the decision sentence. Is it one decision, actionable, and does it name its framing? Any no = fail." |
| 2 — real alternatives | "Is at least one alternative stated that a competent shop could have chosen, with the reason against it? Cite it or its absence." |
| 3 — right decider | "Which role decided, and is the decision inside that role's domain per the role definitions? If not, is an escalation named? Cite." |
| 4 — consequences priced | "For each consequence: what changes, for whom, at what cost? Cite any consequence missing one." |
| 5 — reversibility | "Does the record state how hard the decision is to reverse and, if hard, what would trigger revisiting it? Cite the sentence or its absence." |
