# SQ1 notes — the product-level problem/opportunity artifact at modern companies

Gathered 2026-08-26 via WebFetch/WebSearch. Status per source: opened in full / partial / could not be opened. Quotes are verbatim as returned by the fetch tool. Nothing is summarized from memory; lines prefixed "Note:" are my reading.

## A. SVPG / Marty Cagan

### A1. Product Strategy – Overview
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-strategy-overview/ — opened in full.
- "how do we make the product vision a reality, while meeting the needs of the company as we go?"
- "product strategy helps us decide what problems to solve; product discovery helps us figure out the tactics that can actually solve the problems."
- "Choices means focus. Deciding what few things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't do."
- "insights come from analyzing the data and from learning from our customers. The insights might pertain to the dynamics of our business, our capabilities, new enabling technologies, the competitive landscape."
- "They have product teams that are more accurately feature teams, and they're slaving away, pounding out features all day, but rarely getting closer to their desired outcomes."
- "providing those teams with the strategic context necessary for them to solve the problems we need them to solve."
- "It requires four things that are not easy for most companies: choices on what's important; insights; converting insights into action; and active management."

### A2. Assessing Product Opportunities
URL: https://www.svpg.com/assessing-product-opportunities/ — opened in full.
- "The purpose of a good product opportunity assessment is either to a) prevent the company from wasting time and money on poor opportunities; or b) for those that are good opportunities, to understand what will be required to succeed."
- "I ask product managers to answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this solve? 2. For whom do we solve that problem? 3. How big is the opportunity?"
- "The hardest question to answer is usually the first, which surprises people because it sounds like the easiest."
- "Ask most product managers what problem their product is intended to solve, and you usually get a rambling list of features and capabilities, rather than the a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly the problem that's solved."
- "The purpose of the MRD is to describe the opportunity, not the solution...many companies don't really do MRD's, or if they do, they're essentially product specs that are called MRD's."
- "It is important that the results of the product opportunity assessment be presented and discussed with senior management, and that the company make a clear go or no-go decision."
Note: closest SVPG analogue to a product-level problem statement — short, per-opportunity, problem-first, ends in go/no-go, explicitly distinct from a spec.

### A3. Product vs Feature Teams
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-vs-feature-teams/ — opened in full.
- Feature teams: "they are there to _serve the business_" and are given "a prioritized list that is called the roadmap".
- Product teams: "they are _empowered_ to figure out the best way to solve the problems they've been asked to solve".
- "the product manager is explicitly responsible for ensuring _value_ and _viability_" (product teams) vs. "the _value and business viability are the responsibility of the stakeholder or executive that requested the feature_" (feature teams).
- "the _purpose_ of a product team in this sense _is to solve problems in ways our customers love, yet work for our business_".
- "These feature teams will often think they are doing product discovery, but really it's just design and maybe a little usability testing".

### A4. Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve (Jon Moore & Marty Cagan)
URL: https://www.svpg.com/changing-how-you-decide-which-problems-to-solve/ — opened in full.
- "This is not a difficult step, but simply providing your empowered product teams with problems to solve, and clear measures of success, can go a long way towards generating better solutions."
- "It is not hard to simply take your existing product roadmaps, and for each feature or project, to determine what the underlying problem to solve is."
- "A strong product vision will inspire an organization for many years (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
- "The product strategy begins by focusing on the most critical areas for business success."
- "The product strategy identifies the most critical problems to solve in the quarter, and the product leaders assign those problems to the relevant product teams."
- "We are constantly investigating the quantitative insights, mainly derived from the data that's generated; and also the qualitative insights."
Note: chain is vision (years) → strategy (focus + insights) → quarterly problems → assigned to teams; the problem, not the feature, is the unit handed to a team.

### A5. Product Vision vs. Mission
URL: https://www.svpg.com/product-vision-vs-mission/ — opened in full.
- "A good product vision keeps us focused on the customer" and "serves as the North Star for the product organization so that we have a common understanding of what we are hoping to accomplish together."
- "When each team has their own vision, it's the equivalent of everyone picking out their own star from the sky, and calling it their 'north star' and then heading in their own direction."
- "The product vision, combined with the annual company objectives, drives the product strategy."
- The vision "provides the engineering organization with enough clarity about what's coming in the next several years so they can ensure they have in place an architecture that can serve the need."

### A6. "Problems to solve, not features to build" — could not be opened
https://www.svpg.com/problems-to-solve-not-features-to-build/ (direct and via r.jina.ai) redirects to SVPG home. Not cited; A4 covers the claim.

## B. Product Talk / Teresa Torres

### B1. Opportunity Solution Trees
URL: https://www.producttalk.org/opportunity-solution-trees/ — opened in full (also /opportunity-solution-tree/, same content).
- "Opportunity solution trees are a simple way of visually representing the paths you might take to reach a desired outcome."
- "The root of the tree is your desired outcome—the business need that reflects how your team can create business value."
- "The outcome at the top of an opportunity solution tree sets the scope for discovery. It helps teams understand which opportunities are relevant and keeps them focused on the right types of solutions."
- "An opportunity is an unmet customer need, pain point, or desire."
- "A solution is a product, a service, or a feature that we offer to address an opportunity. The opportunity represents the underlying need, pain point, or desire."
- "The best way to test if an opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there more than one way to address this opportunity?'"
- "Below the solution space are assumption tests. This is how we'll evaluate which solutions will help us best create customer value."
- "One of the key benefits of using an opportunity solution tree is it helps your team externalize and visualize your thinking, so it's easier to align around what to do when."
- "An opportunity solution tree is a living document that should evolve as you learn from your discovery activities."
Note: the opportunity lives independent of any feature; several features may address one opportunity. The tree is per team outcome, not per component.

### B2. "The difference between opportunities and solutions" — could not be opened
https://www.producttalk.org/2021/05/opportunities-vs-solutions/ — 404; no standalone post found. Distinction carried by B1.

## C. Melissa Perri

### C1. What is Good Product Strategy?
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2016/07/14/what-is-good-product-strategy (via r.jina.ai) — opened in full.
- "This isn't a strategy, this is a plan. The problem is that when we treat a product strategy like a plan, it will almost always fail."
- "Product Strategy is a system of achievable goals and visions that work together to align the team around desirable outcomes for both the business and your customers."
- "The vision is your high level, ultimate view of where the company or business line is going...Think long term here, and keep it qualitative."
- "The challenge is the first Business goal you have to achieve on the way to your longer term vision...a strategic objective that helps align and focus your team."
- "The target condition helps break down the Challenge. Challenges are made up of smaller problems you need to tackle along the way...achievable, measurable metrics."
- "This is what the current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be measured and quantified before the work starts."
- "It's the Product Manager and their team's responsibility to determine the user problems and other obstacles standing in the way of achieving that Target Condition."

### C2. The Product Kata
URL: https://melissaperri.com/blog/2015/07/22/the-product-kata — opened in full (worked example).
- Vision: "Make our sellers completely self sufficient in managing their stores."
- Target condition: "Sellers call office less than twice a week".
- Obstacle: "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
- "We weren't building new features for the sellers...we wanted to learn quickly".
- "Every step you take, you also say how you will measure its progress. A step with no measurements can't tell you if you are improving."
Note: the kata records current condition → target condition → obstacle → experiment, so it carries "where we are / where next" as a measured pair.

### C3. Strategy deployment (vision → strategic intents → product initiatives → options) — secondhand only
melissaperri.com/blog/2019/11/1/strategy-deployment → 404. Search results (smartproductpeople.substack.com; medium.com/@lindadao92) report the four-layer model from *Escaping the Build Trap*. Cite only as secondhand.

## D. Basecamp — Shape Up

### D1. Principles of Shaping
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.1-chapter-02 — opened in full.
- "Work in the shaping stage is rough. Everyone can tell by looking at it that it's unfinished."
- "Despite being rough and unfinished, shaped work has been thought through. All the main elements of the solution are there."
- "Shaped work indicates what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
- "When design leaders go straight to wireframes or high-fidelity mockups, they define too much detail too early."
- "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody knows what it means."
- "We have two separate tracks: one for shaping, one for building. During any six week cycle, the teams are building work that's been previously shaped."
- "Setting the appetite and coming up with a solution requires you to be critical about the problem."

### D2. Set Boundaries
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.2-chapter-03 — opened in full.
- "You can think of the appetite as a time budget for a standard team size."
- "Appetites start with a number and end with a design. We use the appetite as a creative constraint on the design process."
- "Our default response to any idea that comes up should be: 'Interesting. Maybe some day.' In other words, a very soft 'no' that leaves all our options open."
- Reframing: from "What could we build?" to "What's really going wrong?"
- "When someone proposes something like 'redesign the Files section,' that's a grab-bag, not a project."
- "The insight wasn't 'computerize the calendar'—that's obvious. What we learned was that 'see free spaces' was the important thing."
- "The best is relative to your constraints. Without a time limit, there's always a better version."

### D3. Write the Pitch
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.5-chapter-06 — opened in full.
- Five ingredients: "Problem — The raw idea, a use case, or something we've seen that motivates us to work on this"; "Appetite — How much time we want to spend and how that constrains the solution"; "Solution — The core elements we came up with, presented in a form that's easy for people to immediately understand"; "Rabbit holes — Details about the solution worth calling out to avoid problems"; "No-gos — Anything specifically excluded from the concept: functionality or use cases we intentionally aren't covering".
- "The purpose of the pitch is to present a good potential bet. It's basically a presentation."
- "People comment on the pitch asynchronously. Not to say yes or no — that happens at the betting table — but to poke holes or contribute missing information."

### D4. Bets, Not Backlogs
URL: https://basecamp.com/shapeup/2.1-chapter-07 — opened in full.
- "Backlogs are a big weight we don't need to carry. Dozens and eventually hundreds of tasks pile up that we all know we'll never have time for."
- "Before each six-week cycle, we hold a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next cycle."
- "There's no giant list of ideas to review. There's no time spent grooming a backlog of old ideas. There are just a few well-shaped, risk-reduced options to review."
- "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle to build. If we don't, we let it go. There's nothing we need to track or hold on to."
- "Anything brought back is brought back with a context, by a person, with a purpose. Everything is relevant, timely, and of the moment."
Note: the unit is the pitch — problem + appetite + rough solution + boundaries — at product level, bet on by stakeholders. Conflict with A/B: Shape Up hands teams a shaped solution; Cagan/Torres hand teams a problem/outcome.

## E. Amazon — Working Backwards / PR-FAQ

### E1. workingbackwards.com PR/FAQ process (Bryar & Carr)
URL: https://workingbackwards.com/concepts/working-backwards-pr-faq-process/ — opened in full (homepage opened; /the-pr-faq 404).
- "Working Backwards is a systematic way to vet ideas and create new products. Its key tenet is to start by defining the customer experience, then iteratively work backwards from that point until the team achieves clarity of thought around what to build."
- "Writing a press release is a forcing function to ensure that the creator of the new product idea is focused on the customer."
- "Problem Paragraph: This is where you describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve. Make sure you write this paragraph from the customer's point of view."
- "A well-written PR defines a specific objective– a destination where there is a treasure. Think of the FAQ section as the map to that destination and a detailed description of the dragons you will need to slay along your journey."
- "A well-written internal FAQ section anticipates the most important questions that senior leaders and stakeholders in the company will ask after reading the PR."
- "The best PR/FAQs are produced through an iterative process requiring discussion, debate, and collaboration with many stakeholders."
- "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should be well understood because it is described in the FAQs. In other words, resources (people, money, fixed cost investments), a rough timeline, and other operational matters are spelled out in the document."
- "Once the PR/FAQ is finalized and approved, the Agile process can be employed to build the product. Amazon frequently used Agile in conjunction with the PR/FAQ process."

### E2. Ian McAllister, Quora (2012)
URL: https://www.quora.com/What-is-Amazons-approach-to-product-development-and-product-management (via r.jina.ai) — opened in full. (Medium repost 404.)
- "We try to work backwards from the customer, rather than starting with an idea for a product and trying to bolt customers onto it."

### F1. RICE

## H. Reforge / Ravi Mehta — Product Strategy Stack

### H1. The Product Strategy Stack

URL: https://review.firstround.com/set-non-goals-and-build-a-product-strategy-stack-lessons-for-product-leaders/ — opened in full.

## I. Linear

### I1. Linear Method — Introduction / Set the product direction
URLs: https://linear.app/method/introduction ; https://linear.app/method/product-direction — opened in full.

# Research report: the product process against modern practice — the product-level artifact, cross-context features, and the record of past, present, and next

## Executive summary

*How to read the labels.* Each finding carries a confidence: **high** —
several sources opened in full agree, at least one primary (the author,
framework, or company's own text); **medium** — one opened source, or
secondary accounts only, or several agreeing sources that are
practitioner report with no controlled comparison; **low** — recall
without a source, or a primary that could not be read. "Secondhand"
marks a quote carried by a secondary account. Confidence is about the
evidence; where a finding predicts an outcome, likelihood is stated in
its own phrase.

*How the sources' vocabulary maps to the shop.* "Product team",
"stream-aligned team", "feature team", and "component team" are all
kinds of team; our Bounded Context shops are context-owning teams
(Team Topologies' preferred mapping). "Initiative", "pitch", "PR/FAQ",
"opportunity assessment", "Intermission", and "project" are the
sources' names for a product-level, problem-first document; "project"
in Linear's sense is a feature-sized unit that can span teams. Our
*framing* is the PM role's recorded statement of a request's problem
and outcome; our *brief* is addressed to one Bounded Context shop; a
*product decision record* is our ADR-form record of one product-level
decision. SAFe is cited only as a contrast, never as a model.

1. **Every modern practice opened puts a written, product-level,
   problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** —
   Cagan's opportunity assessment ("Exactly what problem will this
   solve?"), Torres's opportunity ("an unmet customer need, pain point,
   or desire" — with "more than one way to address" it), Perri's target
   condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page
   Intermission that "never includes solutions", Figma's PRD problem
   section, Linear's initiative. Our process has no such artifact: the
   framing is per request and not persistent, and the brief is already
   addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives, but agree on where the
   decision is made.** One school hands a team a problem and an outcome
   (Cagan: "problems to solve" with "clear measures of success"; Torres;
   Perri); the other hands it a shaped solution with boundaries
   (Shape Up's pitch: problem, appetite, solution, rabbit holes,
   no-gos; Amazon's approved PR/FAQ as "a touchstone" during build).
   Both decide at product level with a recorded go/no-go — Cagan's
   "clear go or no-go decision", Basecamp's betting table, Linear's
   initiative statuses. *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain, not a list:** vision (Cagan: "3-10
   year"), strategy ("choices means focus… insights… converting
   insights into action"), then quarterly problems assigned to teams;
   the roadmap re-typed as problems, themes, or initiatives
   (Perri's problem roadmap with a KPI per problem; McCarthy's themes;
   Bastow's Now/Next/Later "organizes work by levels of confidence
   instead of fixed dates"; Linear's initiatives). Reforge/Mehta
   dissent: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that implement
   the Product Strategy" with goals beneath it. *(High for the chain;
   the dissent is one source.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — explicit
   only in Perri's measured current condition ("measured and quantified
   before the work starts"), Bastow's Now column ("the work in motion"),
   Linear's initiative status and health ("on track, at risk, or off
   track"), GitHub's lifecycle tags (preview → GA → retired), and
   Wardley's test that a map needs "position of components relative to
   some form of anchor and movement". Cagan's vision and objectives
   carry no current-state element. *(Medium — several sources, each
   one element.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies:** what
   shipped — the changelog ("a curated, chronologically ordered list of
   notable changes for each version", "for humans, not machines",
   never "commit log diffs"; Stripe keys it to contract versions with a
   breaking-change flag; GitLab makes the PM responsible for each
   feature's release note) — and why it was decided — product decision
   records ("Every decision has a context", with a "Review Trigger")
   and Productboard's "organizational product memory" ("decisions, the
   reasons behind them, customer evidence"). Only a vendor claims the
   changelog is "an institutional record of product decisions"; the
   decision-record authors say otherwise. *(High that the forms exist
   and differ; medium on their separation as a consensus.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact —
   the industry answer is an artifact above the context brief, with a
   named owner, and a count.** Evans handles cross-context work as a
   *relationship between teams* ("forge a partnership… joint
   management of integration"); the CQRS Journey holds a cross-context
   flow "in a single place, the process manager"; Tune: dashboards and
   journeys are "a composite of capabilities provided by other bounded
   contexts", and journey changes make "multiple business capability
   teams… coordinate" by design; Fowler/Narayan: "Cross-cutting
   initiatives are prioritized by the business or tech leadership.
   Initiatives don't get their own team. They are parceled out to
   pre-existing product-mode teams", with "silo-penetrating…
   solution champions" and "no more than one-third initiative work";
   Team Topologies names time-boxed interaction modes; Linear's
   project "can be shared across multiple teams". The diagnostic is
   frequency: Newman — wrong boundaries "lead to a larger number of
   cross-service changes"; Tune — "corresponding changes between one
   or more systems… serious warning signs". LeSS is the contrast (one
   product backlog, feature teams, context-owning teams as "component
   teams"). Spotify's documented failure: "did not define a common
   process for cross-team collaboration". *(High.)*
7. **The contrast, item by item — the report's judgment.** Our
   *framing* is the opportunity statement's first half (originator,
   problem, outcome) without persistence, status, or a measure. Our
   *brief* is the sources' team-level project document, but it is the
   first artifact where the sources have a product-level one above it.
   Our *product decision record* matches the decision-history half of
   finding 5. We have no vision/strategy artifact, no roadmap of any
   type, no changelog, no current-state measure, and no count of
   cross-context features. The architect's decomposition exists but
   nothing records the product-level intent it decomposes from, so a
   feature crossing contexts has no home and no owner — Spotify's gap.
8. **The proposal — composed from findings 1–7, a judgment, so no
   confidence label.** Five artifacts, two of them existing, in one
   chain:
   *(a) Product strategy* — one document, owned by `lead-pm`: the
   vision (years, qualitative), the strategic choices and what is
   declined (Mehta's non-goals; Cagan's "all the things you won't
   do"), the measures (Perri's target conditions with a measured
   current condition each). Amended by decision record.
   *(b) Initiative* — the missing product-level artifact, owned by
   `lead-pm`, one per problem worth solving: the problem and for whom
   (Cagan's first three questions), the outcome and its measure, the
   appetite (Shape Up), the no-gos, a status lifecycle (proposed →
   active → completed | cancelled — Linear's) with dated updates, the
   framing it came from, and — attached by `lead-solutions-architect`
   — the decomposition: which Bounded Contexts it touches, the
   cross-context flow named in one place (the process manager's home),
   and the relationship kind each pair uses. The PO role derives the
   per-context briefs from it; a brief cites its initiative. An
   initiative is bet on at product level with a recorded go/no-go —
   the authority's review — before any brief exists.
   *(c) Brief* — unchanged in form, now always the child of an
   initiative; a brief with no initiative is a finding.
   *(d) Roadmap* — a Now/Next/Later view of initiatives, generated
   from their statuses, not hand-drawn: Now = active initiatives (where
   we are), Next = planned, Later = proposed; the Completed and
   Cancelled columns are the recent past.
   *(e) Product changelog* — keepachangelog's form, curated by
   `lead-pm`'s assisting agent at each delivery reconciled: one entry
   per delivered change grouped Added/Changed/Deprecated/Removed/Fixed,
   each linking the initiative it served and any decision record; the
   Unreleased section is the active initiatives' expected deliveries.
   The three questions then have homes: *changed* — the changelog and
   the decision records; *now* — the roadmap's Now column and each
   initiative's status and updates, plus the strategy's current
   conditions; *next* — the strategy's choices and the roadmap's Next
   and Later. And the count of initiatives touching more than one
   context, per period, goes to the architect as the boundary-quality
   signal the sources name.
9. **What this changes in the definitions** — for the authority's
   decision: an `initiative` typedef and a `product-strategy` typedef;
   a `roadmap` and `changelog` as generated renderings (no hand
   editing); the brief typedef gains a required `initiative` link; the
   PM role gains the initiative and strategy as accountabilities; the
   architect's decomposition step attaches to the initiative; the
   `discovery-conversation` process's framing step feeds an initiative
   rather than a brief; the PO output check gains the initiative as a
   criteria source alongside the framing. Brief 031's ask 3 (the PO
   typedefs) stands, with the brief typedef amended by this decision.

## Method

Three parallel gather workers in fresh contexts: the product-level
problem artifact (SVPG five essays, Product Talk, Perri two, Shape Up
four chapters, Working Backwards and McAllister, Intercom two, Lenny's
template index and Figma's PRD, Reforge and First Round on the
strategy stack, Linear Method and docs); the record of past, present,
and next (ProdPad, SVPG two, Perri two, McCarthy secondhand, Linear
Method and docs and changelog, keepachangelog, Stripe, GitHub, and
GitLab changelogs, Charak's product decision records, Productboard
two, Metabase, Wardley); cross-context features (Evans's DDD Reference,
Fowler's bliki two, Vernon via InfoQ, the CQRS Journey on sagas,
Brandolini via two secondaries, Tune two, Plöd, Team Topologies three,
Fowler/Narayan "Products Over Projects", Newman two, LeSS two, Lee on
Spotify). Roughly 60 sources opened in full; unreadable: Perri's
strategy-deployment post (404; secondhand), Vernon's IDDD chapter
(403), Product Roadmaps Relaunched (book; notes from a talk), GitLab's
handbook process pages (navigation only), Lenny's PRD guide
(paywalled), SVPG "problems to solve" (redirect). Evidence extracted
quotes-first; an independent fresh-context verification pass followed.

## Findings

### F1 — The product-level, problem-first artifact *(high)*

- Cagan, "Assessing Product Opportunities": "I ask product managers to
  answer ten fundamental questions: 1. Exactly what problem will this
  solve? 2. For whom do we solve that problem? 3. How big is the
  opportunity?"; "a crisp, clear and compelling statement of exactly
  the problem that's solved"; "The purpose of the MRD is to describe
  the opportunity, not the solution".
- Torres, Opportunity Solution Trees: "An opportunity is an unmet
  customer need, pain point, or desire."; "The best way to test if an
  opportunity is really a solution in disguise is to ask, 'Is there
  more than one way to address this opportunity?'"; "a living document
  that should evolve as you learn".
- Perri, product strategy: "The target condition helps break down the
  Challenge… achievable, measurable metrics."; "This is what the
  current reality is compared to the Target Condition. It should be
  measured and quantified before the work starts."
- Basecamp, Shape Up: "When a project is defined in a few words, nobody
  knows what it means."; the pitch's five ingredients — "Problem…
  Appetite… Solution… Rabbit holes… No-gos"; "Shaped work indicates
  what not to do. It tells the team where to stop."
- Amazon, Working Backwards: "Problem Paragraph: This is where you
  describe the problem(s) that your product is designed to solve.";
  McAllister: "Once the project moves into development, the press
  release can be used as a touchstone; a guiding light."
- Intercom: "The Intermission is our quirky name for a project
  brief... It never includes solutions because this comes later.";
  "restricted to less than one page and must succinctly cover the
  problem we're solving"; "Everything in our roadmap is broken down by
  team objective, which is broken down into multiple projects, which in
  turn are broken down into individual releases."
- Figma's PRD (Yamashita): "Describe the problem (or opportunity)
  you're trying to solve. Why is it important to our users and our
  business?"; "Keep track of open issues / key decisions here."
- Linear docs: initiatives "express the goals and objectives an
  organization aims to achieve and to monitor progress towards those
  aims"; projects are "units of work that have a clear outcome or
  planned completion date, such as a new feature's launch" and "can be
  shared across multiple teams".

### F2 — Problem or shaped solution; the decision point *(high)*

- Cagan, "Changing How You Decide Which Problems To Solve": "simply
  providing your empowered product teams with problems to solve, and
  clear measures of success"; "The product strategy identifies the most
  critical problems to solve in the quarter, and the product leaders
  assign those problems to the relevant product teams."
- Cagan, opportunity assessment: "the company make a clear go or no-go
  decision."
- Shape Up, "Bets, Not Backlogs": "Before each six-week cycle, we hold
  a betting table where stakeholders decide what to do in the next
  cycle."; "If we decide to bet on a pitch, it goes into the next cycle
  to build. If we don't, we let it go."
- Working Backwards: "If the new idea is a go, what happens next should
  be well understood because it is described in the FAQs."
- Linear: "Communicate the current stage of the initiative using
  available statuses—Proposed, Planned, Active, Completed, or
  Canceled."

### F3 — Where it is going *(high; the dissent is one source)*

- Cagan, "The Alternative to Roadmaps": "The Product Vision: this
  describes the holistic view of what the organization as a whole is
  trying to accomplish. The Business Objectives: this describes the
  specific, prioritized business objectives for each product team.";
  "It is all about outcome rather than output."; "high-integrity
  commitments… for those situations where we need to actually commit
  to a date".
- Cagan, product vision: "A strong product vision will inspire an
  organization for many years (most are 3-10 year product visions)."
- Cagan, product strategy: "Choices means focus. Deciding what few
  things you really need to do, and therefore all the things you won't
  do."
- Perri, "Rethinking the Product Roadmap": "Instead of focusing on
  features to be developed, we focus on problems to be solved."; "We
  assign a KPI to each team which signifies if the problem has been
  solved successfully or not."
- Bastow, Now-Next-Later: "an outcome-focused product roadmap that
  organizes work by levels of confidence instead of fixed dates";
  "Link each Initiative to the OKRs it supports".
- McCarthy et al. (secondhand, talk notes): the roadmap is "A statement
  of intent and direction, not a promise of deliverables"; themes are
  "The problems / jobs to be done / needs of customers".
- Reforge/Mehta: the roadmap is "the sequence of features that
  implement the Product Strategy"; "Goals are at the bottom of the
  stack, not at the top, because goals should come from the roadmap".
  First Round: "It's important to document those concrete choices —
  not just that we've chosen to do A, but also to explicitly reinforce
  that we're *not* going to do B."

### F4 — Where it is now *(medium)*

- Perri: "It should be measured and quantified before the work
  starts."; the kata's "Sellers call office less than twice a week"
  against "We're not sure how often sellers are calling now".
- Bastow: "Now is the work in motion. These are validated Initiatives
  the team is actively working on, where the problem is well
  understood."
- Linear: "Initiative Health shows whether the latest initiative update
  indicated work was on track, at risk, or off track."
- GitHub changelog: release types "Release", "Improvement", "Retired";
  maturity "generally available" / "public preview".
- Wardley, "On being lost": map elements are "Visual representation,
  context specific, position of components relative to some form of
  anchor and movement of those components"; "Every single diagram I
  was using to determine strategy in business lacked one or more of
  those basic elements."

### F5 — How it has changed *(high that the forms exist and differ; medium on their separation)*

- keepachangelog 1.1.0: "A changelog is a file which contains a
  curated, chronologically ordered list of notable changes for each
  version of a project."; "Changelogs are for humans, not machines.";
  "Added… Changed… Deprecated… Removed… Fixed… Security"; "Using commit
  log diffs as changelogs is a bad idea: they're full of noise."; "Keep
  an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."
- Stripe changelog: named release lines with dated versions, a
  "Breaking change?" column, product grouping.
- GitLab: "For each release, the product manager is responsible for
  creating the MR and files for the feature release note."
- Linear Method: "Writing a changelog benefits both internal and
  external communication. Internally, it helps your team to track
  progress and reflect on what they have achieved."
- Charak, Product Decision Records: "Every decision has a context…";
  fields "Name, Date, Status (Open/Accepted/Rejected), Scope, Context,
  Decision, Consequences, Review Trigger"; "important for decisions to
  be revisited every so often."
- Productboard: "Organizational product memory is the shared record of
  what a product organization has learned. It captures your decisions,
  the reasons behind them, customer evidence, and competitive
  context". Metabase: "Institutional memory is a company's collective
  knowledge of what things mean, how they've changed, and who changed
  them."; "If something is in your face every day, you're more likely
  to keep it up to date."
- Quackback (vendor): the changelog creates "an institutional record of
  product decisions" — the one source conflating the two.

### F6 — Cross-context features *(high)*

- Evans, DDD Reference, Partnership: "Where development failure in
  either of two contexts would result in delivery failure for both,
  forge a partnership between the teams in charge of the two contexts.
  Institute a process for coordinated planning of development and
  joint management of integration."; Customer/Supplier: "Negotiate and
  budget tasks for downstream requirements".
- Fowler, BoundedContext: contexts "share concepts (such as products
  and customers)… Different contexts may have completely different
  models of common concepts".
- CQRS Journey, "A Saga on Sagas": "there may be some business
  processes that involve multiple aggregates, or multiple aggregates in
  multiple bounded contexts"; "the definition of the message flow is
  now located in a single place, the process manager"; "the process
  manager does not perform any business logic. It only routes
  messages".
- Tune: "The dashboard does not belong to the Review system — it's a
  composite of capabilities provided by other bounded contexts";
  "when there are changes to the user journey, multiple business
  capability teams may need to coordinate"; "constant meetings,
  corresponding changes between one or more systems, and teams
  constantly being blocked by others are serious warning signs".
- Fowler/Narayan, Products Over Projects: "For initiatives that cut
  across multiple product-mode teams, it is recommended to appoint
  silo-penetrating, priority-negotiating, dependency-managing solution
  champions"; "Cross-cutting initiatives are prioritized by the
  business or tech leadership. Initiatives don't get their own team.
  They are parceled out to pre-existing product-mode teams."; "aim for
  two-thirds roadmap work and no more than one-third initiative work."
- Team Topologies: Collaboration — "working together for a defined
  period of time to discover new things"; X-as-a-Service; Facilitation.
  Plöd: "Bounded contexts are the preferred way of identifying
  boundaries for teams in the team topology environment."
- Newman: "Getting service boundaries wrong can be expensive. It can
  lead to a larger number of cross-service changes"; a team "decided to
  merge the services back into one big application."
- LeSS: "A feature team is a long-lived, cross-functional,
  cross-component team that completes many end-to-end customer
  features"; "Product Backlog Items are not pre-assigned to the teams."
- Lee, Spotify: "Spotify did not define a common process for
  cross-team collaboration."; "Autonomy requires alignment."

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the brief as the first artifact and let the architect split
  cross-context requests ad hoc.** This is Spotify's documented gap; no
  opened source supports a per-team document as the first product
  artifact. Rejected.
- **Adopt LeSS: one product backlog, no context ownership.** It answers
  "requests against a product" directly but discards the
  context-owning shops the architecture principles and isolation rest
  on. Rejected as a whole; its single-backlog idea survives as the
  roadmap-of-initiatives.
- **Adopt Shape Up whole (pitches, betting, no backlog).** Its pitch is
  the best-formed product-level artifact found, and the appetite and
  no-gos are adopted into the initiative; its rejection of any backlog
  conflicts with the PO role's exclusive domain. Partial adoption.
- **Make the changelog the decision history (Quackback's claim).** The
  decision-record sources separate shipped from decided; conflating
  them loses the reasons. Rejected; both kept, linked.
- **Hand-drawn roadmap.** Every roadmap source warns it drifts into a
  feature list; generating it from initiative statuses keeps it true
  by construction (`single-source-of-truth`). Adopted.

## Limitations

- No controlled comparison of product processes exists; the evidence
  is practitioner texts and company practice, hence medium labels on
  consensus claims.
- Perri's strategy-deployment layers are secondhand; the Product
  Roadmaps Relaunched content is from talk notes.
- GitLab's handbook decision practices could not be read.
- The proposal's artifact names (initiative, product strategy) are the
  sources' most common; the authority may prefer the shop's own.
- What would change the judgment: a source showing that a persistent
  product-level artifact slows small teams more than ad hoc splitting
  costs them; or an authority decision that the framing itself should
  persist and carry the initiative's fields.

## Top three changes

1. **The initiative's status transitions after `planned` have no maker and no process.** Item 8(b) defines the lifecycle "proposed → planned → active → completed | cancelled" and ties only one transition to a decision: "the go/no-go is the PM role's decision, taken in a review, and it is the proposed → planned transition". Item 8(d) then builds the roadmap on the rest: "Now = active, Next = planned, Later = proposed; Completed and Cancelled are the recent past." Nothing says which role moves an initiative to `active` (dispatch to a BC? the architect's assignment?), to `completed` (presumably `reconcile-and-close`, which item 9 amends only to write the changelog entry), or to `cancelled`. So the roadmap's Now column and "where it is now" rest on transitions no process makes. Add to 8(b) the role and process for each remaining transition, and the matching lines in item 9.

2. **The initiative's owner and maker are stated inconsistently, and the PM part-writes what it checks.** Item 8(b): "made by the PO role from the PM role's framing and checked by the PM role through the PO output check". Item 9: "`initiative` typedef (new; owner product-authority; instances owned by `lead-pm`)". Owner-of-instance and maker are different roles with no line saying what "owned" means here versus "made". 3. **Two artifacts have a producer but no process in item 9.** (a) The decomposition "attached by `lead-solutions-architect`" to the initiative (8(b)) — item 9 amends the architect *role* but names no process in which the attachment happens or is checked. Disclosure first: **both loops hit their round cap** — verification ran three rounds with no retraction (attribution and quotation precision each time), and the cold read three rounds, the last finding three closure gaps in the proposal itself, which I closed in the delivered version without a further read. Both residuals are stated in Limitations.

**The answer.** Your gap is real and the industry is unanimous on its shape:

1. **Every modern practice puts a written, product-level, problem-first artifact ahead of any feature or team assignment** — Cagan's opportunity assessment, Torres's opportunity, Perri's target condition, Basecamp's pitch, Amazon's PR/FAQ, Intercom's one-page "Intermission" that "never includes solutions", Linear's initiative. Ours has none: the framing carries no status, measure, or history, and the brief is already addressed to one context. *(High.)*
2. **The sources split on what a team receives** (a problem — Cagan/Torres/Perri; or a shaped solution with boundaries — Shape Up, Amazon) **but agree the decision is made at product level with a recorded go/no-go.** *(High.)*
3. **"Where it is going" is a chain** — vision (years) → strategy (choices, insights) → quarterly problems — with the roadmap re-typed as problems/themes/initiatives, Now/Next/Later by confidence, not dates. *(High; one dissent.)*
4. **"Where it is now" is the least-recorded of the three** — only Perri's measured current condition, Bastow's Now column, Linear's status and health. *(Medium.)*
5. **"How it has changed" is two histories no source unifies** — what shipped (the changelog, keepachangelog's form) and why decided (product decision records with review triggers). *(High/medium.)*
6. **Cross-context features: no DDD source has a "feature" artifact.** The answer is an artifact *above* the context brief with a named owner, parceled to existing teams (Fowler/Narayan: "Initiatives don't get their own team… no more than one-third initiative work"); the cross-context flow named in one place (a saga); and frequency of crossing as the boundary-quality warning sign (Newman, Tune). Spotify's documented failure is exactly the undefined cross-team process. *(High.)*

**The proposal (item 8), five artifacts:** a **product strategy** (vision, choices and non-goals, measured target conditions; owner lead-pm); an **initiative** — the missing artifact: problem and for whom, outcome and measure, appetite, no-gos, lifecycle proposed → planned → active → completed | cancelled, your framing quoted as its first section, the architect's decomposition attached (contexts touched, the cross-context flow, relationship kinds); *made by the PO, checked by you, bet on by you* (go/no-go = proposed → planned); the **brief**, now always an initiative's child; a **roadmap** and a **changelog** as compiler renderings from initiative statuses and reconciled deliveries. Then *changed* = changelog + decision records; *now* = Now column + initiative status + current conditions; *next* = strategy + Next/Later. And the count of cross-context initiatives per period goes to the architect.

**Item 9** lists the definition changes one per line — two new typedefs, two fitness sets, amendments to brief, lead-pm, lead-po, the architect, and four processes. Brief 031's asks 1–2 are unaffected; ask 3 stands with the brief typedef gaining the initiative link.

message.content:
Where does our brief artifact fit? I've been a little confused on the term brief vs how we are using it in the product management lifecycle

Can we get a cold read of the entire system from a product leadership persona? Can this just be done as research? I'd like to get feedback on what we are building from a holistic perspective.

content.text:
Two answers, then the read.

**Where the brief fits — and why it's confusing.** The word carries two things. `decision-brief` is the stakeholder-presentation deliverable *to you* (brief-030, brief-031). The PO's `brief` came across from the frozen corpus on `main`, where it was the lead shop's request document to one BC shop. Same word, two levels, two readers — a `use-defined-terms` failure I carried forward rather than fixed. After yesterday's research the product lifecycle reads: **strategy** (where we're going) → **initiative** (the product-level problem, bet on) → **context brief** (the slice of an initiative one Bounded Context shop is asked to solve, with its scope edge and what it needs to start) → **acceptance scenarios** → **backlog order**. So the PO's brief is the *assignment* document — the initiative's child, per context — not where a problem is first stated. I'd rename it `context-brief` so the level is in the name; that's a one-line decision I'll carry in the read rather than make now.

**The holistic read.** Yes, as research — with one correction from our own findings: the research-prompting report established that expert *personas* don't improve accuracy, so the reader gets a **stated standard** (the product operating model as Cagan, Torres, Perri and the others define it, already gathered) rather than a costume. Three fresh-context readers over the whole basis, each with a different lens; then synthesis, verification against the basis files, and a cold read. Launching.

# Frame — system-read-2026-08

Question (verbatim): "Can we get a cold read of the entire system from a product leadership persona? Can this just be done as research? I'd like to get feedback on what we are building from a holistic perspective."

Consumer: the product authority (David), who holds lead-pm. Decision served: what to change, keep, or stop in the system as a whole — the roles, processes, principles, artifact types, and their fit — before Phase 2 (the first feature) begins.

What is read: the definition corpus on the `rebaseline` branch, working directory /home/vscode/rebaseline — basis/README.md, basis/principles.md, basis/architecture-principles.md, basis/experience-principles.md, basis/glossary.md, basis/roles/*, basis/processes/*, basis/artifacts/*, basis/guidelines/*, basis/fitness/*, basis/types/*, basis/experience/*, .claude/shop/primer.md; and the five research reports on the `research` branch (git show research:research/<id>.md), especially product-process-2026-08.md, which proposes an initiative/strategy layer not yet built. Also main:drafts/migration-plan.md for the phases.

Standard, not persona (the shop's research-prompting report found expert personas do not improve accuracy): read against the modern product operating model as the shop's own research reports document it — Cagan's product operating model (vision → strategy → discovery → delivery; empowered teams given problems not features; the four risks each owned; product teams vs feature teams), Torres's continuous discovery, Perri's strategy stack and build-trap diagnosis, Shape Up's shaping/betting, Amazon's working backwards, Team Topologies and DDD on team and context boundaries — plus the shop's own nine working principles as its stated definition of good.

Scope: the system as designed — is it a coherent product operating model; would it let a small team ship, learn, and steer; where is it over-defined or under-defined; what would a product leader arriving cold not understand; what does it get right that most startups don't; what is missing that every product org has; where do its own principles conflict with each other or with practice. Out of scope: line-level document quality (the cold-reviewer screens cover that).

Sources policy: primary = the basis files themselves, quoted by path and line; the research reports; model knowledge of the product literature is admissible only where the reports already carry the source, cited by report; nothing else is opened from the web.

Confidence scheme: high — the claim is read directly from the quoted basis text and the standard it is judged against is one the reports carry; medium — an inference from several documents, or a judgment of fit; low — a prediction about how the system will behave in use, which no run has yet shown. Confidence and likelihood stated separately.

Assumptions: the system is judged as a design, since no feature has yet run through it; Phase 2 will be its first test.

Banned words: "seat", "surface".
EOF
cat > $S/hol/plan.md <<'EOF'
Three readers, fresh contexts, same corpus, different lens; each returns notes with quotes (path + heading/line) and a numbered list of observations with a confidence per the scheme:
R1 Product operating model lens — vision/strategy/discovery/delivery; are the four risks owned; problems vs features; is the PM's accountability real; does the initiative gap (product-process report) break the model; what a Cagan/Torres/Perri reader would say is missing or wrong.
R2 Operating-model coherence lens — trace one imagined feature end to end (request → framing → [initiative] → brief → scenarios → check → assignment → BC build → reconcile → conformance → changelog): where does the chain break, which artifacts have no producer or consumer, which principles conflict (e.g. least-context vs governed-context; single-source vs renderings; define-good-up-front vs one person holding two roles), where are loops without measured feedback, what is over-defined for a one-person lead shop.
R3 Cold-arrival lens — a product leader reads the primer and README first, then whatever they link: what can they understand in an hour, what jargon blocks them, what is the system for (is that stated anywhere), how many definitions must one read to make one decision, what would they cut, what would they copy.
EOF

# R3 — Cold arrival notes (system-read-2026-08)

Reader: a product leader with no context, one hour, no web. Working directory `/home/vscode/rebaseline`. Confidence per the frame's scheme (high / medium / low); likelihood stated separately where the claim is a prediction.

## Reading order taken (16 documents, ~1 hour)

1. `.claude/shop/primer.md` (full)
2. `basis/README.md` (full)
3. `basis/principles.md` (full)
4. `basis/glossary.md` (full)
5. `basis/artifacts/definition.md` (full)
6. `basis/roles/lead-pm.md` (full)
7. `basis/processes/discovery-conversation.md` (full)
8. `basis/artifacts/brief.md` (full)
9. `basis/artifacts/decision-brief.md` (full)
10. `basis/fitness/brief.fitness.md` (full)
11. `basis/processes/po-output-check.md` (full)
12. `basis/processes/stakeholder-presentation.md` (header + flow)
13. `basis/roles/lead-po.md` (opening + accountabilities)
14. `basis/architecture-principles.md` (opening + one principle)
15. `basis/guidelines/base-writing-style.md` (first half)
16. `main:drafts/migration-plan.md` via `git show` (first 60 lines + headings) and `basis/experience/core-tasks.md` (entries table) — opened last, only because nothing earlier said what the product does.

Why this order: the primer names `basis/README.md` as the index; the README lists directories in the order principles → glossary → artifacts → types → processes → guidelines → fitness → roles; I followed that order but jumped to `roles/lead-pm.md` after the glossary because the primer says the authority "holds lead-pm" and a product leader wants to find their own job first. From lead-pm I followed its two linked processes and the PO check chain to reach one concrete decision.

## What the system is for — is it stated?

Not in the first hour's path, and not plainly anywhere I opened.

- The primer opens: "This is the `rebaseline` branch: the greenfield tree of the shopsystem-product migration" (`.claude/shop/primer.md`, opening paragraph). It says what the branch is, not what the product is or who it serves.
- The README opens: "The `basis/` tree is the shop's definition corpus. Every activity on the `rebaseline` branch operates through these definitions; nothing here is advisory." (`basis/README.md` §Basis index). Again: what the tree is, not what it is for.
- The nearest thing to a purpose statement is in the glossary: "**shop** — the entity that builds, operates, and evolves part of the product. Two types: the lead shop ... and the BC-shop" (`basis/glossary.md` line 117). "The product" is never defined.
- The only place the product's substance shows is the core-task list, found at minute ~55: every row is a task of the shop system itself — "start a run", "answer an ask", "submit output for a check", "raise a clarify" (`basis/experience/core-tasks.md` §Entries). From that I inferred the product IS the system for running AI-agent shops — a product that builds products. That inference is mine; no document says it.
- The migration plan (`main:drafts/migration-plan.md`) has no purpose heading either: headings run "How to rule", "Open rulings", "Summary", "Execution phases (RULED model — R27...)", action tables.

## What I could understand in the hour

- The governance mechanism: every document has a type, a typedef, a guideline, a fitness set, a Document History; changes go through a producing process; renderings (skills, flow diagrams) are compiled and never hand-edited. Clear by document 5.
- The maker/checker split between PM and PO and the "definition change" exit when a check finds something no criterion names (`basis/processes/po-output-check.md` §Guiding statement: "A finding the criteria cannot name is a missing criterion, and the decision that follows is a definition change, not a verdict on the maker").
- The four product risks and their owners (`basis/roles/lead-pm.md` §Knowledge and skills: "value and viability here; feasibility with the solutions architect; usability with the product designer").

## What I could not understand in the hour

- What the product does for whom (above).
- What a "BC-shop" concretely is in practice — a repo? a team? an agent? The glossary defines it structurally ("owns and produces exactly one Bounded Context", line 119) but 18 documents reference BC-shops and none I opened shows one.
- Where a *framing* lives. It is "the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`" and the criterion every check runs against, but there is no `basis/artifacts/framing.md`; `ls basis/artifacts | grep -i fram` returns nothing. The brief typedef requires `framing (link to the framing it serves)` (`basis/artifacts/brief.md` §Required frontmatter) — a link to an artifact type that has no typedef.
- How work actually reaches a BC-shop after a brief is checked: the brief says "Consumed by: the receiving Bounded Context shop" (`basis/artifacts/brief.md` §Identity and ancestry) but the dispatch step belongs to a process I did not reach, and the primer says "no dispatches" anyway.
- What `bd create` is (`basis/processes/discovery-conversation.md` step `open`, `run: bd create --title ...`) — an undefined tool.

## Terms that blocked me, and where each was finally defined

| Term | Where it first blocked me | Where defined (or not) |
|---|---|---|
| shop, lead shop, BC-shop | primer, para 1 | `glossary.md` line 117, document 4 |
| definition chain | primer §Current state ("meta-chains") | `glossary.md` line 55 — "the six linked definitions of good for one artifact type"; the six are never enumerated; I reconstructed them from the README and was still unsure at the end |
| meta-chain | primer §Current state | never defined; not in the glossary |
| cold read / cold reviewer | primer §Operating rules; principles Document History | `roles/cold-reviewer.md` exists; meaning inferred from `po-output-check.md` step `screen` ("fresh-context: true") — document 11 |
| anchor | `roles/lead-pm.md` §Accountable for | `glossary.md` line 70 — but only made sense after `discovery-conversation.md` |
| framing | `roles/lead-pm.md` opening | `glossary.md` line 141, and inline in lead-pm; no artifact type |
| screen / screen verdict | `roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment | inline in lead-pm; the `screen-review` type not opened |
| ask | `roles/lead-pm.md` | `glossary.md` line 151; inline in lead-pm |
| Bounded Context | glossary | `glossary.md` line 113, with Evans cited — good |
| keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call | glossary | defined there — but all are migration-mechanics terms a product leader does not need, sitting between the terms they do need |
| session record, work item, run, hold | discovery-conversation | glossary — but `work item` is not an entry; `bd` is nowhere |
| SCQA, BLUF | `artifacts/decision-brief.md` §Required sections | not defined; cited under Sources only |
| CEL | `po-output-check.md` frontmatter `condition-language: cel` | not defined anywhere I opened |
| pkg:shopsystem-knowledge | `discovery-conversation.md` §Data | not defined; a foreign package referenced from the "single source of truth" |

## Documents needed to make one concrete decision

Decision picked: **approve a brief** (the PM's pass/fail/definition-change verdict in the PO output check).

Minimum path from cold: primer → README → glossary → `roles/lead-pm.md` → `processes/po-output-check.md` → `fitness/brief.fitness.md` → `artifacts/brief.md` = **7 documents (~1,300 lines)** before I could say what "pass" means and what I would be looking at. Strictly, the process says the PM decides from the `screen-review` alone ("Decide from the quotes in the review", `po-output-check.md` step `decide`), so in steady state the decision needs one document (the review) plus the framing; the 7 are the cost of understanding the rules once. Reasonable for a founder, heavy for anyone joining.

To approve a *decision-brief*: primer → README → `artifacts/decision-brief.md` → `processes/stakeholder-presentation.md` = 4 documents, and the brief itself is designed to be decidable in one reading ("≤ ~400 words", `decision-brief.md` §Commitment). This is the best-designed decision path in the corpus.

## Observations

1. **The product is never named or described.** No document on the newcomer's path states what the product does or for whom; the closest are the glossary's `shop` entry and the core-task list, from which a reader infers "a system for running AI-agent shops that build a product". A product leader would ask this in the first five minutes and the corpus cannot answer. Confidence: high (searched `basis/` for "the product is", "vision", "customer" — only the architect role's "technical vision" and the architecture set's "how the product is designed" appear).

2. **The primer is a branch primer, not a system primer.** Its four sections are governing instruments, current state, operating rules, session close — migration mechanics. No sentence of the form "we are building X so that Y". Confidence: high.

3. **The README is a directory map, not an orientation.** Nine directories, one line each; no "read these three first"; no statement of the shape (roles → processes → artifacts → checks) the reader must reconstruct. Confidence: high.

4. **The mechanism is understandable in an hour; the purpose is not.** By document 5 I could explain typedef/guideline/fitness/process/Document History and the compile-never-edit rule. By document 16 I still could not say what a customer gets. Confidence: high for the first half; medium for the second.

5. **The glossary mixes three vocabularies with no grouping.** Type-system terms, governance/migration terms (keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call), and product-model terms (Bounded Context, framing, originator, intent) are interleaved in arrival order. The ~12 migration terms are noise for anyone but the migration operator. Confidence: high.

6. **"Definition chain" is central and never enumerated where it is defined.** Glossary line 55: "the six linked definitions of good for one artifact type" — the six are not listed. "Meta-chain" (primer) is not a glossary term. `types/definition-chain.md` exists but nothing on the path links to it. Confidence: high.

7. **Framing has no home.** It is the pivot of the whole product model — the PM's exclusive decision, the criterion every check runs against, a required frontmatter link in the brief typedef — and there is no framing artifact type, template, or example. A brief cannot currently satisfy its own frontmatter. Confidence: high.

8. **The lead-pm role reads like a real product role.** "outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem to solve, never a feature to build" (`roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment); four risks named and assigned; "Never decides: feasibility and the stack ... how a Bounded Context builds a behavior". The Anti-rationalization list ("'The PO knows what I meant.' → A framing is recorded or it does not exist") is the sharpest writing in the corpus. Confidence: high.

9. **Unusually strong, to a product leader:** (a) the maker/checker split with a third exit — "definition-change" — so an unnamed defect fixes the standard rather than blaming the maker; (b) the decision-brief discipline — answer first, asks with defaults, a budget, an independent cold read; (c) every loop declaring its exit (round caps, `hold-after`); (d) Document History as the only change record, with the ledger deliberately retired. Most product orgs have none of these written down. Confidence: high for the reading; medium for "unusually strong".

10. **What would make a product leader walk away:** the ratio of governance to product. In the hour I read roughly 2,000 lines about how documents are checked and zero lines describing a user, a problem, or an outcome the product serves. Nine working principles, an architecture set, an experience set, six roles, twelve processes, nineteen typedefs, nine fitness sets and eleven guidelines exist before the first feature; Document Histories show three to seven review rounds per definition. It reads as an organisation that has built a very good factory and not yet decided what to manufacture. Confidence: medium (fit judgment); likelihood Phase 2 changes this: unknown, no run yet.

11. **Processes are written as executable programs, which helps the machine and hurts the newcomer.** YAML steps, CEL conditions (`review.findings.all(f, f.criterion == "uncovered")`), `run: bd create ...`, `$ref ... from: pkg:shopsystem-knowledge/...` — none of `bd`, CEL, or `pkg:` is defined on the path. The compiled mermaid flow and the prose outcomes ("O1 ... witnessed by") are the readable part; a newcomer should be able to stop there. Confidence: high.

12. **`use-defined-terms` is honoured about the corpus and violated about its tools.** The glossary is disciplined about its own vocabulary (12 versions, stumble-driven additions) but `bd`, CEL, SCQA, BLUF, `pkg:shopsystem-knowledge`, `work item`, "meta-chain" pass through undefined. Confidence: high.

13. **Seven documents to one decision is the price of rules; one document per decision is the design.** The PO output check excludes the artifact from the decider's inputs (O2: "the artifact reaches the PM role only through the findings' quotes"). A real least-context design. Whether a PM will accept deciding on a brief they have not read is untested. Confidence: high for the design; low for use.

14. **The two "briefs" collide.** `brief` (PO → BC-shop, a problem statement) and `decision-brief` (PM → authority, a request for decisions) share a word and an ancestry (`request`) but run in opposite directions. A newcomer hearing "approve the brief" cannot tell which is meant. Confidence: high.

15. **The corpus leans on the `main` it forbids reading.** Brief typedef history v1, brief fitness intro ("the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference"), lead-po ("until they exist, the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference") all point at a branch the primer says "Never copy from ... outside an import step". The newcomer is told the answer exists and told not to look. Confidence: high.

16. **Cut:** migration-mechanics terms from the glossary (to a migration-plan appendix); the repeated "What a good principle looks like" block in each principle set (the architecture set admits it is "a rendering, not a second authority" — then render it); the `tools`/`maxTurns` agent frontmatter on roles a human holds (lead-pm: "the person holding the role is bound by the definitions, not by the tool list"). Confidence: medium.

17. **Merge:** primer and README into one two-screen orientation with the missing first paragraph — what the product is, who it serves, what the lead shop does, what phase we are in — then the directory map. Also `brief` and `request`: the brief already carries the request's sections "by equivalence" (`artifacts/brief.md` history v2). Confidence: medium.

18. **Copy into any product org:** the decision-brief typedef and stakeholder-presentation loop wholesale; the Anti-rationalization section of role definitions; the "definition-change" exit of the PO output check; the Document History table with `update | review | state` kinds. Confidence: high that they are portable; medium that they survive a team that did not write them.

19. **A newcomer cannot tell how close the system is to running.** "The shop is frozen: no dispatches"; the brief typedef is `status: draft`; core-tasks rows are all `hypothesis`; `bd` is invoked but not present. Nothing states what has ever executed end-to-end. Confidence: high; the corpus should say so itself.

20. **Prediction:** a product leader hired into this system would spend week one on the operating model and week two asking "where is the product strategy" — and would find the research branch proposes a strategy/initiative layer not yet built (per the frame; not opened here). The absence is structural, not wording. Confidence: low (prediction); likelihood: high given observations 1, 7, 10.</result>

| screen / screen verdict | `roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment | inline in lead-pm; the `screen-review` type not opened |
| ask | `roles/lead-pm.md` | `glossary.md` line 151; inline in lead-pm |
| Bounded Context | glossary | `glossary.md` line 113, with Evans cited — good |
| keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call | glossary | defined there — but all are migration-mechanics terms a product leader does not need, sitting between the terms they do need |
| session record, work item, run, hold | discovery-conversation | glossary — but `work item` is not an entry; `bd` is nowhere |
| SCQA, BLUF | `artifacts/decision-brief.md` §Required sections | not defined; cited under Sources only |
| CEL | `po-output-check.md` frontmatter `condition-language: cel` | not defined anywhere I opened |
| pkg:shopsystem-knowledge | `discovery-conversation.md` §Data | not defined; a foreign package referenced from the "single source of truth" |

## Documents needed to make one concrete decision

Decision picked: **approve a brief** (the PM's pass/fail/definition-change verdict in the PO output check).

Minimum path from cold: primer → README → glossary → `roles/lead-pm.md` → `processes/po-output-check.md` → `fitness/brief.fitness.md` → `artifacts/brief.md` = **7 documents (~1,300 lines)** before I could say what "pass" means and what I would be looking at. Strictly, the process says the PM decides from the `screen-review` alone ("Decide from the quotes in the review", `po-output-check.md` step `decide`), so in steady state the decision needs one document (the review) plus the framing; the 7 are the cost of understanding the rules once. Reasonable for a founder, heavy for anyone joining.

To approve a *decision-brief*: primer → README → `artifacts/decision-brief.md` → `processes/stakeholder-presentation.md` = 4 documents, and the brief itself is designed to be decidable in one reading ("≤ ~400 words", `decision-brief.md` §Commitment). This is the best-designed decision path in the corpus.

## Observations

1. **The product is never named or described.** No document on the newcomer's path states what the product does or for whom; the closest are the glossary's `shop` entry and the core-task list, from which a reader infers "a system for running AI-agent shops that build a product". A product leader would ask this in the first five minutes and the corpus cannot answer. Confidence: high (searched `basis/` for "the product is", "vision", "customer" — only the architect role's "technical vision" and the architecture set's "how the product is designed" appear).

2. **The primer is a branch primer, not a system primer.** Its four sections are governing instruments, current state, operating rules, session close — migration mechanics. No sentence of the form "we are building X so that Y". Confidence: high.

3. **The README is a directory map, not an orientation.** Nine directories, one line each; no "read these three first"; no statement of the shape (roles → processes → artifacts → checks) the reader must reconstruct. Confidence: high.

4. **The mechanism is understandable in an hour; the purpose is not.** By document 5 I could explain typedef/guideline/fitness/process/Document History and the compile-never-edit rule. By document 16 I still could not say what a customer gets. Confidence: high for the first half; medium for the second.

5. **The glossary mixes three vocabularies with no grouping.** Type-system terms, governance/migration terms (keeper, rewrite-forward, close-out, snapshot tag, authority-call), and product-model terms (Bounded Context, framing, originator, intent) are interleaved in arrival order. The ~12 migration terms are noise for anyone but the migration operator. Confidence: high.

6. **"Definition chain" is central and never enumerated where it is defined.** Glossary line 55: "the six linked definitions of good for one artifact type" — the six are not listed. "Meta-chain" (primer) is not a glossary term. `types/definition-chain.md` exists but nothing on the path links to it. Confidence: high.

7. **Framing has no home.** It is the pivot of the whole product model — the PM's exclusive decision, the criterion every check runs against, a required frontmatter link in the brief typedef — and there is no framing artifact type, template, or example. A brief cannot currently satisfy its own frontmatter. Confidence: high.

8. **The lead-pm role reads like a real product role.** "outcomes, not outputs — you frame a problem to solve, never a feature to build" (`roles/lead-pm.md` §Standard of judgment); four risks named and assigned; "Never decides: feasibility and the stack ... how a Bounded Context builds a behavior". The Anti-rationalization list ("'The PO knows what I meant.' → A framing is recorded or it does not exist") is the sharpest writing in the corpus. Confidence: high.

9. **Unusually strong, to a product leader:** (a) the maker/checker split with a third exit — "definition-change" — so an unnamed defect fixes the standard rather than blaming the maker; (b) the decision-brief discipline — answer first, asks with defaults, a budget, an independent cold read; (c) every loop declaring its exit (round caps, `hold-after`); (d) Document History as the only change record, with the ledger deliberately retired. Most product orgs have none of these written down. Confidence: high for the reading; medium for "unusually strong".

10. **What would make a product leader walk away:** the ratio of governance to product. In the hour I read roughly 2,000 lines about how documents are checked and zero lines describing a user, a problem, or an outcome the product serves. Nine working principles, an architecture set, an experience set, six roles, twelve processes, nineteen typedefs, nine fitness sets and eleven guidelines exist before the first feature; Document Histories show three to seven review rounds per definition. It reads as an organisation that has built a very good factory and not yet decided what to manufacture. Confidence: medium (fit judgment); likelihood Phase 2 changes this: unknown, no run yet.

11. **Processes are written as executable programs, which helps the machine and hurts the newcomer.** YAML steps, CEL conditions (`review.findings.all(f, f.criterion == "uncovered")`), `run: bd create ...`, `$ref ... from: pkg:shopsystem-knowledge/...` — none of `bd`, CEL, or `pkg:` is defined on the path. The compiled mermaid flow and the prose outcomes ("O1 ... witnessed by") are the readable part; a newcomer should be able to stop there. Confidence: high.

12. **`use-defined-terms` is honoured about the corpus and violated about its tools.** The glossary is disciplined about its own vocabulary (12 versions, stumble-driven additions) but `bd`, CEL, SCQA, BLUF, `pkg:shopsystem-knowledge`, `work item`, "meta-chain" pass through undefined. Confidence: high.

13. **Seven documents to one decision is the price of rules; one document per decision is the design.** The PO output check excludes the artifact from the decider's inputs (O2: "the artifact reaches the PM role only through the findings' quotes"). A real least-context design. Whether a PM will accept deciding on a brief they have not read is untested. Confidence: high for the design; low for use.

14. **The two "briefs" collide.** `brief` (PO → BC-shop, a problem statement) and `decision-brief` (PM → authority, a request for decisions) share a word and an ancestry (`request`) but run in opposite directions. A newcomer hearing "approve the brief" cannot tell which is meant. Confidence: high.

15. **The corpus leans on the `main` it forbids reading.** Brief typedef history v1, brief fitness intro ("the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference"), lead-po ("until they exist, the frozen corpus on `main` is the reference") all point at a branch the primer says "Never copy from ... outside an import step". The newcomer is told the answer exists and told not to look. Confidence: high.

16. **Cut:** migration-mechanics terms from the glossary (to a migration-plan appendix); the repeated "What a good principle looks like" block in each principle set (the architecture set admits it is "a rendering, not a second authority" — then render it); the `tools`/`maxTurns` agent frontmatter on roles a human holds (lead-pm: "the person holding the role is bound by the definitions, not by the tool list"). Confidence: medium.

17. **Merge:** primer and README into one two-screen orientation with the missing first paragraph — what the product is, who it serves, what the lead shop does, what phase we are in — then the directory map. Also `brief` and `request`: the brief already carries the request's sections "by equivalence" (`artifacts/brief.md` history v2). Confidence: medium.

18. **Copy into any product org:** the decision-brief typedef and stakeholder-presentation loop wholesale; the Anti-rationalization section of role definitions; the "definition-change" exit of the PO output check; the Document History table with `update | review | state` kinds. Confidence: high that they are portable; medium that they survive a team that did not write them.

19. **A newcomer cannot tell how close the system is to running.** "The shop is frozen: no dispatches"; the brief typedef is `status: draft`; core-tasks rows are all `hypothesis`; `bd` is invoked but not present. Nothing states what has ever executed end-to-end. Confidence: high; the corpus should say so itself.

20. **Prediction:** a product leader hired into this system would spend week one on the operating model and week two asking "where is the product strategy" — and would find the research branch proposes a strategy/initiative layer not yet built (per the frame; not opened here). The absence is structural, not wording. Confidence: low (prediction); likelihood: high given observations 1, 7, 10.</result>
