# Artifact type: feature

## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `feature` — a Gherkin Feature: one capability described
  from the user's or agent's point of view, with the scenarios that
  state, as requirements, what counts as done for it. A product-level
  artifact: it belongs to the initiative whose outcome it serves and
  may hold scenarios owned by several Bounded Contexts. The scenario is
  the atom; the feature is its grouping; a Bounded Context's scenario
  register is the subset of scenarios, across all features, tagged to
  it. Scenarios are executed by the owning shops; the feature as a
  document is judged by the [feature fitness set](../fitness/feature.fitness.md),
  never executed there.
- **Produced by:** the [PO role](../roles/lead-po.md), with the shops
  that own the behaviors (scope and wording from the PO; steps and edge
  cases from each owning shop; usability and accessibility criteria
  from the product designer role); checked by the
  [PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md); its scenarios
  assigned to Bounded Contexts by the solutions architect role in the
  [scenario assignment](../processes/scenario-assignment.md) process.
  **Consumed by:** the shops, each receiving the scenarios tagged to it;
  the interaction conformance check for the interaction types named;
  the changelog, when its scenarios are reconciled.

## Required frontmatter

`type: feature`, `id`, `status` (draft | checked | returned |
pending-definition | assigned — replaces `checked` when the solutions
architect role has tagged every scenario), `version`, `date`, `name`
(the Feature's name), `framing` (link to the framing it serves; the
initiative, once that type exists), `owner`, `created`, `updated`.

## Required sections

1. **Feature** — the Gherkin `Feature:` line with its name, and the
   narrative beneath it: who the capability is for, what they can do,
   and the outcome it serves, in the framing's words.
2. **Contributors** — each owning shop named as the source of the
   steps and edge cases of the scenarios it owns; where the capability
   has an interaction, the product designer role's usability acceptance
   criteria and the accessibility criteria.
3. **Interaction types** — those the capability must hold on, from the
   [core-task list](../experience/core-tasks.md), where it has an
   interaction.
4. **Scenarios** — optionally a `Background:`, then each scenario with
   a tag naming the feature, a `@bounded-context:<name>` tag once
   assigned, and a hash field; Given/When/Then with one action or event
   in the When and an outcome observable in the running system in the
   Then; no step names an implementation detail.
5. **Edges** — each failure or boundary case the framing or a shop's
   contribution names, as a scenario above or marked out of scope with
   a reason.

## Rules

- A scenario's `@bounded-context:` tag is written by the solutions
  architect role at assignment, never by the PO role; a feature's
  scenarios may carry different contexts.
- The hash is of the scenario's text; a changed text is a new
  scenario. Whether the hash matches is a mechanical check, to be filed
  as a lint.
- A scenario written without the shop that owns its behavior is not
  co-produced and fails the check.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

A feature is done when it has passed the PO output check against its
fitness set and the framing, and every scenario carries a
`@bounded-context:` tag. **Consequence on failure:** it is returned
with the criterion named and no scenario enters a register.

## Sources

Gherkin (Feature, narrative, Background, Scenario, tags); Cucumber's
guidance on the three amigos (co-production); the experience
principles `core-task-parity` and `accessible-by-standard`; the
[feature fitness set](../fitness/feature.fitness.md).

## Derived review checklist

- Feature line and narrative present, tied to the framing. *(§Required sections 1; fitness 6)*
- Each scenario one observable behavior, no how. *(§Required sections 4; fitness 1)*
- Owning shops and both designer criteria present. *(§Required sections 2; fitness 2)*
- Feature tag and hash on every scenario; bounded-context tag once assigned. *(§Required sections 4; §Rules; fitness 3)*
- Named edges covered or excluded with reason. *(§Required sections 5; fitness 4)*
- Interaction types named. *(§Required sections 3; fitness 5)*

# Guideline: feature

**Voice principle.** Write the feature for the person or agent it
serves and for the shops that will run its scenarios against the real
system: a narrative that says who and why, then scenarios that each
state one action and one observable outcome, with nothing about how.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** a Feature
line and a narrative — who, what, the outcome, in the framing's words ·
one When, one observable Then, no how · each owning shop named as the
source of its scenarios' steps and edges · usability and accessibility
criteria where there is an interaction · feature tag and hash on every
scenario; the bounded-context tag is the architect's · every named edge
covered or excluded with a reason · the interaction types named.

**Layers:** this guideline adds feature rules on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
beats the [feature typedef](../artifacts/feature.md), which beats this
guideline. Gherkin's own syntax governs the Feature, Background, and
Given/When/Then form. Every rule feeds the
[feature fitness set](../fitness/feature.fitness.md), scored in the
[PO output check](../processes/po-output-check.md).

---

## Rules

**1. A narrative that says who and why.**
Before: "Feature: Run list" with scenarios beneath and no narrative.
After: "Feature: Failed runs visible in the run list / An operator
checking last night's runs / can see which failed without opening each
/ so that a failed run is noticed within one glance (the framing's
outcome)."
*Test:* read the Feature line and the lines beneath it. *Criterion:*
they name who the capability is for, what they can do, and the outcome
it serves, and the outcome is the framing's. *Decision:* yes/no per
feature.
*Derived check:* judged — feature fitness scenario 6.

**2. One action, one observable outcome, no implementation.**
Before: "When the user clicks the red button and the API returns 200,
Then the database row is updated."
After: "When the operator lists runs, Then each failed run is marked as
failed in the list."
*Test:* for each scenario, count the actions in the When and check the
Then against what a person or agent could observe from outside the
system. *Criterion:* one action or event; an outcome observable in the
running system; no step names a component, call, storage, or
algorithm. *Decision:* yes/no per scenario.
*Derived check:* judged — feature fitness scenario 1.

**3. Name who wrote what, per owning shop.**
Before: a feature with no contributors section.
After: "Contributors: the reporting shop supplied the steps and edge
cases for the list scenarios; the export shop for the CSV scenarios;
the product designer role supplied the usability criterion (marked
within one glance) and the accessibility criterion (failure not by
color alone)."
*Test:* read the Contributors section. *Criterion:* each shop that owns
a behavior is named as the source of its scenarios' steps and edges;
where the capability has an interaction, both designer criteria are
present. *Decision:* yes/no per feature.
*Derived check:* judged — feature fitness scenario 2.

**4. Tag and hash every scenario; leave the bounded-context tag to
assignment.**
Before: a scenario with a title only; or a scenario the PO role tagged
`@bounded-context:reporting` before the architect assigned it.
After: `@failed-runs-visible` and `hash: 3f9a…` above the scenario; the
`@bounded-context:` tag absent until assignment writes it.
*Test:* read each scenario's header. *Criterion:* a feature tag and a
hash field are present; no `@bounded-context:` tag was written by the
PO role. *Decision:* yes/no per scenario.
*Derived check:* judged — feature fitness scenario 3.

**5. Cover the named edges or exclude them with a reason.**

# Process: Scenario assignment

**Purpose:** Turn a checked feature into work the Bounded Context shops
can take up: the solutions architect role tags each scenario with the
context that owns its behavior, records the feature as assigned, and
sends each shop the scenarios tagged to it — the scenarios, never a
document of the shop's own.

**Guiding statement:** The decomposition decides, not the wording.
Which context owns a behavior is read from the decomposition and the
contexts' contracts; a scenario no context can own is the architect's
finding, not a guess.

**Outcomes:**
- O1. Every scenario in the feature carries exactly one
  `@bounded-context:` tag, or the feature is returned with the
  scenarios no context owns named — witnessed by `assign`'s output and
  `route`.
- O2. Each shop receives its scenarios by the message type the
  pre-state selects — witnessed by `dispatch`'s `run`.
- O3. The feature's status becomes `assigned` and the assignment is
  recorded in its Document History — witnessed by `record`.
- O4. A question the decomposition cannot answer — whether a behavior
  is in scope at all — leaves the run as an ask to the PM role with a
  default — witnessed by `assign`'s `asks` and the `ask` value.

**Roles:** assigner —
[`../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md`](../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md)
(decides which context owns each scenario; its exclusive decision on
the decomposition). the [PM role](../roles/lead-pm.md) — answers asks.
Bounded Context shops — receive their scenarios; not a role of this
process.

**Carried by:**
[`../skills/scenario-assignment/SKILL.md`](../skills/scenario-assignment/SKILL.md)
— generated from this definition by
[`../tools/compile_process.py`](../tools/compile_process.py), never
edited by hand.

## Data

Each entry names a process-local value. Simple types use JSON Schema
names inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined type with
an explicit source. Conditions are CEL expressions over these names.
`decomposition` is the path of the solutions architect's structural

## Steps

```yaml
start: assign
parameters: [feature, decomposition]
result: feature
steps:
  - id: assign
    name: Tag each scenario with its owning context
    run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent}
    inputs: [feature, decomposition, ask]
    outputs: [feature, unowned, contexts]
    asks: [lead-pm]
    prompt: |
      Read the decomposition and the feature. For each scenario, decide
      which Bounded Context owns the behavior it states — from the
      decomposition and the contexts' contracts, never from the
      scenario's wording alone — and write a single
      @bounded-context:<name> tag on it. A scenario whose behavior no
      context owns, or that two contexts would each have to own, goes
      to unowned with the reason; do not guess. List every context
      tagged in contexts. If deciding needs what the decomposition
      cannot say — whether a behavior is meant to be in the product at
      all — return an ask to lead-pm (kind: scope) with the question,
      the default you will apply, and a checkpoint of the tags written
      so far; on the first pass ask is absent, and if it carries an
      answer or resolved defaulted, act on it. Return the tagged
      feature.
    next: route

  - id: route
    name: Route on ownership
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [unowned]
    branches:
      - label: "success exit: every scenario owned"
        when: size(unowned) == 0
        next: dispatch
      - else: return

  - id: return
    name: Return the feature with the unowned scenarios named
    run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent}
    inputs: [feature, unowned]
    outputs: [feature]
    prompt: |
      Write a review entry into the feature's Document History naming
      each unowned scenario and its reason, set the feature's status to
      "returned", and return it to the PO role — the decomposition may
      need a change, which is this role's to raise as a decision
      record, or the scenario may need a split, which is the PO role's.
    next: end

  - id: dispatch
    name: Send each shop its scenarios
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [feature, contexts]
    run: |
      for ctx in ${contexts}; do
        shop-msg send --bc "$ctx" --type assign_scenarios \
          --feature ${feature} --tag "@bounded-context:$ctx"
      done
    next: record

  - id: record
    name: Record the assignment
    run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent}
    inputs: [feature, contexts]
    outputs: [feature]
    prompt: |
      Set the feature's status to "assigned" and write a state entry
      into its Document History listing the contexts each scenario was
      tagged to and the message sent to each. Return the feature.
    next: end

# Cold screen — feature chain, round 1

Material: `basis/artifacts/feature.md` (v4), `basis/fitness/feature.fitness.md` (v4), `basis/guidelines/feature.md` (v3). Read once, in that order, after the role, the three typedefs, the base style, the glossary v14, the two lead roles, and the PO output check process.

## 1. `basis/artifacts/feature.md` — verdict: **findings**

The instance's file form is unstated, and the required sections are not Gherkin-legal — an author cannot write an instance and a validator cannot check one.** (Commitment: "a validator can check any instance from it alone and an author can write a conforming instance".) The artifact-typedef rule says "A section is a markdown heading", and §Required sections lists five headings: Feature, Contributors, Interaction types, Scenarios, Edges. §Sources says "Gherkin (Feature, narrative, Background, Scenario, tags)". Gherkin has no headings, no "Contributors" or "Edges" block, and no "hash field" — free text is legal only under `Feature:`/`Scenario:` lines, and a bare `hash: 3f9a…` line above a Scenario (the guideline's rule 4 After) is a parse error. So either the instance is a markdown document with an embedded Gherkin block that shops extract, or it is a `.feature` file and the non-Gherkin sections and the hash must be carried as tags or comments. The typedef says neither. Quote: "each scenario with a tag naming the feature, a `@bounded-context:<name>` tag once assigned, and a hash field". *Required:* state the instance form (recommend: markdown with YAML frontmatter; §4 Scenarios holds one fenced Gherkin block that is the executable unit shops receive), and state where the hash lives in Gherkin-legal form (a tag such as `@hash:3f9a…`, or a `#` comment line) so the lint the Rules promise can find it.

**F2. Who "owns a behavior" before assignment is not stated, so §2 Contributors and the co-production Rule cannot be decided against the later tag.** §2 requires "each owning shop named as the source of the steps and edge cases"; §Rules says "A scenario written without the shop that owns its behavior is not co-produced and fails the check"; but the same Rules say ownership is written by the architect "at assignment, never by the PO role" — after the check. The lead-po role resolves this (the decomposition is admissible evidence "for where a scenario lands"; the architect "supplies context ownership" during co-production), but the typedef does not, and it does not say what happens when the tag the architect writes names a context other than the Contributors' shop. *Required:* one sentence in §2 or §Rules: the owning shop named in Contributors is the one the solutions architect's decomposition places the behavior in; at assignment the tag confirms or corrects it, and a corrected assignment returns the scenario for co-production with the newly named shop (or whatever the owner decides).

**F3. The named edges have no required home, so §5 and fitness 4 have nothing to read.** §5 covers "each failure or boundary case the framing or a shop's contribution names", and the guideline's rule 5 test reads cases "the Contributors section names" — but §2 only requires each shop to be "named as the source of the steps and edge cases", not that the edge cases be listed. A judge can find the framing's edges; the shops' edges exist only if a scenario or an exclusion already mentions them, which makes the check circular. *Required:* §2 (or §5) requires the list: the failure and boundary cases each contributing shop and the framing named, each pointing at its scenario or its out-of-scope reason.

**F4. Status transitions are incomplete.** "`status` (draft | checked | returned | pending-definition | assigned — replaces `checked` when the solutions architect role has tagged every scenario)". Stated: checked → assigned. Not stated: what follows `returned` and `pending-definition` (back to draft? resubmitted as is?), and which process writes `assigned` (the linked scenario-assignment process, presumably — say so, since the PO output check declares its values "this process's until the artifact typedefs define their own" and this typedef now owns them). *Required:* the full transition list with the writer of each value.

**F5. Undefined frontmatter field `date`.** "`version`, `date`, `name`" sits beside `created`/`updated`; nothing says what `date` is. *Required:* define it or remove it. (Also: the artifact-typedef says every instance carries the identity base including `approved` when applicable — state that `approved` does not apply to a feature, since its terminal state is `assigned`.)

The solutions architect role's assignment of a checked feature's
scenarios: for each Bounded Context tagged, the vehicle chosen from

schema:

for ctx in ${assignment.entries[].context}; do
  vehicle=$1; shift

The vehicle is the role's posture ("pre-state determines the vehicle") and sits under the scenario-register-loop accountability. # Cold-read screen: scenario-assignment process (v4) and its skill — round 3 (final)

**Verdict: clean.** All six fitness scenarios pass. All three round-2 required changes were made, and every round-2 stumble was addressed. Right-sized for one reading; nothing to defer. Three stumbles remain, none a fail; polish in place if wanted.

## Round-2 changes confirmed

## The `dispatch` run under the typedef as now written

`${assignment.entries[].vehicle}` and `${assignment.entries[].context}` each yield one shell word per entry in entry order (v5 rule, field path admitted by v6). `set --` loads the vehicles as positionals; the `for` walks the contexts; `$1; shift` pairs them positionally — the form the typedef names. `${feature}` is a scalar. The template's only stdout is what `shop-msg send` prints, so `sent` is that stdout line-split (v6 rule). Every reference (`assignment`, `feature`) is a declared input; `sent` the declared output. A reader can say from the run alone that the `--type` of each message is that entry's vehicle. **O2's witness is true.**

Process prompt: "A scenario whose behavior no context owns, that two contexts would each have to own, or whose owning context differs from the shop named as its source in Contributors, goes to unowned with the reason; do not guess." Feature typedef Rules: "a scenario whose owning context differs from its Contributors' shop is treated as unowned with that reason, so the feature returns (`returned`) for co-production with the newly named shop." The `return` step sets `returned` and names each unowned scenario with its reason. Consistent; the feature's status writers ("a feature the assignment process returns goes to `returned`") match. # Artifact type: initiative

## Identity and ancestry

- **Type:** `initiative` — the product-level problem artifact: one
  problem worth solving, stated for the product, not for any Bounded
  Context, with the outcome it serves and how that outcome will be
  measured, the appetite the product will spend on it, what it will
  not do, and — once the solutions architect has decomposed it — which
  Bounded Contexts it touches. It is the home of the framing: the PM
  role's recorded statement of what a request is about is the
  initiative's first section, not a separate record. Features cite it;
  a feature with no initiative is a finding. The initiative is one page
  by design, so the framing check is real and there is no second
  document to keep in step.
- **Produced by:** the [PM role](../roles/lead-pm.md), from a discovery
  conversation — the role's assisting agent drafts, the PM decides its
  content; screened by the cold reviewer against the
  [initiative fitness set](../fitness/initiative.fitness.md), which is
  the check of record since the authority holds the PM role in person;
  bet on by the authority in a review (the proposed → planned
  transition). The solutions architect role attaches the decomposition
  and its feasibility verdict; the product designer role attaches its
  usability evidence where the problem has an interaction.
  **Consumed by:** the PO role, which makes features from it; the
  solutions architect role; the roadmap and changelog renderings the
  research report `product-process-2026-08` on the `research` branch
  proposes; the PO output check, as a criteria source beside the
  framing it carries.

## Required frontmatter

`type: initiative`, `id`, `status`, `version`, `name`, `owner`
(`lead-pm`), `created`, `updated`. `approved` does not apply; the
lifecycle below stands in. Status values and their writers: `proposed`
(the PM role, on drafting — the framed-but-unbet state; a request
declined at this stage becomes `cancelled`, so the record of what was
declined survives); `planned` (the authority's go/no-go in a review,
replacing `proposed`); `active` (the PO output check's record step, on
the first feature derived from it passing); `completed` (the
`reconcile-and-close` process, when the last delivery under it is
reconciled and the measure is recorded against its target);
`cancelled` (the PM role's decision in a review, with the reason
recorded, from any state).

## Required sections

1. **Framing** — the originator (who expressed the intent, in their own
   words, quoted), the problem taken to be worth solving, the outcome
   it serves, and the contract — product or operational — it entered
   through. The PM role's exclusive decision.
2. **For whom** — who has the problem and how the product will know
   the outcome was reached: one measure with its current condition and
   its target.
3. **Appetite** — how much the product will spend on it — time, or
   capacity — as a bound the features stay within; and the no-gos: what
   this initiative will not do, each with its reason.
4. **Feasibility and usability** — the solutions architect role's
   feasibility verdict with its reasons, and, where the problem has an
   interaction, the product designer role's usability evidence or the
   hypothesis it stands on; each attached before the go/no-go or
   marked "not yet" with the ask that requests it.
5. **Decomposition** — attached by the solutions architect role: the
   Bounded Contexts the initiative touches, the relationship kind of
   each contract between them it relies on, and the cross-context flow
   in one place — the saga or process manager that will carry it, or
   "none" when the contexts need no flow between them. "Not yet" until
   attached.
6. **Features** — the features made from it, by id, as they are made;
   empty until the first.

## Rules

- The framing is written here and nowhere else; a check that names the
  framing as a criterion reads this section.
- An initiative names no solution and no interface form; naming the
  interaction types the outcome must hold on is a what.
- An initiative touching more than one Bounded Context is counted, per
  period, as the boundary signal the solutions architect role reads.
- A decision the initiative records — the go/no-go, a cancellation —
  is carried by a product decision record linked from the Document
  History.

## Commitment (Definition of Done)

An initiative is done — able to be bet on — when it has passed the
cold reviewer's screen against its fitness set, its feasibility
verdict is attached, and its measure has a current condition and a
target. **Consequence on failure:** it stays `proposed` with the
criterion named; no feature is made from it.

## Sources

Cagan's product opportunity assessment (the problem, for whom, how
big); Torres's opportunity as distinct from any solution; Perri's
target condition with a measured current condition; Basecamp's pitch
(appetite, no-gos); Linear's initiative statuses (proposed → planned →
active → completed | cancelled); the CQRS Journey's process manager and
saga for the cross-context flow; all as the research report
`product-process-2026-08` carries them; the shop's `define-good-up-front`
principle for the check of record.

## Derived review checklist

- Framing carries originator quoted, problem, outcome, contract. *(§Required sections 1; fitness 1)*
- One measure with current condition and target. *(§Required sections 2; fitness 2)*
- Appetite bounded; every no-go reasoned. *(§Required sections 3; fitness 3)*
- No solution or interface form named. *(§Rules; fitness 4)*
- Feasibility and usability attached or asked. *(§Required sections 4; fitness 5)*
- Decomposition attached or "not yet"; cross-context flow named or "none". *(§Required sections 5; fitness 6)*
- One page. *(§Identity; fitness 7)*

## Document History

| Version | Date | Kind | Entry |

| 1 | 2026-08-28 | update | Authored by owner direction as the product-level artifact the brief's retirement left missing — the system-read report's 13(a): the framing absorbed as its first section, made by the PM role, screened by the cold reviewer as the check of record, bet by the authority; lifecycle from Linear, appetite and no-gos from Shape Up, the measured condition from Perri, the decomposition from the product-process report. |

# Fitness set: initiative

An initiative is the product-level problem artifact the PM role makes:
the framing, the measure, the appetite and no-gos, the feasibility and
usability attachments, and the decomposition. These scenarios are the
check of record on it — the cold reviewer's screen — since the
authority holds the PM role in person and no other role checks the
PM's framing. Evaluated by the `cold-reviewer` role, never executed.
The judge reads only the criteria set and the initiative; every fact a
scenario judges is one the initiative must carry. The judge's model
and prompt version are recorded with each round verdict.

## Scenarios

Scenario 1: the framing is complete and in the originator's words
  Given the Framing section
  When it is read
  Then it quotes the originator's own expression, states the problem
  taken to be worth solving and the outcome it serves, and names the
  contract the intent entered through

Scenario 2: the outcome has a measure, a current condition, and a target
  Given the For whom section
  When it is read
  Then it names who has the problem and one measure with its current
  condition, quantified, and its target

Scenario 3: appetite bounded, no-gos reasoned
  Given the Appetite section
  When it is read
  Then it states a bound in time or capacity, and every no-go carries
  its reason

Scenario 4: the problem, not the solution
  Given every section
  When they are parsed for design or implementation choices
  Then no technology, structure, or interface form is named; an
  interaction type named is a what

Scenario 5: feasibility and usability attached or asked
  Given the Feasibility and usability section
  When it is read
  Then the solutions architect's verdict is present with reasons, and,
  where the problem has an interaction, the designer's evidence or
  hypothesis is present — or each absent one is marked "not yet" with
  the ask that requests it

Scenario 6: decomposition attached or not yet
  Given the Decomposition section
  When it is read
  Then it names the Bounded Contexts touched, each relied-on
  contract's relationship kind, and the cross-context flow or "none"
  — or it is marked "not yet"

Scenario 7: one page
  Given the initiative alone
  When it is read in one sitting
  Then it fits one page — about five hundred words outside the
  Document History — and a reader can say what the bet is from the
  first two sections

## Compile mapping (each Then → one judge-rubric assertion)

| Scenario Then | Judge-rubric assertion |
|---|---|
| 1 — framing complete | "Is the originator quoted? Are problem, outcome, and contract each stated? Cite any missing." |
| 2 — measured outcome | "Who has the problem? Quote the one measure, its quantified current condition, and its target; any absent = fail." |
| 3 — appetite and no-gos | "Is a bound in time or capacity stated? For each no-go, is a reason given? Cite any without." |
| 4 — no solution | "List every sentence that names a technology, structure, or interface form (an interaction type is not a form). Empty list = pass." |
| 5 — attachments | "Feasibility verdict present with reasons, or 'not yet' with an ask? Usability evidence or hypothesis present where there is an interaction, or 'not yet' with an ask? Cite." |
| 6 — decomposition | "Contexts, relationship kinds, and flow-or-none present, or 'not yet'? Cite." |
| 7 — one page | "Word count outside the Document History; can the bet be stated from the Framing and For whom sections alone? Cite." |

## Document History

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2026-08-28 | update | Authored with the initiative typedef as the check of record on the PM role's framing; one scenario per required section plus the no-solution and one-page rules. |

id: initiative-guideline
target-type: initiative
owner: product-authority

# Guideline: initiative

**Voice principle.** Write the initiative for the authority who must
bet on it in one reading and for the PO role who must make features
from it with no one to ask: the problem in the originator's words, one
measure, a bound, what it will not do — and nothing about how.

**Highlights (the layer compiled into generating context):** the
originator quoted, the problem and outcome stated, the contract named
· one measure, its current condition quantified, its target · an
appetite in time or capacity; every no-go with a reason · no
technology, structure, or form · feasibility and usability attached or
asked · contexts, relationship kinds, and the cross-context flow, or
"not yet" · one page.

**Layers:** this guideline adds initiative rules on top of the
[base writing style](base-writing-style.md); the base always applies
and is never overridden. When rules conflict, an approved principle
beats the [initiative typedef](../artifacts/initiative.md), which beats
this guideline. Every rule feeds the
[initiative fitness set](../fitness/initiative.fitness.md), scored by
the cold reviewer as the check of record.

---

## Rules

**1. Quote the originator; state the problem, the outcome, the contract.**
Before: "Operators have asked for better visibility into failures."
After: "Originator (operator, 2026-08-20, through the operations
contract): 'I open every run to find the one that failed.' Problem:
failed runs are not distinguishable from the run list. Outcome: a
failed run is noticed within one glance."
*Test:* read the Framing section. *Criterion:* the originator's words
are quoted; the problem, the outcome, and the contract are each one
statement. *Decision:* yes/no per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 1.

**2. One measure, a current condition, a target.**
Before: "Success: operators are happier with the run list."
After: "Measure: time from a run's failure to an operator noticing it.
Now: median 40 minutes (sampled 2026-08 from the run log). Target:
under one minute."
*Test:* read the For whom section. *Criterion:* exactly one measure,
its current condition quantified with its source, its target stated.
*Decision:* yes/no per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 2.

**3. Bound the appetite; reason every no-go.**
Before: "We'll do what it takes; notifications are out of scope."
After: "Appetite: two weeks of the reporting shop. No-gos: notifying
on failure — a separate initiative (alerting) serves it; historical
failure analysis — no originator has asked."
*Test:* read the Appetite section. *Criterion:* a bound in time or
capacity is stated; every no-go carries its reason. *Decision:* yes/no
per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 3.

**4. No solution.**
Before: "Add a status column backed by the failures table and a `--failed`
flag."
After: "The outcome holds on the command line and the graphical
interaction; how a failure becomes visible is the shops'."
*Test:* list every sentence naming a technology, structure, or
interface form. *Criterion:* the list is empty; an interaction type
named is a what. *Decision:* yes/no per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 4.

**5. Attach feasibility and usability, or ask.**
Before: silence on feasibility.
After: "Feasibility (architect, 2026-08-21): feasible within the
current stack; the run log already records failure. Usability: not yet
— ask to the product designer role, default 'a hypothesis stands until
the first user test'."
*Test:* read the Feasibility and usability section. *Criterion:* the
verdict with reasons is present, and the usability evidence or
hypothesis where there is an interaction — or each absent one is
marked "not yet" with the ask that requests it. *Decision:* yes/no per
initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 5.

**6. Name the contexts and the flow, or "not yet".**
Before: "Touches reporting and maybe export."
After: "Decomposition (architect): reporting, export; contract
reporting → export: customer–supplier; cross-context flow: none — each
context reads the run log directly." or "Decomposition: not yet."
*Test:* read the Decomposition section. *Criterion:* contexts,
relationship kinds, and the flow or "none" are stated, or the section
says "not yet". *Decision:* yes/no per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 6.

**7. One page.**
Before: a twelve-section document with a history of the reporting
area.
After: six sections, about five hundred words, the bet readable from
the first two.
*Test:* count words outside the Document History; read the first two
sections alone. *Criterion:* about five hundred words or fewer; the
bet is statable from the Framing and For whom sections. *Decision:*
yes/no per initiative.
*Derived check:* judged — initiative fitness scenario 7.

# Cold-read screen — initiative chain, round 1

Material: `basis/artifacts/initiative.md` v1, `basis/fitness/initiative.fitness.md` v1, `basis/guidelines/initiative.md` v1. Context read as instructed; note the PM role file on disk is lead-pm **v9** (the brief named v8) — v9's only change is the initiative accountability, and it is what I judged against. Banned words "seat"/"surface": none in any of the three (grep).

## Verdicts

| File | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `basis/artifacts/initiative.md` | **findings** (6 required changes) |
| `basis/fitness/initiative.fitness.md` | **findings** (3 required changes) |
| `basis/guidelines/initiative.md` | **findings** (2 required changes) |

Cross-cutting first, since three of the findings repeat across files.

## On the check of record and `define-good-up-front`

The principle's letter is met: the definition of good (the fitness set) is stated up front, it drives both the writing (guideline highlights) and the check, and the check sits with the cold reviewer — a different role with a different accountability (the round's verdict) from the PM who makes and the authority who bets. The feasibility attachment adds a second independent role on the one risk it covers.

Two things stop it from being a check in fact rather than in name:

1. **No process carries the screen.** The typedef says "screened by the cold reviewer"; the fitness set says "the judge's model and prompt version are recorded with each round verdict"; the commitment says done "when it has passed the cold reviewer's screen." No process is named that invokes the reviewer on an initiative, applies the "stays `proposed` with the criterion named" consequence, records the round, or declares an exit. `po-output-check` does not fit — its maker is `lead-po`, its `framing` input is the initiative's own first section, and the initiative is not among its inputs. Under `no-orphan-activities` the check of record is presently an orphan activity. Required: name the carrying process, existing or pending, in the typedef's Produced-by — for example an `initiative-check` process mirroring `po-output-check` with maker `lead-pm` (agent-assisted), screener `cold-reviewer`, decider the authority.
2. **What the check covers should be said plainly.** The fitness set checks the initiative's completeness and form — originator quoted, one measure, bound, no solution, attachments. It does not and cannot check whether the problem is worth solving; the same person frames and bets, and the typedef's "check of record since the authority holds the PM role in person" reads as if that gap were closed. It is not, by design. State that the value judgment stands unchecked and rests on the recorded originator words and the measure — then the principle is satisfied for what the definition of good actually defines, and no reader takes the screen for more than it is.

## `basis/artifacts/initiative.md` — findings

**1. Status lifecycle: three of five transitions have no carrying process, and one names a process that does not do what is claimed.** (§Required frontmatter)

- `proposed` — "the PM role, on drafting." The discovery-conversation process (linked from lead-pm) is the evident writer; the typedef names no process and does not link it.
- `planned` — "the authority's go/no-go in a review." No process named. The Rules say the go/no-go "is carried by a product decision record linked from the Document History" — see finding 3.
- `active` — "the PO output check's record step, on the first feature derived from it passing." The `po-output-check` v4 record step writes the **feature's** status (`checked`/`returned`/`pending-definition`); the initiative is not among its inputs or outputs, so it cannot write `active`. Either amend that process (and say the amendment is pending) or move the writer.
- `completed` — "the `reconcile-and-close` process." Exists (the architect role links it); not linked here, and whether it records "the measure against its target" I could not verify from the allowed reads.
- `cancelled` — "the PM role's decision in a review … from any state." No process named. "From any state" includes `completed`; bound it to the non-terminal states.

Required: for each value, name the process (path) that writes it, or mark it "pending — process not yet authored"; link the ones that exist.

**2. The Commitment and section 4 disagree on whether feasibility may be "not yet".** (§Required sections 4, §Commitment)

Section 4: "each attached before the go/no-go or marked 'not yet' with the ask that requests it" — feasibility included. Commitment: done "when … its feasibility verdict is attached." Fitness 5 and guideline rule 5 follow section 4 and pass a feasibility "not yet". So an initiative can screen clean and still not be done, with no criterion named — contradicting the consequence clause "stays `proposed` with the criterion named." Required: split the two — feasibility must be present (fitness 5 fails on "not yet"); usability may be "not yet" with its ask. Also drop "before the go/no-go" — sequencing belongs to the carrying process.

**3. "Product decision record" is undefined and its writer conflicts with `po-output-check`.** (§Rules, last bullet)

"A decision the initiative records — the go/no-go, a cancellation — is carried by a product decision record linked from the Document History." The term is in no glossary and no typedef. Where it appears (`po-output-check` use-when, lead-pm Accountable) it is **PO output checked by the PM** — so this rule has the authority's bet carried in an artifact the PO makes and the PM checks. Required: either define the record and its writer, or drop the bullet and let the Document History state entry carry the decision with its reasons, as the primer's decision practice already does.

**4. Scenario-4 scope and the one-page bound have no home in the typedef.** (§Rules, §Derived review checklist)

- "One page" is stated in Identity as prose; the number (~500 words) lives only in fitness 7 and guideline rule 7 — two downstream homes, none authoritative (`single-source-of-truth`). The checklist cites "§Identity; fitness 7", citing prose, not a rule. Required: a Rule — "at most N words outside the Document History" — with fitness and guideline referring to it.
- The no-solution rule ("names no solution and no interface form") applies to "an initiative", but sections 4 and 5 by definition name the stack, contexts, and "the saga or process manager." State the rule's scope: sections 1–3.

**5. The boundary-signal rule names no consumer and undefined terms.** (§Rules, third bullet)

"An initiative touching more than one Bounded Context is counted, per period, as the boundary signal the solutions architect role reads." "Boundary signal" and "per period" are defined nowhere; the architect role v6 carries no such accountability; no resulting action is named (`feedback-loops-with-consumers`). Required: define the signal, the period, the consumer accountability, and the action — or file it as a gap and remove the rule.

**6. Insider references and undefined terms a cold reader trips on.** (§Identity, §Required sections)

- "the roadmap and changelog renderings the research report `product-process-2026-08` on the `research` branch proposes" — a consumer that does not exist, described by an insider reference. Base style: explain in one plain sentence or cut. Cut from Consumed-by; the Sources section already cites the report.
- "a feature with no initiative is a finding" — of which check? Name it or cut.
- "check of record", "bet"/"bet on", "go/no-go", "saga", "process manager" arrive undefined. The first two are important terms (a reader must know them to check the work): define "check of record" and "bet" once — glossary or inline at first use.
- "`ancestry: [initiative]`" — the artifact-typedef form says ancestry runs "from the generic root"; the feature typedef states why it names none. Say the same here or add the root.
- "Contract — product or operational" here versus the glossary v15 `framing` entry (originator, problem, outcome — no contract). Not this file's defect, but the two now disagree; reconcile.

Clean: Required sections order and headings; Sources present; no pinned example links; every checklist entry cites a clause.

## `basis/fitness/initiative.fitness.md` — findings

**1. Scenario 4 fails every initiative with an attached decomposition or feasibility verdict.** "Given every section … Then no technology, structure, or interface form is named." Section 5 names Bounded Contexts, relationship kinds, and a saga or process manager; a feasibility verdict with reasons names the stack. Required: Given "the Framing, For whom, and Appetite sections" (matching typedef finding 4). Rubric row 4 follows.

**2. Scenario 5 is not falsifiable from the initiative alone.** "Where the problem has an interaction" is a fact the initiative is not required to carry — no section states whether it has an interaction (the feature typedef has an Interaction types section for exactly this reason). The judge must infer it, breaking the preamble's own rule "every fact a scenario judges is one the initiative must carry." Required: either the typedef adds "interaction types the outcome must hold on, or 'none' with the reason" (section 2 or 4) and scenario 5 reads it, or scenario 5 requires usability present-or-"not yet" unconditionally. And per typedef finding 2, feasibility "not yet" must fail here.

**3. The carrying process is unnamed.** "The judge's model and prompt version are recorded with each round verdict" — by nothing that exists. Required: name the process (existing or pending) in the preamble, and drop the third restatement of the check-of-record rationale (typedef Identity, typedef Produced-by, this preamble, guideline Layers all carry it — one home).

Otherwise: Thens 1, 2, 3, 6 falsifiable from the criteria and the initiative; scenario 7 decidable ("about five hundred words" — the rubric row should carry the number, which after typedef finding 4 it takes from the typedef); compile mapping one for one, 7 rows for 7 Thens; frontmatter guardrails present; not under `features/`.

## `basis/guidelines/initiative.md` — findings

**1. Rule 2 is stricter than scenario 2.** Criterion: "its current condition quantified **with its source**." Scenario 2 and rubric 2 ask for the quantified condition only. Either the source goes into scenario 2 (and the typedef's section 2) or leaves the criterion. Rule 1 has the same drift in miniature: "each one statement" against scenario 1's "states" — decide which and align.

**2. Rule 5 and rule 7 criteria do not match their scenarios once the typedef is repaired.** Rule 5 admits feasibility "not yet" (typedef finding 2). Rule 7's "about five hundred words or fewer" is two bounds in one phrase; take the number from the typedef's rule.

Stumbles, polish in place: rule 1 After says "through the operations contract" — the defined term is *operational contract*; rule 5 Before "silence on feasibility" is not text — quote an empty or evasive section so the pair is a before/after on real prose. Examples are generic (a failed-run/operator domain, no real initiative) and stay one domain across all seven rules — good.

Clean: voice principle one sentence; Highlights present and shorter than the rules; Layers state precedence; all seven rules carry before/after, test, criterion, yes/no decision, and a named judged check.

## Consistency with lead-pm v9 and the feature typedef

- lead-pm v9 Accountable ("the initiative … the rest drafted by the assisting agent and decided here; screened by the cold reviewer as the check of record") and Never-decides (feasibility, usability) match the typedef's Produced-by and sections 4–5. Consistent.
- Feature v7 `initiative` frontmatter link ("its framing is that document's first section") and initiative §6 Features (by id) are a consistent two-way reference. One seam to note: the feature's commitment checks "against its fitness set and the framing" through `po-output-check`, whose `framing` input is a URI reference — it now must point at a section of the initiative, and the typedef also calls the initiative "a criteria source beside the framing" for that check, which the process's Data does not admit (criteria set = fitness set or guideline). Say which it is.

## Overload

Typedef 923 words, fitness 616, guideline 751 — each readable in one sitting; the typedef's Identity bullet is the one dense passage (a 90-word sentence) and would read better as three.

## Summary of required changes, most important first

1. Name the process that carries the cold reviewer's screen on an initiative, existing or pending (typedef, fitness).
2. Give every status transition a named writer process, existing or pending; fix `active` (po-output-check does not write it); bound `cancelled` to non-terminal states (typedef).
3. Make feasibility mandatory for done and let only usability be "not yet"; align fitness 5 and rule 5 (all three).
4. Scope the no-solution rule to sections 1–3; fix scenario 4 and rubric 4 (typedef, fitness).
5. Make "has an interaction" a fact the initiative carries, or make scenario 5 unconditional (typedef, fitness).
6. Define or drop "product decision record" as the go/no-go's vehicle; resolve the writer conflict with po-output-check (typedef).
7. Put the one-page bound in a typedef Rule; downstream refer to it (all three).
8. Define or remove the boundary-signal rule with its consumer and action (typedef).
9. Align rule 2 (source) and rule 1 (one statement) with their scenarios (guideline).
10. Cut the research-report consumer; define "check of record" and "bet"; reconcile the glossary `framing` entry's missing contract.</result>

content.text:
Brief 032 is delivered (`briefs/brief-032.md`, annex `annex-032.md` with the diagram and tables; pushed `69183ca`). Disclosure first: **the cold read hit its four-round cap** — the decision layer runs ~600 words against ~400 because the six sub-process lines and the batch-to-definition mapping are on the page at your request, and the last read still wanted five terms glossed earlier. All three count errors it found are repaired; the residual is stated at the top of the brief.

**The answer first.** Discovery ends at a session record, and nothing carries an idea from there to a scenario a shop can take up. The whole path is one top-level process, **`product-flow`**, composed of six sub-processes — three exist, three are new — built in five batches, four screens, about five sessions. Recommendation: approve the model, the build order, and block approval.

**Ask 1 — the model.** One run per initiative:
1. `discovery-conversation` (amended) — you and the assisting agent, in one of three forms (brainstorm first), leave an initiative `proposed` or `cancelled`.
2. `initiative-check` (new) — architect and designer attach feasibility, decomposition, usability; the cold reviewer screens; you take the bet inside the check (`proposed` → `planned`).
3. `backlog-ordering` (new, one step) — the PO places it in the order; the PO output check screens.
4. `feature-authoring` (new) — the PO drafts one feature, co-produces scenarios with the owning shops by asks the run waits on (marked hypotheses while shops are frozen); the designer adds criteria.
5. `po-output-check` (amended) — screens the feature; the initiative goes `active` on its first pass.
6. `scenario-assignment` (draft) — the architect tags contexts, chooses the vehicle, dispatches; loop until every feature is assigned.

**Ask 2 — build order and block approval.** A `initiative-check` (re-screens the initiative chain and decision-record amendment; 1 session) → B discovery amendment (with A; ½) → C `feature-authoring` + `backlog-ordering` (re-screens the feature chain and PO guidelines; 1–2) → D the `po-output-check` amendment + `scenario-assignment` (½) → E `product-flow` + the primer's missing first paragraph, screened end to end (1). The fourteen already-drafted definitions are approved with their batch, not one by one. The last three days ran ~forty screen rounds; this runs four. Defaults to proceeding in this order on silence.

**Ask 3 — five exclusions:** `completed` and the changelog (set on the reconcile side), the roadmap rendering, the `router` role, discovery forms beyond three. Accepted on silence.

On your word for ask 1, batch A starts.

content.text:
It's the **`stakeholder-presentation` process** — and it is deliberately generic. Its use-when: "before delivering any report, review material, or status update longer than ~300 words." Its steps are frame → compose → cold read ↺ → deliver, its result is a `decision-brief`, and the primer makes it a standing rule: "deliveries to the authority longer than ~300 words go through the `stakeholder-presentation` process — no exceptions." Briefs 030, 031, and 032 all came out of that process.

What you're noticing, though, is real: the rule says *when* it fires, but nothing records *what invoked it*. The process actually has the hook — its first parameter is `request: request` (the request artifact type: what is asked, from whom) — so each run is supposed to know its origin. In practice I've been invoking it directly from our conversation without writing that request down, so the brief's provenance lives in the transcript, which the shop's own rules say is never a governed record. Concretely:

- **Brief 030** came from your ask in a discovery conversation ("do some research on what should be in a role definition… make a plan to import the skills").
- **Brief 031** came from "work through 1–3 and present the results to me" — a work conversation's delivery.
- **Brief 032** came from "model the whole process… and present the plan" — same.

So the honest description: `stakeholder-presentation` is a **cross-cutting sub-process any conversation or process invokes when its delivery to you exceeds the budget** — the invoking run is "how we got here." Under the conversation model it should run as a *branched conversation*, its anchor recording the parent; under `intent-provenance` the brief should be traceable to the expression that asked for it.

The one-line gap, if you want it closed: the `decision-brief` frontmatter (or its Document History's first entry) records the requesting conversation or run — "requested in the work conversation of 2026-08-28, 'model the whole process… present the plan'." That's a small amendment to the decision-brief typedef and a habit change in the deliver step, not a new process. In the `product-flow` world this also falls out naturally: the brief-producing runs would hang off named steps (the `initiative-check`'s decide step, batch E's end-to-end screen), and the ad hoc case — like this one — stays covered by the generic rule plus the recorded request.

Happy to make that typedef amendment part of batch A's screen set, or leave it as is — your call.

content.text:
From the `initiative` typedef (§4–5) and the two roles' definitions — this is what the `attach` step in `initiative-check` requires of each, before the cold reviewer screens and you bet:

**The solutions architect attaches two things:**

1. **The feasibility verdict — mandatory.** "Whether the product can be built as framed with the stack, capacity, and time it has, with its reasons recorded" (its first accountability since your feasibility decision). The fitness set makes this hard: scenario 5 fails the screen if the verdict is absent, so an initiative cannot reach your bet without the architect having answered. Its evidence rules apply — the verdict is read from the decomposition record and the contexts' contracts, not from the initiative's wording — and "infeasible" doesn't kill the initiative; it returns the problem to you for re-framing (the lead-pm rule: infeasible never decides what's worth solving).
2. **The decomposition (§5) — may be "not yet" at the screen.** Three specifics: which Bounded Contexts the initiative touches; the relationship kind of each contract between them it relies on (customer–supplier, conformist, ACL, etc. — the context-mapping catalogue); and the cross-context flow named in one place — the saga or process manager that will carry it, or "none" when the contexts need no flow between them. This is also where the crossing gets counted: an initiative whose §5 names more than one context feeds the quarterly count the architect reads as its decomposition-review signal.

**The product designer attaches one thing, conditionally:**

3. **Usability evidence (§4) — where §2 names an interaction type.** Either real evidence — a user test, a tested prototype, or measured task completion, per its admissible-evidence list — or, honestly labeled, *the hypothesis it stands on*; or "not yet" with the text of the ask that requests it. So a bet can proceed on a stated hypothesis, but never on silence. (The interaction types in §2 themselves come from the designer's core-task list, so the designer's corpus shapes the initiative before this step too.)

The net effect at the bet: all four risks are on the table before you spend the appetite — value and viability are your judgment (unchecked by design, the typedef says so), feasibility is answered with reasons, usability is evidenced or explicitly hypothetical, and the decomposition tells you the coordination cost you're buying.

What's deliberately *not* specified yet: the attach step's prompts, its asks (both roles can ask you mid-step), and its ordering within `initiative-check` — those are batch A's drafting work, inside ask 1's "prompts, caps, wording" default.

content.text:
**Co-production in `feature-authoring` — the mechanics as designed, and the seam in them.**

What the definitions fix: the feature typedef requires a named source shop per scenario ("the shop the solutions architect's decomposition places the behavior in"), the steps and edge cases come *from that shop*, and the rule has teeth — "a scenario written without the shop named as its source is not co-produced and fails the check." The PO brings scope and wording; the shop brings steps and edges; that's the three-amigos split from the PM/PO research, encoded.

How the exchange actually travels is batch C's drafting work, and there's a seam to decide there: the annex says "by asks the run holds for," but an ask's `to` is a **role id inside the lead shop** — a BC-shop isn't a role. So co-production needs one of two channels: extend the ask type so a shop can be an addressee, or use the messaging contract the shops already speak (`shop-msg`, the same channel `clarify` rides — effectively a clarify in reverse: the lead shop asking the shop a question). The second is more honest to the architecture (everything crossing the boundary goes through a contract); the run still holds-and-resumes either way. While shops are frozen, the fallback stands: the PO writes the shop's part itself, marked `hypothesis`, and the first real co-production replaces it.

**The architect's contribution to feature authoring — what exists, and a real gap.**

What exists today:
- **Before the feature:** the decomposition (which shop owns which behavior — this is what tells the PO who to co-produce with) and the feasibility verdict, both attached at the initiative.
- **Standing guidance, not per-feature:** the stack ADRs and **platform guardrails** — the architect's mode is "bounds, never approves": shops choose within the guardrails, and a choice outside them is raised as a contract question, not vetoed. Plus **enabler recommendations** into the backlog order (placed or declined by the PO with reasons), and **clarify answers** on structure, stack, contracts, and decomposition.
- **After the feature:** assignment — the `@bounded-context:` tags, the vehicle from each context's pre-state, and the correction return if ownership doesn't match Contributors.

The gap: the feature carries the **designer's** criteria (usability, accessibility) but has **no slot for the architect's non-functional constraints**. The SA research was explicit that NFRs "ride as constraints on the definition of done" — which in our system means they belong on the feature's scenarios, exactly where the designer's criteria sit. Right now a performance bound, a data-retention rule, or an integration constraint has nowhere to land between the initiative's decomposition and the shop's build.

So technical guidance is delivered at three levels — standing (guardrails, ADRs, contracts), per-initiative (feasibility, decomposition), per-question (clarifies) — and is missing at the per-feature level. My recommendation, folded into batch C rather than decided now: the feature's Contributors section gains "the solutions architect role's non-functional constraints, where the decomposition names them" parallel to the designer's criteria, with fitness scenario 2 widened one clause. One line in the typedef, no new artifact.

content.text:
You've put your finger on an industry practice I imported without re-deriving it for this architecture. Let me re-derive it honestly.

**Why three amigos exists in industry.** Cucumber's warning — the domain expert writing scenarios alone is "a weak-ass move" — is aimed at two failure modes in *human* teams: scenarios that aren't testable as written, and shared understanding that lives only in the writer's head. The developer and tester in the room contribute implementation-aware wording, hidden edge conditions, and — mostly — the shared memory that the team then carries. That last one is the real product of the meeting.

**Why most of that evaporates here.** Our shops are agents, component teams, "a simpler execution unit." Shared human memory isn't the mechanism — records are; provenance replaces the meeting. And the specific contributions decompose:

- **Testability** — enforced by the check, not the meeting: fitness scenario 1 fails any Then that isn't observable in the running system, and a shop that receives a genuinely unrunnable scenario has a return path. The safeguard survives without co-authoring.
- **Step definitions** — you're right, and I conflated two things. The Gherkin *steps* (the Given/When/Then lines) are the requirement; the step *definitions* (the code binding them) are internal to the shop, by isolation. The shop's implementation knowledge shaping the requirement's wording is exactly what "what, never how" and the isolation principles say should *not* happen — the design is authoritative over the shop, not negotiated with it.
- **Edge cases** — what I meant: failure and boundary conditions of the *behavior* (the empty list, the cancelled run, permission denied, the concurrent change). These matter, but their sources are the framing, the designer's error principle, the contract, and the architect's decomposition — all readable by the lead shop. The one thing only the shop knows that's relevant is **what scenarios it already holds** — and the architect already reads that: the register sweep at assignment is precisely how a new scenario that conflicts with or tightens held behavior gets caught, and it's what drives the vehicle choice.

**What the shop's voice should be, then:** not a synchronous conversation during specification, but the two asynchronous channels that already exist — the **register sweep before dispatch** (architect's, catches conflicts) and the **clarify after receiving work** (shop's, catches what specification missed), plus the shop's standing right to recommend scenario splits to the PO. Cycles are spent only when something actually surfaces, instead of one held exchange per context per feature every time.

**My recommendation for batch C:** drop the `co-produce` step. Contributors becomes: the PO as author, the designer's criteria, and (per the last discussion) the architect's non-functional constraints; the feature typedef's co-production rule is replaced by "a scenario's conflicts with held behavior are caught by the register sweep at assignment; a shop's objection travels as a clarify or a return." The marked-hypothesis machinery for frozen shops disappears entirely — a nice simplification, since it existed only to simulate a conversation we'd now not have.

The one thing I'd preserve from the three-amigos idea is its *diversity of lenses*, which we get anyway: PO writes, designer and architect constrain, cold reviewer screens fresh, shop can object after the fact. Five perspectives, none requiring a meeting.

Shall I fold this into brief 032's model (it simplifies `feature-authoring` to draft → criteria → check), or hold it for batch C's screen?

Quotes come before claims — no claim enters the evidence without the passage it rests on. Note where sources conflict. ``` ## synthesize — Synthesize the findings Run by an agent in role `researcher`. reads: evidence, frame, confidence_scheme, report_typedef_path · writes: draft. - then: `verify` Prompt: ```text Write the draft report in the form the typedef at report_typedef_path requires: executive summary answer-first; method; findings each with a confidence label from the scheme and its sources; alternatives considered and why the findings stand; limitations; sources with their opened status. Mark any claim resting on model knowledge as knowledge-only with lowered confidence. ``` ## verify — Verify independently Run by an agent in role `researcher` (fresh context every run). reads: draft, evidence · writes: review. - then: `route-verify` Prompt: ```text You have not seen how this draft was reasoned — that is the point. For each finding, write the verification question it must survive, answer it from the evidence entries and by reopening the sources those entries identify, and check every reference exists and says what the finding claims. Can you act on the executive summary without the body? Report stumbles in reading order with quotes, every term that arrives before the report explains it, and whether each finding's confidence label is reproducible from its stated sources. Record read_round in the report's Document History. ``` ## advance-round-read — Advance the cold-read round Run by the runtime — no agent, no prose. reads: read_round · writes: read_round. ```yaml set: read_round: read_round + 1 next: cold-read ``` ## deliver — Deliver the report Run by an agent in role `lead-pm`. reads: report, report_path, consumer, verify_round, read_round, round_cap, index_path · writes: report. - then: `end` Prompt: ```text Set the report's status to delivered, push the research branch, and add or update the report's row in the research index at index_path (id, question, date, status, location). content.content:
- A scenario's `@bounded-context:` tag is written by the solutions architect role at assignment, never by the PO role — a writer rule the assignment process enforces; the check does not judge the tag's presence, since a re-verified or resubmitted feature may carry it. built (the shops' and the architect's); which context owns a
  behavior (the architect's).

**Admissible evidence:** the PM role's recorded framing; every
Bounded Context's scenario register read in full, never one context's
copy of another's; the solutions architect's decomposition, for where
a scenario lands; the owning shop's steps for a scenario. Not
authoritative: a stakeholder document transcribed into tickets; a
scenario written without the owning shop; this role's own memory of
what the PM meant.

**Interfaces:**
- The PM role: framed intent in; requirements artifacts, backlog
---F
   `@hash:<sha>` (a hash of the scenario's text), and, once assigned,
   `@bounded-context:<name>`; Given/When/Then with one action or event
   in the When and an outcome observable in the running system in the
   Then; no step names an implementation detail.
5. **Edges** — a table of every failure and boundary case the framing
   or a contributing shop named: case · who named it · the `Scenario:`
   name that covers it, or "out of scope" with the reason.

## Rules

---G
assignment; its presence is not this rule's).
*Test:* read each scenario's tag line. *Criterion:* `@feature:` and
`@hash:` are present. *Decision:* yes/no per scenario.
*Derived check:* judged — feature fitness scenario 3.

**5. List every edge and cover or exclude it.**
Before: a happy path only, with the cancelled-run case the shop named
absent from the Edges table.
After: an Edges row "cancelled run · reporting shop · Scenario: a
cancelled run is not marked failed" and a row "runs older than
the retention window · framing · out of scope: the archive feature
owns them".
*Test:* read the Edges table and the cases the framing names.
*Criterion:* every row names a covering scenario or a reasoned
exclusion, and every case the framing names has a row. *Decision:*
---S
    outputs: [feature, unowned, assignment]
    asks: [lead-pm]
    prompt: |
      Read the decomposition and the feature. For each scenario, decide
      which Bounded Context owns the behavior it states — from the
      decomposition and that context's contract at contracts, never
      from the scenario's wording alone — and write a single
      @bounded-context:<name> tag on it. A scenario whose behavior no
      context owns, that two contexts would each have to own, or whose
      owning context differs from the shop named as its source in
      Contributors, goes to unowned with the reason; do not guess. Then, for each context
      tagged, read its pre-state — its contract at contracts and its view of
      the register at registers, the full register where a scenario
      could conflict — and choose the vehicle: assign_scenarios for net-new
      behavior, request_bugfix for a scenario the register already
      holds and the system fails, request_maintenance for a tightening
      of held behavior. Write one assignment entry per context with
      its vehicle, the @hash: values of its scenarios, and the
      pre-state read. If deciding needs what the decomposition
      cannot say — whether a behavior is meant to be in the product at
      all — return an ask to lead-pm (kind: scope) with the question,
      the default you will apply, and a checkpoint of the tags written
      so far; on the first pass ask is absent, and if it carries an
      answer or resolved defaulted, act on it. Return the tagged
      feature.
    next: route

  - id: route

message.content: Scenario register has the sound of a specific artifact and one that has a different use. The features and scenarios are artifacts held in the lead shop. They live in a directory. A scenario register, which is another feature is a tracker for *implemented* scenarios pulled from the shops. The architect would work with the feature [repository - possible name] and potentially cross-reference the register if any conflicts are detected to find implementation status.

content.text:
That splits an overload I'd built into one term — and the single-source-of-truth principle was already straining under it. Let me play it back and test the edges.

**The split as I read it:**

- **Feature repository** (name open) — the directory of feature artifacts in the lead shop. The scenarios *as specified*: texts, hashes, `@bounded-context:` tags once assigned. Existence and assignment live here because they live in the artifacts themselves — no second record to keep in sync. This is what the architect works from at assignment.
- **Scenario register** — a tracker of *implemented* scenarios, populated by pulling from the shops asynchronously. Implementation status only. Consulted as a cross-reference when a conflict shows up, to learn what state the colliding behavior is actually in.

What this fixes in what I wrote last commit: I had the register as "the lead shop's one record of every scenario with hash/state/assignment" — assignment duplicated out of the artifacts into a tracker, which violates single-source-of-truth the moment a tag and a register row disagree. Under your split, the repository *is* the artifacts; only the thing the lead shop genuinely can't know from its own files — what the shops have actually implemented — gets a maintained record.

Two places where the register enters earlier than "only on conflict," and I want to check whether that's intended or something to redesign:

1. **Vehicle choice.** `request_bugfix` is defined as "a scenario the shop holds and the system fails" — distinguishing bugfix from net-new assignment requires implementation status, not just the repository. So as currently written the architect reads the register per assignment, not just per conflict. Either that's fine (vehicle choice is a legitimate register use), or vehicle choice should be re-derived: the repository tells whether the scenario was previously assigned, and bugfix/maintenance is only chosen when a *conflict or failure report* already put the register in hand.

2. **Pre-state verification.** You earlier said the register exists partly so the architect can verify pre-state without querying shops. Pre-state is exactly implementation status, so that stays a register read — which means "cross-reference only if conflicts are detected" understates it slightly; pre-state is a routine read, conflict lookup is the exceptional one. Unless you want pre-state to also come from somewhere else.

One more reading to confirm: "a scenario register, which is another feature" — do you mean the register is *itself a feature to be built through the product process* (specified, assigned, implemented like anything else), rather than basis infrastructure I define into existence? That would make the basis carry only the term and its interface, with the tracker arriving as Phase 2+ product work — a meaningful difference from what I did last commit, where I defined it as standing infrastructure.

If we converge on this, the touch-set is contained: the glossary entry splits in two, the architect role and `scenario-assignment`'s inputs/prompts separate repository-reads from register-reads, and lead-po's evidence line points at the repository. I'll hold off until you've answered the vehicle-choice and register-as-feature questions.

content.content:
two Bounded Contexts relate, drawn from the context-mapping catalogue (Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*): customer–supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language, shared kernel, or separate ways. - **vehicle** — the message type a request to a Bounded Context shop travels in; chosen from the pre-state, never from the request's wording. - **pre-state** — what a Bounded Context actually is before a change, read from its contracts and its view of the scenario register — both lead-shop-held records — never from its internals and never by querying the shop. - **framing** — the PM role's recorded statement of what a request is about: the originator, the problem taken to be worth solving, the outcome it serves, and the contract it entered through; the exclusive decision of `lead-pm`; written as the first section of an initiative and nowhere else. - **initiative** — the product-level problem artifact: one problem worth solving, stated for the product, with its framing, one measured outcome, an appetite and no-gos, the feasibility and usability attachments, and the solutions architect's decomposition; made by the PM role, screened by the cold reviewer, bet on by the authority; features are made from it. - **acceptance scenario** — a Gherkin scenario in a feature that states, as a requirement, what counts as done for one behavior; authored by the PO role; assigned to its owning context by a `@bounded-context:` tag the solutions architect writes; recorded in the scenario register. - **scenario register** — the lead shop's one register of every acceptance scenario in the system, with each scenario's hash, state, and `@bounded-context:` assignment; read as per-context views. Maintained asynchronously — assignment writes to it when scenarios are dispatched, and reconcile-and-close confirms and updates it when a shop's work returns — never by querying shops on demand. # Process: Scenario assignment

**Purpose:** Turn a checked feature into work the Bounded Context shops
can take up: the solutions architect role tags each scenario with the
context that owns its behavior, reads each tagged context's pre-state
to choose the message type its scenarios travel in, records the
feature as assigned, and sends each shop its scenarios.

**Guiding statement:** The decomposition decides, not the wording.
Which context owns a behavior is read from the decomposition and the
contexts' contracts; a scenario no context can own is the architect's
finding, not a guess.

**Outcomes:**
- O1. Every scenario in the feature carries exactly one
  `@bounded-context:` tag (judged in `assign`), or the feature is
  returned with the scenarios no context owns named — witnessed by
  `assign`'s outputs and `route`.
- O2. Each tagged context's vehicle is chosen from its pre-state — its
  contracts and scenario register, declared inputs of `assign` — and
  carried in `assignment`; `dispatch` sends one message per entry with
  that entry's vehicle — witnessed by `dispatch`'s `run`, which pairs
  `entries[].context` with `entries[].vehicle`.
- O3. The feature's status becomes `assigned` and the assignment,
  with the messages sent, is recorded in its Document History —
  judged in `record` from `assignment` and `sent`.
- O4. A question the decomposition cannot answer — whether a behavior
  is in scope at all — leaves the run as an ask to the PM role with a
  default — witnessed by `assign`'s `asks` and the `ask` value.

**Roles:** assigner —
[`../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md`](../roles/lead-solutions-architect.md)
(decides which context owns each scenario — its decomposition
decision right — and which vehicle each context's scenarios travel
in — its scenario-register-loop accountability, under its posture
that the pre-state determines the vehicle). The [PM role](../roles/lead-pm.md) — answers asks.
Bounded Context shops — receive their scenarios; not a role of this
process.

**Carried by:**
===SA 84-100===
  dispatch --> record
  record --> __end
```


## Data

Each entry names a process-local value. Simple types use JSON Schema
names inline; every structured shape is a `$ref` to a defined type with
an explicit source. Conditions are CEL expressions over these names.
`decomposition` is the path of the solutions architect's structural
model, and `contracts` the path under which each Bounded Context's contracts
are read, and `registers` the path of the lead shop's scenario
register (per-context views); none of
the three has a typedef on this branch — an unfiled gap, named here —
so each names the record the architect maintains, an approved source
by the role's own admissible evidence.
===SA 185-225===
  - id: dispatch
    name: Send each shop its scenarios
    run-by: {execution: runtime}
    inputs: [feature, assignment]
    outputs: [sent]
    run: |
      set -- ${assignment.entries[].vehicle}
      for ctx in ${assignment.entries[].context}; do
        vehicle=$1; shift
        shop-msg send --bc "$ctx" --type "$vehicle" \
          --feature "${feature}" --tag "@bounded-context:$ctx"
      done
    next: record

  - id: record
    name: Record the assignment
    run-by: {role: lead-solutions-architect, execution: agent}
    inputs: [feature, assignment, sent]
    outputs: [feature]
    prompt: |
      Set the feature's status to "assigned" and write a state entry
      into its Document History listing, from assignment, each
      context's scenario hashes and vehicle, and, from sent (the tool's
      standard output, one line per message — its output contract is
      pinned when the messaging package is imported), the message sent to each. Return
      the feature.
    next: end
```

| O3 | status `assigned` and a state entry listing vehicles and messages | judged | `record` |
| O4 | `assign` carries `asks`; process carries `ask-cap`; `ask` listed in inputs | mechanical | `assign`, frontmatter |
